en: The Scripture Spoken by the Great Śākyan Nirgrantha, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter One: The Introduction. Chapter One: The Introduction.
Homage to the Buddha Vairocana, the Ocean of Great Wisdom. This phrase appears at the beginning of all sūtras in the foreign (Indian) editions.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Bhagavān was staying in the city of Ujjayinī, in the royal garden belonging to the king named Ugratejas. The extraordinary splendor and adornments of that garden were beyond measure, namely:

It was adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of various exquisite groves of trees, including *śāla* trees, *tāla* trees, *tamāla* trees, *karnikāra* trees, *nyagrodha* trees, *pārśa* trees, *udumbara* flower trees, *vārṣika* flower trees, *dhanuṣkāra* flower trees, *atimuktaka* flower trees, *campaka* flower trees, *aśoka* flower trees, and *pāṭala* flower trees.
Furthermore, there are various kinds of water with diverse characteristics, namely:

spring water and ocean water; water flowing straight and water flowing in curves; *tāla* water; pond water; water pouring down from above and water gushing up from below. Thus, these waters, possessing hundreds of thousands of such wondrous characteristics, serve as adornments.
Furthermore, there were various kinds of exquisite and diverse flowers, namely:

the *utpala*, the *padma*, the *kumuda*, the *puṇḍarīka*, the *tāra*, the *mahātāra*, the *roca*, and the *mahāroca*. Thus, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of such wonderful flowers served as an adornment.
Furthermore, there are various birds with exquisite voices, namely:

geese, *kūṇapa* birds, *kukkuṭa* birds, *kunāla* birds, *kuta* birds, *guda* birds, parrots, mynas, *jīvajīvaka* birds, and *kalaviṅka* birds; it is adorned by hundreds of thousands of such diverse and wondrously vocal birds.
Furthermore, there were various bees of exquisite colors flying in the void, linked together in succession like a net that completely covered the area above as an ornament.
Furthermore, there were various kinds of grasses of many colors, soft, fragrant, and pure, adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of different patterns and hues that graced the ground.

Within this garden, so exquisitely adorned, he was together with a great assembly of bhikṣus numbering seventy-two hundred thousand million, and others among the great multitude, whose names were as follows:

The venerable Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Aniruddha, Subhūti, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākapphiṇa, Revata, Nanda, Nadīkāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Kuvangapa, Paṃtakas, Cuḷapaṃtaka, Tissa Mātṛputra, Khaṇḍa, Tiṣya, Cunda, Mahākauṣṭhila, Rāhula, and the venerable Ānanda—these and others were the leaders among the great assembly of seventy-two hundred thousand million billion followers.
All cultivate practices within the realm of the *dharmadhātu* as it truly is; all enter the true nature of the *dharmadhātu*;
all attain the supreme and wondrous practices of the unobstructed and unhindered realm of space;
all attain practices free from attachment; and all are liberated from the stains of afflictions and all fetters.
All enter the sphere illuminated by the Tathāgata’s Dharma-nature; all realize the same Dharma-nature and the great wisdom of equality;
all attain the manifestation of the gates of omniscience of all Tathāgatas;
all attain the path of great bodhi that is eternally uninterrupted; and all attain the turning back of non-retrogression.
They turn toward the path of great bodhi; all attain the realization of the non-retrogressive mind of great bodhi;
all reach the foremost shore of the wisdom and vision of prajñā; and all attain the ultimate shore of the wisdom of skillful means.
Furthermore, there were eight thousand bhikṣuṇīs, headed by the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī and the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, who stood as the foremost among hundreds of thousands of millions of bhikṣuṇīs.

They have all fully perfected and gathered all sublime, pure dharmas; they have all skillfully entered the path to omniscience; they are all close to the wisdom of omniscience; they have all entered the nature of non-existence; they are all able to contemplate all phenomena as signless; they have all well-faithed in the limit of phenomena which is itself limitless; they have all attained unobstructed liberation; and they have all attained the ability to manifest the form-body of a Buddha according to the conditions of sentient beings who may be transformed.
Accompanied by a great assembly of seventy-two hundred thousand million billion bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, their names were as follows:
Bodhisattva Mahāvega, Bodhisattva Mahāvegadhara, Bodhisattva Mahāvikrama, Bodhisattva Mahāvikramarāja, Bodhisattva Mahāvīryavikrama, and Bodhisattva Mahāśūravikrama.
[Sākyamuni], together with the Bodhisattva Mahāvikrāntavikrama, the Bodhisattva Mahābalavikrama, the Bodhisattva Mahāgaṇeśvara,
the Bodhisattva Mahāgandhahastin, the Bodhisattva Mahācandra, the Bodhisattva Sucandra,
the Bodhisattva Candraguṇa, the Bodhisattva Ratnacandra, the Bodhisattva Candraprabhasamantaprabha, and the Bodhisattva Dharma...
The Bodhisattva Vimalacandra, the Bodhisattva Candraprabha, the Bodhisattva Candrakīrti, the Bodhisattva Candrābhāsa,
the Bodhisattva Pūrṇacandra, the Bodhisattva Ghoṣadatta, the Bodhisattva Ghoṣeśvararāja, the Bodhisattva Bhūmigarjita, the Bodhisattva Dharmadhātugarjita, and the Bodhisattva Sarvatrāsasamtrāsana.
The Bodhisattva Roaring in the Palace of Māra, the Bodhisattva Producing the Sound of the Dharma Drum, the Bodhisattva Universal Cognition Sound,
the Bodhisattva Non-discriminative and Detached from Discrimination Sound, the Bodhisattva Lion’s Roar Ground Valiant Sound, the Bodhisattva Obstructing All Sounds,
the Bodhisattva Universal Treasury, the Bodhisattva Treasury of Merit, and the Bodhisattva Universal Illumination.
Gandhagarbha Bodhisattva, Ratnagarbha Bodhisattva, Candragarbha Bodhisattva, Sūryagarbha Bodhisattva,
Sūryaprabhāgarbha Bodhisattva, Padmagarbha Bodhisattva, Puṇyagarbha Bodhisattva,
Jñānavijayagarbha Bodhisattva, Mahāmati Bodhisattva, Vijayamati Bodhisattva, Yaśomati Bodhisattva, and...
The Bodhisattva Swift Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Supreme Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Increasing Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Boundless Wisdom,
the Bodhisattva Vast Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Buddha-Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Inexhaustible Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Lamp of Mount Meru,
the Bodhisattva Kindling the Great Lamp, the Bodhisattva Dharma-Lamp, and the Bodhisattva Pervasive...
The Bodhisattva Lamp-Light of the Ten Directions, the Bodhisattva Universal Illumination, the Bodhisattva Lamp-Light that Universally Extinguishes All Darkness,
the Bodhisattva Lamp-Light that Universally Illuminates All Realms of Existence, the Bodhisattva Lamp-Light that Constantly Emits Great Radiance,
the Bodhisattva Moonlight Lamp-Light, the Bodhisattva Sunlight Lamp-Light, and the Bodhisattva Departure from Evil Paths.
Mārajit Bodhisattva, Mahāmārajit Bodhisattva, Āścaryasambhava Bodhisattva,
Durjayottaraṇa Bodhisattva, Durmāna Bodhisattva, Durvijñeyajñāna Bodhisattva, Kṣīṇāpāya Bodhisattva,
Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, and Mañjuśrī.
The Bodhisattvas who are Dharma-Prince heirs were the leaders of a multitude numbering seventy-two hundred thousand million.
All such Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had attained the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood;
all had attained all dhāraṇīs; all had attained the ocean of all samādhis; all had...
They attained the unimpeded eloquence of boundless joy in teaching; all became fearless in expounding the Dharma;
all reached the foremost shore of the forest of merit with sovereign mastery at will;
all attained the great supernormal powers and the vigor of mastery to travel to the lands of all Buddhas; and all attained unimpeded self-...
In the liberation of body and mind, they all attain ultimate knowledge and vision that is entirely unobstructed and unhindered;
they all attain the universal manifestation of the Buddha-body to travel through all the ten directions, even to those buddha-lands where no Buddha resides;
they all attain the correct wisdom of reality to turn the Great Wheel of Dharma without error or fault; they all attain [the power] to accord with the ten...
They are now fit to hear the teaching for the sake of sentient beings; all have attained the gate of *dhāraṇī* and speak of all things as neither non-dharma nor dharma;
all have attained the true reality of the *dharmadhātu*, which is without grasping or abandoning;
all have attained unimpeded ability to explain the meaning of the emptiness of all phenomena; and all are able to let out the lion’s roar. All...
All were able to subdue non-Buddhists; all were able to destroy the enemies that are Māras;
all attained the various supreme and wondrous practices of bodhisattva supernormal powers; all attained liberation from all enmity and hatred;
all attained the great mind of equanimity regarding earth, water, fire, and wind; and all attained entry into the profound [teachings] of all Tathāgatas.
In this secret place, all are able to perform the Buddha-work for the sake of all sentient beings;
all are praised, extolled, and rejoiced in by all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas as they proclaim their sublime practices;
all are able to fully maintain and uphold [these practices] throughout boundless kalpas; and all are able to maintain and uphold that which was taught by the Tathāgata.
When the Wheel of Dharma was preached, they all attained the supreme and wondrous radiance of the great jewel-treasure of the Dharma;
they all attained the ability to expound the merit of inexhaustible, supreme practices;
they all attained sovereign mastery over all worlds; they all attained the full accomplishment of their past vows; they all attained...
The realm of faith and practice of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, is such that they have all fully attained the virtuous deeds cultivated in the past;
they have all fully attained the pure, stainless wisdom of the Buddhas;
they have all attained constant and uninterrupted courageous diligence in making offerings to all Buddhas, Tathāgatas; they have all attained...
With courageous exertion, they resolutely attained the stage of non-retrogression; all of them realized the manifestation of great compassion,
all of them attained liberation through a deeply pure mind of intrinsic nature, all of them became free from the afflictions of doubt,
regret, and attachment to precepts, and all of them were empowered by the spiritual power of the Buddhas of the past.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable *upāsakas* and *upāsikās*.

There were also, throughout the trichiliocosm, the various devas and deva-kings of superior and inferior realms who possessed great majesty and virtue; the various nāgas and nāga-kings; the various yakṣas and yakṣa-kings; the various gandharvas and gandharva-kings; the various asuras and asura-kings; the various garuḍas and garuḍa-kings; the various kiṃnaras and kiṃnara-kings; the various mahoragas and mahoraga-kings; as well as humans and human kings. At that time, all these great assemblies, each with hundreds of thousands of millions of retinues, gathered together and sat in attendance.

At that time, the World-Honored One was seated in the full lotus posture upon a lion throne—the supreme treasury of merit adorned with hundreds of thousands of millions of blessings—surrounded by a great assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis who paid him reverent homage.
The majestic power and radiance of the Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body are uniquely distinguished; its brilliance shines forth, eclipsing all the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings.
It is like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, emerging from the great ocean; its majestic light is preeminent, shining forth and eclipsing all lesser hills.

Likewise, the World-Honored Tathāgata, the Great Sumeru King, seated upon a wondrous lion throne adorned with hundreds of thousands of merits, possesses a uniquely distinguished majesty that shines forth and eclipses the entire assembly.
Just as the crescent moon, its orb gradually increasing until it reaches fullness, possesses a preeminent radiance that shines forth and outshines the light of all the stars;

so too is it with the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, who sits upon a sublime lion throne adorned with hundreds of thousands of millions of merits—his majestic brilliance is extraordinary, shining forth and outshining the entire assembly of devas and humans.

For example, just as the sky is pure and stainless, free from all clouds, mists, and dust, and within it the solar orb emits a great radiance—its light so sublime that it shines forth and eclipses all the light of insects and fireflies so that they no longer appear;

even so, when the Tathāgata-solar orb sits upon the wondrous lion throne adorned with hundreds of thousands of millions of merits, his majestic brilliance is extraordinary, shining forth and outshining the lights of all Śakras, Brahmā kings, and the Four Heavenly Kings until their radiance does not appear.
Just as when a great wheel of fire is set ablaze atop a mountain peak in the darkness of night, its light is preeminent, shining forth so that all may see it;

likewise, the Tathāgata, like a mountain fire, seated upon a sublime lion throne adorned with hundreds of thousands of millions of merits, possesses a most extraordinary radiance that shines forth so that all who have a karmic connection may behold him—thus it is.
For example, just as the lion, the king of beasts, dwelling in the deep mountains, possesses supreme majesty and power that shines forth and subdues all insects and wild animals;

so too is it with the Tathāgata, the lion and king of all dharmas, who sits upon a sublime lion throne adorned with hundreds of thousands of merits, his majestic radiance uniquely distinguished, shining forth and subduing all heterodox teachers and sentient beings of divergent views.

For example, suppose a stainless eight-faceted *maṇi* wish-fulfilling jewel were placed atop a high banner; it would emit great radiance and, according to the wishes of sentient beings, rain down [precious things] to satisfy them. Its light is sublime, shining forth and manifesting, illuminating the ten directions everywhere.

In the same way, the Tathāgata-maṇi, seated upon a wondrous lion throne adorned with hundreds of thousands of merits, possesses the brilliance of great wisdom and extraordinary majestic light; shining forth and manifesting, it illuminates the ten directions everywhere and fulfills the wishes of sentient beings. Thus it is.

For example, just as the sovereign Wheel-Turning Sage King possesses preeminent majesty and virtue, shining and manifesting so as to subdue all across the four continents, with none able to oppose him;

likewise, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, the Wheel-Turning King of the Dharma, seated upon the wondrous lion throne adorned with hundreds of thousands of millions of merits, possesses extraordinary majestic radiance, shining and manifesting to subdue all demons and hostile adversaries—thus it is.

For example, it is like Śakra Devānām Indra, who, having fastened a necklace of the divine *maṇi* jewel of Śakra around his neck, dwells among the hosts of gods in the Sudharmā Hall; his majestic virtue is preeminent, shining forth and manifesting so as to subdue the entire assembly of devas.

In the same way, the Tathāgata-Śakra, seated upon a wondrous lion throne adorned with hundreds of thousands of merits, possesses extraordinary radiant light that shines forth and manifests, eclipsing all other heavenly beings.

Chapter Two: Questions and Doubts At that time, the noble Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva, seeing the vast assembly of immeasurable beings gathered like clouds, and observing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, manifesting a great, supreme, wondrous, and rare sign, reflected thus:
"For what purpose has the World-Honored One now manifested this sign?"
I have a matter of doubt that I should now ask. Why is this?

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is seated upon a sublime lion throne adorned with hundreds of thousands of merits; his majestic radiance is extraordinary, shining forth and manifesting clearly. Such a vast assembly as this is difficult to encounter.

Having formed this thought, he immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and joined his palms toward the Buddha. He then praised the Tathāgata in verse, speaking these words:
“World-Honored One, hero of the ten powers, Among gods, humans, and all worlds, In the three realms there is none equal to you; How could there be anyone who surpasses you?”
Just as Sumeru, the king of mountains, rises above the great ocean and its minor peaks,
firm and unshakable, providing peace and security to all the devas;
so too is the Tathāgata, the king of Sumeru, who has transcended the ocean of birth and death of the sages.
Abiding in all virtues, dwelling securely and immovable,
with a body like Mount Sumeru of merit, he manifests throughout all worlds;
entirely relying upon the Tathāgata, he dwells in peace within nirvāṇa.
Just as the empty sky is unobstructed, and the full moon alone shines with brilliance,
while the light of all the stars is eclipsed and cannot appear;
so too the Tathāgata’s ten powers are pure, and the moon of his wisdom is luminous and clear.
The assembly of disciples with supernormal powers is like the light of the stars.
Just as the orb of the sun’s radiance illuminates all worlds,
extinguishing all darkness so that lesser lights do not appear;
The sun-disk of the Tathāgata’s wisdom Shines to dispel the darkness of the world;
The lights of the Brahmā kings and others Are eclipsed and cannot appear.
It is like lighting a fire at night And placing it upon the peak of a high mountain.
Because its essence is luminous and pure, all darkness throughout the ten directions is seen;
the Tathāgata’s great blazing fire, the mountain of wisdom, stands high and manifest,
illuminating the realm of the darkness of afflictions and causing the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) to open and appear.
Just as the lion king, Majestic and fierce, outshines all other beasts,
Without manifesting an expression of wrath, All other beasts are subdued;
So too the Tathāgata, the Lion King, Is fully endowed with the power of fearlessness.
All non-Buddhists, through the power of loving-kindness, are naturally subdued.
Just as a maṇi jewel emits light that illuminates the world, fulfilling all the wishes of sentient beings with a rain of everything they need; so too does this compassion.
The Tathāgata’s maṇi-jewel, the banner of wisdom shining afar,
can rain down the great Dharma rain, fulfilling the vows of sentient beings.
Like a wheel-turning monarch, who is fully endowed with the merit of the seven treasures.
Wandering through the four continents, he transforms enemies into friends;
the Tathāgata, a Wheel-Turning King, is fully endowed with the jewels of the ten powers,
gathering the hosts of the four Māras so that they all return to the path of the Tathāgata.
Just as Śakra, the King of Gods and Lord of the Thirty-three,
Arranges the Hall of Righteous and Good Dharma, which all devas joyfully receive;
So too is the Tathāgata Śakra, the Great Dharma King of the three realms.
With a compassionate mind observing all realms of existence, Seated in the Dharma-hall of Nirvana,
he raises great clouds of loving-kindness and compassion, Raining down the nectar of the Dharma rain;
Gods and humans receive it with joy, Cultivating the unsurpassed path.
At that time, the noble Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva, having praised the Buddha with these verses, joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata is thus able to expound for the great assembly this Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s Practice of Skillful Means, the Sphere of Activity, and the Manifestation of Power. By hearing this sutra, all sentient beings with roots of goodness who have faith and delight in the unsurpassed Mahāyāna will resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; even those sentient beings who believe in the narrow and inferior Hīnayāna will likewise resolve their minds upon unsurpassed bodhicitta. Those who have already resolved upon the unsurpassed Great Mind will be able to increase their thoughts of bodhi; those sentient beings of narrow conduct and limited views will be able to give rise to great practice; those who have regressed from the Path will be able to advance toward the path of great bodhi; and those who have attained the superior path to bodhi will be able to enter into the profound and secret Dharma of the Tathāgata’s wisdom-adornment.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, saying: “Mañjuśrī!

Regarding all the profound and secret dharmas of the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—which are difficult to believe, difficult to know, difficult to awaken to, difficult to discern, difficult to measure, and difficult to enter—all devas and humans do not know by what intention the Tathāgata has spoken them.”
Mañjuśrī! Regarding such a profound and subtle Dharma as this, if there are sentient beings who practice evil deeds, they do not know this Dharma and do not recognize this Dharma;
those who violate the precepts likewise do not know this Dharma and do not recognize this Dharma.
Those who delight in minor practices do not believe in this Dharma;
those with a corrupted mind do not believe in this Dharma;
and those who are under the influence of evil associates do not enter into this Dharma.
Those who are not sustained by spiritual friends do not enter this Dharma;

those who are not upheld by the Buddhas for the sake of sentient beings do not hear this Dharma—it is impossible for anyone, except those sustained by the empowering power of the Tathāgatas, to hear this Dharma or to believe in it.
At that time, the World-Honored One, reiterating this meaning, spoke in verse:
“Son of the Dharma with a beautiful voice, you have been able to ask me about this matter.
Now listen with a sincere mind; I shall explain it for you.”
Sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance; possessing only small minds of faith, they do not believe when they hear this Mahāyāna Dharma, and thus I do not speak of it to them.
If, throughout immeasurable eons, they had [served] under the various Buddhas of the past...
Those sentient beings who have practiced various virtuous deeds and whose roots of goodness are fully matured,
are constantly sustained by the empowerment of the Tathāgata;
upon hearing this teaching, they give rise to joy and are thus able to believe and accept it with true clarity.
If one is befriended by evil associates and bitten by the venomous snake,
being separated from virtuous friends and failing to hear the nectar-like Dharma,
one gives rise to a mind of negligence regarding all sublime teachings.
Falling into the pit of great false views, they hear the teaching but do not give rise to faith.
The minds of sentient beings are narrow and inferior; unable to receive the Great Dharma, they retreat upon hearing it and fail to believe, giving rise to a mind of slander.
"Having fallen into evil realms for a long night, they shall never again hear the Buddha-dharma;
out of compassion for them, I do not speak quickly.
At that time, the noble Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This great assembly is entirely well-purified; they have well practiced all deeds, are well able to make offerings to all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, are well able to protect and sustain all spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), are well able to cultivate and accumulate the eye of pure faith, are well able to enter the realms of great wisdom and believe in all states, and are well endowed with a pure profound mind and a straightforward mind.”
All those in this great assembly are well able to contemplate all realms; they are able to know this Dharma and are able to recognize this Dharma.
Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will, for our sake and for the hearts of this assembly who joyfully desire to hear it, skillfully expound this Dharma.
And he spoke in verse:
"The sentient beings in this assembly have, throughout immeasurable kalpas,
planted roots of goodness in the presence of all Buddhas until they are fully perfected."
May these sentient beings likewise be able to enter the realm of the Buddha;
for the sake of fulfilling the vessels of the Dharma, we pray that the Buddha will now speak swiftly.
All gaze with reverence upon the face of the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
With reverent palms joined, they gaze upon him, their eyes fixed without turning away out of thirsty longing.
May the World-Honored One, out of compassion for these beings whose hearts thirst and long,
rain down the great rain of the sublime Dharma, so that the sprouts of wholesome dharmas may grow.
I now entreat the Tathāgata, the unsurpassed Great Dharma King,
to open the gate of ambrosia and turn the most supreme wheel of Dharma.
May all these sentient beings, upon hearing what the Buddha has spoken, [attain liberation].
"Able to practice the unsurpassed path, They will ultimately realize the dharma of nirvāṇa.

Chapter Three: The One Vehicle (Part One) The Sūtra Spoken by the Mahāsaccaka Nirgrantha, Chapter Three: The One Vehicle (Part One) At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, the Holy Dharma Prince, had thus questioned, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"O Dharma Prince!
Excellent, Mañjuśrī! You have now skillfully questioned the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding this profound dharma-gate of the bodhisattva's practice."
Why is this? Mañjuśrī!

You have perceived the true meaning of all phenomena before you without any doubt, having reached the ultimate, supreme shore of the perfection of wisdom (jñānapāramitā). It is because you desire to benefit immeasurable sentient beings and lead them into the unsurpassed path of the bodhisattvas that you ask about such a Dharma.
Mañjuśrī! It is excellent, excellent, that you have asked about such a Dharma in order to kindle the great lamp of wisdom and extinguish all darkness for the sake of future sentient beings.
Well done, well done!
“Mañjuśrī! Listen attentively now; I shall explain for you the Dharma-gate of the Vigorous Display within the Sphere of Skillful Means in the Bodhisattva Practice.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We wish most earnestly to hear it.
Then the entire assembly of bodhisattvas, with one mind and in unison, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We wish to hear it with joy.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to expound this Dharma, addressed the great assembly:
“O sons of good family!
If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who ultimately accomplish twelve dharmas, they will then be able to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
What are the twelve?
First, one generates the bodhicitta out of an inherent faith in the Mahāyāna teachings, in order to abandon the narrow and inferior mind of the Hīnayāna.
Second, one generates the bodhicitta through the natural accomplishment of great compassion, desiring to fulfill all pure dharmas (*śukladharma*).
Third, with a straightforward mind and firm fundamental practice, one generates the bodhicitta in order to weary of birth and death and head toward the other shore;
fourth, by skillfully accumulating all merits, one generates the bodhicitta in order to cultivate and fulfill all vows and practices;
fifth, being able to skillfully make offerings to all Buddhas, one generates the bodhicitta in order to skillfully give rise to all pure dharmas (*śukladharma*).
Sixth, one generates the bodhicitta for the sake of purifying the actions of body, speech, and mind, in order to abandon all unwholesome conduct;
seventh, one generates the bodhicitta for the sake of distancing oneself from evil associates and drawing near to virtuous friends;
eighth, one generates the bodhicitta for the sake of practicing according to the teachings as they have been heard, so as not to deceive sentient beings with falsehoods.
Ninth, one generates the bodhicitta for the sake of benefiting all beings by maintaining the necessities of life without greed or stinginess;
tenth, one generates the bodhicitta because of receiving the empowerment of all Buddhas, in order to remain free from the influence of all Māras;

eleventh, one generates the bodhicitta by constantly giving rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings and being able to relinquish all internal and external things, in order to abandon stinginess and envy.
Twelfth, they possess the power of practicing the Dharma, generating the bodhicitta for the sake of being able to accomplish all meritorious qualities.
Good son! These are called the twelve sublime dharmas.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family accomplishes these twelve dharmas, they will then be able to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Good son! Furthermore, there are twelve kinds of supreme dharmas that a bodhisattva accomplishes, which are called ‘generating the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.’”
What are the twelve?
First is the mind of peace and security—generating the bodhicitta for the sake of bestowing happiness upon all sentient beings;
second is the mind of compassionate mindfulness—generating the bodhicitta because one can endure and protect oneself when others inflict evil upon one, without giving rise to thoughts of resentment.
Third is the mind of great compassion—generating the bodhicitta for the sake of bearing the heavy burden of sentient beings;
fourth is the mind of great loving-kindness—generating the bodhicitta for the sake of uprooting the suffering of all evil realms;
fifth is the pure mind—generating the bodhicitta because one does not give rise to aspiration or delight in other vehicles.
Sixth, the undefiled mind—generating the bodhicitta for the sake of leaving behind all turbidity of afflictions;
seventh, the luminous mind—generating the bodhicitta for the sake of seeking the unsurpassed, self-natured, pure radiance of illumination;
eighth, the illusory mind—generating the bodhicitta because one is able to know that all phenomena are ultimately without substantiality.
Ninth, the mind of non-substantiality—because it is able to know that all things are non-existent, one generates the bodhicitta;
tenth, the firm mind—because it cannot be moved among all phenomena, one generates the bodhicitta;
eleventh, the non-retrogressive mind—because it is able to realize the ultimate exhaustion of all phenomena, one generates the bodhicitta.
"Twelfth, one should deliver all sentient beings without giving rise to a mind of weariness—because one practices according to what is taught—one should resolve upon Bodhicitta.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"O sons of good family, if there are any sentient beings..."
Desiring to cultivate all pure dharmas and achieve the stainless dharma,
being able to maintain a mind moistened by compassion that is equal toward both enemies and kin—
such bodhisattvas are said to have "aroused the bodhicitta."
If there are sentient beings who, throughout immeasurable eons,
have guarded against evil associates, made offerings to virtuous friends,
protected the gateway to bodhi, and given rise to various great vows and practices,
Such bodhisattvas as these are said to have awakened the bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who can recollect the events of the past, spanning immeasurable billions of kalpas,
with a resolve as firm and stable as the king of mountains, [they too are called those who have awakened the bodhicitta].
With a mind of diligence free from weariness, constantly practicing without rest—
such Bodhisattvas as these are said to have "aroused the bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who abandon all unwholesome dharmas,
Endowed with a heart of compassion, Accomplished in a mind of peace and security,
They mindfully show all sentient beings The paths of all wholesome karma;
Such bodhisattvas Are said to have resolved upon bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who, upon seeing those of supreme wisdom,
bring to mind great enlightenment and unsurpassed, sublime merit,
and whose minds remain pure and untainted even while seeking within other vehicles;
Such bodhisattvas are said to have awakened the bodhicitta.
Having attained a pure mind, the bodhisattva is free from false conceptualization;
they perceive the world and nirvana as equal and without distinction.
Though one acts to transform sentient beings, it is like seeing a reflection in a mirror;
one who generates the mind in this way possesses the true bodhicitta.
Having already departed from the faults of affliction and all worldly defilements, [it is] thus.
Pure like space, unstained by defilements,
With all signs eternally stilled and extinguished, Transcending the path of speech—
This is called the fulfillment of cultivation, The pure bodhicitta.
Such bodhisattvas as these will, before long, sit at the site of enlightenment;
they shall attain great dhāraṇīs and unsurpassed, supreme eloquence,
and possess bodies endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics.
They are able to abide within the fundamental nature and virtues of all Buddhas.

"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are able to abide within such supreme virtues, there are twelve kinds of sublime practices of giving that bring great benefit and lead swiftly to Bodhi; these are the practices of the *dānapāramitā* that Bodhisattvas should perform."
What are the twelve?
First, because giving can swiftly increase the merit and benefits of unsurpassed bodhi, a bodhisattva should practice the *dānapāramitā*.
Second, because giving results in birth in a place of abundance where inexhaustible treasures constantly emerge from one's hands, a bodhisattva should practice the *dānapāramitā*.

Third, because through giving one may be born according to one's wishes as a Śakra or Brahmā Deva King, or within great noble families, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā);

fourth, because giving can eliminate the fault of all stingy and greedy minds and cause one to relinquish all states of existence without generating longing or attachment, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of giving;
fifth, because giving can abandon the bonds of worldly greed and defilement, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of giving.
Sixth, because giving opens the gate to escape the realm of hungry ghosts and brings one away from all evil destinies, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of generosity;

seventh, because giving allows one to abandon the common property shared by many in the world and attain the uncommon property of enlightenment, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of generosity;
eighth, because giving can satisfy the joyful hearts of sentient beings, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of generosity.
Ninth, because giving enables one to relinquish both internal and external things and to practice the conduct of a Buddha, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).
Tenth, because giving allows one to remain free from the stains and harms of attachment toward all cherished objects, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of generosity.
Eleventh, because the practice of giving can fulfill the unsurpassed perfection of generosity, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of generosity.

Twelfth, because the practice of giving can follow the Tathāgata’s teachings and bring the fulfillment of one's vows, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*). Good son!

These are called the twelve kinds of practices through which a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) to obtain great benefit, dedicating them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) with these verses,
speaking them again: "If one seeks the unsurpassed path, And practices all manner of meritorious virtues,
To shatter the mind of stinginess and greed, Generosity is the foremost."
When a Son of the Buddha practices the mind of equanimity, seeing those who come to beg,
he is able to give rise to a heart of joy and has no stinginess toward anything.
Whether it be his kingdom, city, wife, or children, even up to the rank of a celestial king, he gives it all away.
One’s own flesh and limbs, head, eyes, marrow, and brain,
And one’s pure, stainless eyes— having given these away with a joyful heart,
To practice such a mind of relinquishment is called *dānapāramitā*.
All Tathāgatas, who have fulfilled all merits and possess the supreme path to nirvāṇa,
have attained this entirely through the practice of giving. Therefore,
O sons of the Buddha, those who wish to seek the unsurpassed path [should likewise practice giving].
One should always cultivate a mind of equanimity and practice the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Through generosity one attains awakening and does not abide in the world;
therefore, all bodhisattvas should always practice a mind of equanimity.
Generosity can sever poverty and enrich one with the seven kinds of pure wealth;
it exhausts the mind of stinginess, envy, and jealousy, leading to the pure enlightenment of a Buddha.
Through giving, one can achieve fulfillment and accomplish the ten masteries.
Therefore, all Tathāgatas praise the merit of practicing generosity.
Seeing this benefit, the Bodhisattva, in order to fulfill the pāramitās,
cultivates a mind of relinquishment and constantly gives away all things.
“Good son! Furthermore, there are twelve kinds of upholding the precepts through which a bodhisattva attains great benefit; a bodhisattva should thus practice the śīlapāramitā.
What are these twelve?
First, because maintaining ethical discipline can encompass all roots of goodness, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā);
second, because maintaining ethical discipline leads one into the bodhisattva path, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of ethical discipline;
third, because maintaining ethical discipline liberates one from the bonds of all afflictions, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of ethical discipline.
Fourth, because observing the precepts enables one to transcend all evil realms, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā);
fifth, because observing the precepts enables one to uproot sentient beings suffering in the evil realms, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of ethical discipline;

sixth, because observing the precepts ensures that one’s actions of body, speech, and mind are not censured by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of ethical discipline.
Seventh, because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, always praise the upholding of precepts, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā);
eighth, because through upholding precepts one can enter into all states of existence without negligence, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of ethical discipline;
ninth, because upholding precepts bestows fearlessness upon sentient beings, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of ethical discipline.
Tenth, because the observance of precepts accomplishes the excellence of the actions of body, speech, and mind, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā);
eleventh, because the observance of precepts enables one to attain mastery in accordance with all phenomena, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of ethical discipline;

twelfth, because the observance of precepts accomplishes the meritorious karma of the foremost perfection of the further shore (pāramitā), a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of ethical discipline.
"Good son! These are called the twelve kinds of practices of the śīla-pāramitā by which a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains great benefit and dedicates it toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) with these verses, speaking them once more:
"Those who wish to leave behind all birth and death, And reach nirvana in peace and security— All Tathāgatas have declared: The upholding of precepts is foremost."
Precepts are like a cool, refreshing pond, capable of producing all manner of virtuous flowers;
they are also like a fierce, blazing fire, capable of burning away all weeds of evil.
For one who skillfully maintains the practice of the precepts, it is like a bird soaring through the void.
They have no fear of falling into birth and death, nor among the various realms of the evil paths.
When the great venomous dragons of the evil paths and the rākṣasas of ignorance see one who maintains pure precepts, they show reverence and abandon their harmful intent.
All Tathāgatas dwell peacefully in nirvāṇa, having severed the paths to all evil realms;
this is entirely due to the power of upholding the precepts.
Therefore, O sons of the Buddha, those who wish to seek the unsurpassed path [should likewise uphold the precepts].
Firmly establishing all roots of goodness, one maintains the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
A bodhisattva should reflect thus: "Abiding well within the category of morality, I shall be liberated from the bonds of affliction and close the gates to the evil realms."
If you wish to maintain pure precepts, you should be like a yak;
for the sake of protecting a single hair, guard yourself unto death, not sparing even your life.
Thus guarding all karmic actions is what is called being a person who maintains the precepts.
The Tathāgata always praises those who are able to maintain pure precepts; whatever they seek shall be accomplished.
Such are their merits, and for this reason, all bodhisattvas should always maintain pure precepts.
When the actions of body, speech, and mind are pure, and all evils are not committed,
one can reach Bodhi, and omniscience will manifest before them.
By maintaining the precepts without negligence, all virtues become firm and steadfast.
Attaining mastery within the Dharma, they are able to purify the precepts of all Buddhas.
When Bodhisattvas uphold the pure precepts, they view all beings without distinction between enemy and kin;
with a mind of equanimity toward all living creatures, those who see them feel no fear.
I dwelt in that place, constantly practicing heedfulness;
therefore, I have now attained liberation from all evil realms.
Having reached the supreme further shore, I abide on the ground of qualities as they truly are.
Therefore, all Bodhisattvas should always maintain pure precepts.
If a Bodhisattva desires to seek awakening and the virtues of a Buddha,
they should maintain the precepts like a yak and constantly remain mindful and heedful.
Such bodhisattvas as these are called wise ones;
they are able to swiftly reach the other shore and abide in the fruit of Buddhahood, Bodhi.
"O son of good family!

After the bodhisattva has thus practiced all dharmas, there are furthermore thirteen kinds of contemplations for practicing the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*) that yield great benefit; the bodhisattva should therefore practice the perfection of patience.
What are the thirteen?
First, because one can realize the emptiness of all phenomena by practicing patience and enduring all afflictions, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Second, because one does not perceive a self that is harmed by others when practicing patience, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of patience.
Third, because in the practice of patience one perceives no sentient beings as either enemies or kin, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of patience;
fourth, because in the practice of patience one does not perceive one's own or another's body as something that can be harmed, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of patience;
fifth, because in the practice of patience the mind remains ever unmoved upon hearing disparagement or praise, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of patience.
Sixth, because the practice of patience can sever the various fetters and latent tendencies of affliction, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of patience;
seventh, because the practice of patience can sever the fetters and latent tendencies of anger and resentment, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of patience;
eighth, because the practice of patience can bring to fulfillment the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of patience.
Ninth, because the practice of patience can lead one away from rebirth in the evil realms and cause birth in the Brahma heavens, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of patience;
tenth, because the practice of patience can transcend all realms of harm, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of patience;
eleventh, because the practice of patience can attain the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of patience.
Twelfth, because the practice of patience can subdue all realms of evil Māras, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of patience;
thirteenth, because the practice of patience enables one to see the Tathāgata’s body adorned with immeasurable merits, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of patience.
"Good son! These are called the thirteen kinds of contemplative cultivation of the pāramitā of kṣānti by which a bodhisattva attains great benefit and dedicates it toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the perfection of patience with these verses, speaking them once more:
"If one wishes to act as a place of refuge for all sentient beings,
causing them to give rise to a mind free from fear, patience is the foremost."
Those who are able to practice patience bring joy to all who see them;
their enemies abandon their poisonous hearts, and all conceive thoughts of them as close friends.
All Tathāgatas have accomplished a mind of equanimity.
That sentient beings have a refuge to turn to is entirely due to the practice of patience.
Therefore, O sons of the Buddha, those who seek the unsurpassed path and wish to serve as a reliance for all beings should make their endurance firm and steadfast.
If a bodhisattva wishes to abide in the awakening of all buddhas,
they should contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena and that sentient beings cannot be apprehended.
Practicing patience in this way, one is able to fulfill the qualities of a buddha.
Therefore, all bodhisattvas should constantly cultivate patience.
If a bodhisattva cultivates patience, they should remain far removed from the two extremes,
seeing neither their own body nor the bodies of others as capable of causing harm or benefit.
The Tathāgata, in his great compassion, praised such contemplation;
therefore, all bodhisattvas should constantly cultivate patience.
If one desires to attain the knowledge of exhaustion and extinguish all latent afflictions, [one must practice thus].
Cultivating patience without cowardice, Always free from a discriminating mind,
Observing all phenomena in this way, One fulfills the perfection of patience;
Therefore, all bodhisattvas Should always cultivate forbearance.
The Bodhisattva, wishing to adorn the body with the marks and signs of a Tathāgata,
is reborn in the Brahma-world; having departed from all paths of Māra,
he delights in practicing the conduct of patience, and thus achieves everything.
Therefore, all bodhisattvas should maintain firm patience.
The power of patience is supreme; among all practices, there is none that surpasses it.
All virtues and merits abide within the practice of patience.
The four powers of Māra are difficult to overcome, but the power of patience can eliminate them;
for this reason, all bodhisattvas should constantly cultivate forbearance.
*Sāṃkathyaviniścaya-sūtra*, Volume One.
The Scripture Spoken by the Great Śākyan Nirgrantha, Volume Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Part Two of Chapter Three: The Single Vehicle. Part Two.

“Good son! Furthermore, there are twelve kinds of generating a courageous mind through which a bodhisattva practices the *vīrya-pāramitā* and attains great benefit; thus, a bodhisattva should practice the *vīrya-pāramitā*.
What are the twelve?

First, because diligence enables one to swiftly awaken to and realize the ocean of all Buddha-dharmas, a bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of great valor and practice the perfection of diligence;
second, because diligence enables one to swiftly proceed to the presence of all Buddhas, a bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of great valor and practice the perfection of diligence.

Third, because diligence enables one to universally make offerings to and revere all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, a bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of great courage and vigor to practice the perfection of diligence;

fourth, because the deeds performed through diligence accord with the intentions of all Buddhas, a bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of great courage and vigor to practice the perfection of diligence;

fifth, because diligence enables one to diligently transform and deliver all sentient beings without ever becoming weary or satisfied, a bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of great courage and vigor to practice the perfection of diligence.

Sixth, because diligence can establish sentient beings within the teachings of all Buddhas and lead them toward the gate of liberation, a bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of great valor and practice the perfection of diligence;
seventh, because diligence can swiftly cause all sentient beings to be free from all ignorance, a bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of great valor and practice the perfection of diligence;
eighth, because diligence can swiftly bestow upon all sentient beings the wisdom of all Buddhas, a bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of great valor and practice the perfection of diligence.
Ninth, because diligence can swiftly purify all Buddha-fields, a bodhisattva should resolve upon great valor and courage to practice the perfection of diligence;

tenth, because the practice of diligence can establish [the bodhisattva] throughout all kalpas until the end of the future, enabling them to perform the bodhisattva deeds for the sake of all sentient beings without giving rise to weariness, a bodhisattva should resolve upon great valor and courage to practice the perfection of diligence;

eleventh, because the practice of diligence can plant all roots of goodness throughout all Buddha-fields within a single thought-moment, a bodhisattva should resolve upon great valor and courage to practice the perfection of diligence.

Twelfth, because diligent practice enables one to travel to all Buddha-lands to accomplish the Unsurpassed Way and turn the Great Wheel of Dharma, a bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of great valor and courage to practice the perfection of diligence.

“Good son! These are called the twelve kinds of generating a courageous mind by which a bodhisattva practices the *vīryapāramitā* (perfection of vigor), attains great benefit, and dedicates it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment).”
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the perfection of diligence with these verses, speaking them once more:
"If one wishes to act for the sake of sentient beings, Cultivating the practices of a bodhisattva,
And swiftly attain the unsurpassed path, Diligence is the foremost [virtue]."
Throughout immeasurable kalpas, the Tathāgata has been able to endure all the various ascetic practices he performed,
because he never gave rise to cowardice or weakness. Therefore, you sons of the Buddha,
if you wish to swiftly attain the path of Buddhahood, [you must likewise cultivate such endurance].
One should always diligently practice the perfection of vigor.
When a bodhisattva practices vigor, they can swiftly reach the supreme state;
passing through hundreds of thousands of lands, they make offerings to and contemplate all Buddhas.
The Bodhisattva seeks great bliss in order to uproot the suffering of sentient beings;
practicing the path of a bodhisattva with firm resolve and without turning back,
they are able, for the sake of all sentient beings, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas—
Enduring suffering without indolence is entirely due to diligence.
May I always be diligent in purifying the Buddha-lands;
furthermore, may I be able to awaken to and know all the teachings of the Buddhas.
Able to pervade all Buddha-lands, turning the great and wondrous wheel of Dharma.
May all classes of sentient beings fully awaken to this knowledge,
all entering the Mahāyāna, and leaving behind other vehicles and the realm of Māra.
Fulfilling all great vows, they swiftly reach the stage of fearlessness;
through the bodhisattva’s diligence, they are able, in a single thought-moment,
to awaken to the dharma of great bodhi and reveal the gate of nirvana.
Manifesting immeasurable bodies, they pervade the lands of the ten directions.
To benefit sentient beings, they display such supreme deeds.
"O son of good family!

Furthermore, there are twelve kinds of contemplations through which a bodhisattva practices the perfection of dhyāna and attains great benefit; thus, a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of dhyāna.
What are these twelve?

First, because meditative concentration can extinguish all defilements of the various afflictions, a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), remaining forever free from a mind of discrimination;

second, because the mind abides in tranquility through meditative concentration and mindfulness is not distracted, a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of meditation, not grasping at any sensory objects;

third, because the mind has no attachments through meditative concentration and is able to fulfill all practices, a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of meditation, being able to transcend the three realms.

Fourth, because meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) can transcend the world and remain unattached to any state of existence (*bhava*), a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*); for it surpasses the mundane world.
Fifth, because meditative concentration can contemplate the sublime Dharma with a mind free from weariness, a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of meditation; for it is never satisfied.

Sixth, because meditative concentration is supple and sovereign, and does not lead to rebirth through the power of dhyāna, a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of meditation; for it exercises mastery over all states of dhyāna.

Seventh, through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one attains the signless mind (*animitta-citta*) and does not perceive external objects; therefore, a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), because it is free from all signs.

Eighth, through meditative concentration, the mind is purified and can illuminate immeasurable realms; therefore, a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of meditation, because it transcends all limited samādhis and reproves their faults.

Ninth, through meditative concentration, one can extinguish the observing mind and no longer perceives the observer; therefore, a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of meditation, because it attains a state of quiescent mind.

Tenth, because meditative concentration realizes a supple mind and extinguishes all discursive thoughts (*vitarka* and *vicāra*), a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) in order to achieve mastery over the mind;

eleventh, because the mind in meditative concentration can attain tranquil extinction through single-pointed observation and remain unmoving in its faculties, a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of meditation in order to subdue the unwholesome roots;

twelfth, because the mind in meditative concentration possesses great skillful means regarding all phenomena, a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of meditation in order to never abandon the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*).
Why is this? Because all bodhisattvas dwell in the dhyānapāramitā, they do not give rise to a mind of arrogance;
because they dwell in the dhyānapāramitā, they do not give rise to a mind of false views.
Because they abide in the *dhyānapāramitā*, they do not give rise to feelings of aversion or attachment.
For this reason, all bodhisattvas are able to surpass all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists who practice various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and enter into dhyāna-trance.
"Good son! These are called the twelve kinds of practices of the bodhisattva’s dhyānapāramitā that yield great benefit, dedicated toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the dhyāna-pāramitā with these verses:
"If one wishes to cultivate untainted wisdom, To emerge from the mire of desire,
And to eliminate all karmic obstructions, Dhyāna-concentration is the foremost."
This meditative concentration is inconceivable; it is the realm of all Buddhas.
The śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary worldlings cannot know this samādhi.
Even the great earth, its mountains, and its oceans can be consumed and eliminated by the fires at the end of an eon.
If the mind abides in meditative concentration, it is peaceful and free from harm.
The Tathāgata’s sun of wisdom and the stainless maṇi jewel do not arise from any other place; they emerge from the ocean of meditative concentration.
Therefore, all you sons of the Buddha, who seek the great wisdom-treasure of the Buddhas,
should eliminate a distracted mind and contemplate the perfection of dhyāna.
The meditative concentration of the bodhisattvas pacifies and extinguishes all afflictions.
Therefore, the wise say that one who excels in this meditation surpasses those who practice other dhyānas.
With a deeply settled mind always in quiescence, taking no delight in sensory realms,
they are able to gather in all distracted thoughts and abide in the supreme state of nirvāṇa.
The Bodhisattva cultivates meditative concentration, dwelling nowhere within the three realms;
therefore, he does not rely upon them, for they are not places of reliance.
The Bodhisattva’s meditation can transcend both the mundane and the supramundane.
Therefore, this samādhi is supreme, surpassing both the world and the two vehicles.
The Bodhisattva’s dhyāna is supple; acting according to his will without hindrance, he is thus able to turn back and take birth within the desire realm.
The dhyāna practiced by Bodhisattvas surpasses all other forms of contemplation;
since other meditations are not ultimate, the Buddha declared these to be superior.
The immeasurable dhyānas of Bodhisattvas arise from the most excellent objects.
Free from all marks of sentient beings, And free from all defiled phenomena, Therefore,
the meditative concentrations practiced by the Bodhisattvas Are superior to those cultivated by others, As well as all partial concentrations.
The Bodhisattva contemplates exclusively, purifying all objective realms;
such cultivation of dhyāna arises from wisdom and skillful means,
with right knowledge as its foundation, never giving rise to a mind of false views.
Therefore, the dhyāna of the bodhisattva is beyond reproach or suspicion.
When the bodhisattva enters meditative concentration, he does not dwell within existence or non-existence;
because he contemplates the reality of the object, he is able to transcend the marks of existence and non-existence.
Such supreme wisdom and meditation are unlike any other realm;
even the arhats and pratyekabuddhas have their wisdom utterly bewildered by them.
"O son of good family!
Furthermore, there are twelve kinds of contemplation through which a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā and attains great benefit; thus, a bodhisattva should cultivate the prajñāpāramitā.
What are the twelve?

First, because prajñā is able to distance itself from all defilements and give rise to radiance, a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), for it is able to leave behind all dharmas of darkness.

Second, because prajñā is fully capable of awakening to and comprehending all obscurations of darkness, a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of wisdom, for it is able to illuminate and eliminate the dense forest of afflictions (kleśa).
Third, because Prajñā can radiate all the light of wisdom, a Bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in order to be free from all ignorance;

fourth, because Prajñā is like a plow that tills the earth and removes weeds and filth, a Bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of wisdom in order to uproot the very foundation of ignorance (avidyā);
fifth, because Prajñā is like a sharp iron hook that carves and hews at will, a Bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of wisdom in order to hook and sever the net of craving (tṛṣṇā).
Sixth, prajñā is like a vajra, which cannot be destroyed by any object; a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of wisdom because it can shatter the mountains of afflictions.
Seventh, prajñā is like the great sun disk, free from all clouds and mists; a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of wisdom because it can dry up the mire of all afflictions.
Eighth, prajñā is like a great mass of fire that burns away all foul weeds; a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of wisdom because it can incinerate the trees of karma and affliction.

Ninth, because prajñā is like a maṇi jewel that can illuminate all things, a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), so as not to have a mind obscured by darkness and thus not to be deluded regarding all dharmas;
tenth, because prajñā can abide in the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi) of quiescent cessation, a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of wisdom, because there is nothing [to be grasped];
eleventh, because prajñā can extinguish the mind of signs and be free from discrimination, a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of wisdom, because it is signless (animitta).

Twelfth, because Prajñā can accomplish the mind of wishlessness and the absence of seeking for pleasure, a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā), as it transcends the three realms.
“Good son! These are called the twelve kinds of practices through which a bodhisattva cultivates the perfection of wisdom and attains great benefit.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the perfection of wisdom with verses, speaking them as follows:
"Having ultimately severed the seeds of existence, One enters nirvana in peace and security.
Among all the pāramitās, Wisdom is the foremost.
Just as a lamp in the world Can dispel all darkness,"
Like a flame atop a high banner, they are the most supreme sight in the world.
All Tathāgatas have emerged from the flow of existence, having subdued the hosts of the four Māras; wisdom serves as their valiant general.
O sons of the Buddha, if you wish to benefit yourself and all sentient beings,
you should always diligently practice the Prajñāpāramitā.
It is like plowing a field, which can remove all weeds and impurities.
Wisdom extinguishes the weeds of doubt and craving, just as a plow tills the pure earth.
As Śakra’s vajra destroys the evil asuras, so too does wisdom shatter the mountain of afflictions; its power of destruction is likewise.
All Tathāgatas speak of the power of wisdom;
it is like the sun in summer, and also like a lamp in the world.
It can exhaust the ocean of afflictions and illuminate away the darkness of ignorance.
Because its essence transcends the world and possesses the brilliance of the untainted fire,
wisdom is able to cut through the tree of the darkness of ignorance and delusion,
just as a sharp blade shears away all the small weeds.
Wisdom is like a mani jewel, Illuminating the world with equanimity;
Like space, it is free from discrimination, And does not abide in either existence or nirvana.
The mind of wisdom is sovereign, Having certainty regarding all things.
Able to sever all doubts and regrets, And to resolve every inquiry,
He speaks of the evil retributions of the world, And reveals the fruit of nirvāṇa.
He universally shows all sentient beings Like a bright lamp in the darkness.
The Buddhas possess the bright moon-eye, Directly perceiving the characteristics of all phenomena;
All Bodhisattvas are likewise, Practicing with stainless wisdom.
Just as a person holding a lamp at night Sees clearly wherever they go,
Within the dark gloom of birth and death, the light of wisdom can deliver one across it.

"Good son! Furthermore, there are twelve kinds of spheres for a bodhisattva; by practicing skillful means within these spheres, one attains great benefit. Therefore, a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of skillful means."
What are the twelve?

First, because they manifest the turbid realms of the world while not departing from the pure realm of nirvāṇa through skillful means, bodhisattvas should cultivate the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*).

Second, because they manifest the bustling and noisy realms of the world while not departing from the tranquil realm of a single place through skillful means, bodhisattvas should cultivate the perfection of skillful means.

Third, because they employ skillful means (*upāya*) without departing from the profound realm of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), yet manifest the worldly realm of royal palaces, Bodhisattvas should cultivate the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*).

Fourth, because they employ skillful means without departing from the pure realm of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*), yet manifest the worldly realm of effortful activity, Bodhisattvas should cultivate the perfection of skillful means.

Fifth, because they employ skillful means without departing from the true realm of non-arising (*anutpāda*), yet manifest the various worldly realms of birth here and decline there, or decline here and birth there, Bodhisattvas should cultivate the perfection of skillful means.

Sixth, because they are able to transcend all realms of the four māras through skillful means while manifesting the realm of subduing māras within the world, a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of skillful means;

seventh, because they do not depart from the realm of all noble ones through skillful means while manifesting the realm of ordinary worldlings within the world, a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of skillful means;

eighth, because they do not depart from the realm capable of transcending the world through skillful means while abiding in the realms of existence within the world, a bodhisattva should cultivate the perfection of skillful means.

Ninth, because they do not depart from the realm of all-encompassing wisdom through skillful means, yet manifest the realm of worldly ignorance, Bodhisattvas should cultivate the perfection of skillful means;

tenth, because they do not depart from the Bodhisattva’s realm of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) through skillful means, yet manifest the realms of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas should cultivate the perfection of skillful means;

eleventh, because the power of skillful means enables them to thoroughly know that all phenomena are signless (*animitta*), yet they can manifest the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics to teach and transform sentient beings, Bodhisattvas should cultivate the perfection of skillful means.

Twelfth, because they are able to enter all realms of equality through the power of skillful means (*upāya-bala*), yet can manifest all realms of Māra, a bodhisattva should abide in the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*).
“Good son! This is called the great benefit obtained by a bodhisattva through the twelve kinds of dwelling in the perfection of skillful means.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the perfection of skillful means with these verses, saying:
"All Bodhisattvas who practice the various pāramitās,
if they lack skillful means, cannot reach the other shore.
[Yet through them] they benefit themselves and others, abiding in both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa."
Thus there is neither purity nor defilement; all is due to skillful means.
All the spheres of activity traversed by the Tathāgatas are inconceivable to those of the two vehicles; this is due to the power of skillful means.
Therefore, all you sons of the Buddha, who wish to perform the deeds of the Tathāgata,
should always diligently practice the perfection of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā).
The Bodhisattva is ever pure, using skillful means to benefit sentient beings.
In truth, they are free from the defilements of desire, yet they manifest the practice of stained conduct.
Bathing in the pool of nirvāṇa, they skillfully appear within all realms of existence;
these are called bodhisattvas, who do not abide in either extreme.
Body, speech, and mind are ever-abiding in the ultimate truth of quiescence;
yet for the benefit of sentient beings, they employ skillful means in accordance with the world.
Like a bee entering a forest of flowers, it does not focus exclusively on gathering from a single flower.
The bodhisattva’s practice of skillful means encompasses all realms of experience.
He may manifest various appearances, his body exquisitely adorned,
appearing among the palace women and engaging in acts of indulgence.
Sometimes appearing in the hells, they rescue all suffering sentient beings;
though manifesting such forms, they never abandon meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Without relinquishing any *samādhi*, they appear amidst distraction.
Manifesting acts of harm is called the power of skillful means.
Having already been able to leave behind all conditioned activities,
the Bodhisattva possesses no discursive mind regarding existence or non-existence.
Though manifesting all manner of defilements, they do not give rise to the fire of deluded desire;
through skillful means they manifest within them, discerning the characteristics of the conditioned.
Regarding all states of existence, the Bodhisattva neither gives rise to them nor does he regress.
Manifesting the events of birth and decline through the power of skillful means and wisdom,
they abandon the realms of demonic activity and dwell within the sphere of the Buddhas.
With wisdom that is neither timid nor weak, they manifest all manner of demonic deeds.
Through the power of great compassion, the Bodhisattva employs the swift wisdom of skillful means;
abiding in the noble, unsurpassed state, he manifests the affairs of ordinary beings.
By entering into the characteristics of all phenomena, he knows that the essence of all phenomena is empty.
Constantly abiding in nirvāṇa, yet not abandoning the world;
all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, tranquil, and signless,
yet for the benefit of sentient beings, his body is adorned with the marks and signs of excellence.
Without delusion yet appearing as ignorance, without anger yet appearing as lack of compassion,
yet able to benefit sentient beings— this is called skillful means.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in such a state,
This is called the manifestation of the various skillful means of the sages.
"Furthermore, sons of good family!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has yet another skillful means, which you should know."
Why is this? Sons of good family!

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess twelve kinds of supreme and wondrous merits that are like clarified butter (*ghṛta*); among all flavors, they are the most excellent, pure, and foremost. They are able to purify all Buddha-lands, and within them, the Tathāgatas attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
What are the twelve?
First, manifesting the defilement of the eon;
second, manifesting the defilement of the time;
Third, manifesting the defilement of sentient beings;
fourth, manifesting the defilement of afflictions;
fifth, manifesting the defilement of lifespan.
Sixth, manifesting the turbidity of the distinctions between the three vehicles;
seventh, manifesting the turbidity of impure buddha-fields;
eighth, manifesting the turbidity of sentient beings who are difficult to transform.
Ninth, manifesting the teaching on the turbidity of various afflictions;
tenth, manifesting the turbidity of the confusion of non-Buddhists;
eleventh, manifesting the turbidity of Māra.
Twelfth is the manifestation of the turbidity of Māra’s deeds. Good son!
All the lands of all Buddhas are adorned with supramundane merits, fully perfected and pure, and are devoid of any turbidity.
"Such manifestations as these are all displayed through the power of the skillful means of the Buddhas for the benefit of sentient beings; you should know this.
At that time, the noble Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has spoken of these twelve supreme merits of a pure Buddha-field; in what kind of land, then, will the Tathāgata attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"First, the sentient beings in that buddha-land will ultimately be able to bring about a supreme and pure kalpa, free from the turbidity of the kalpa and endowed with all merits; in such a pure land, the Tathāgata attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Second, the sentient beings in that buddha-land will ultimately be able to bring about the most excellent and wondrous time, wherein the dharma-practices of all Buddhas do not miss their proper seasons; in such a pure land, the Tathāgata attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Third, the sentient beings in that Buddha-land will ultimately be able to become the most excellent vessels for the Dharma and receive the Tathāgata’s true Dharma; in such a pure land, the Tathāgata attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Fourth, the sentient beings in that Buddha-land will ultimately be able to become an ocean of pure and wondrous wisdom, purifying all stains of affliction; in such a pure land, the Tathāgata attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Fifth, the sentient beings in that Buddha-land will ultimately be able to achieve a supple and gentle mind, wherein there is always the taming of sentient beings; in such a pure land, the Tathāgata attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Sixth, the sentient beings in that Buddha-land will ultimately be able to accomplish the most supreme and wondrous vehicle; being able to attain ultimate, unsurpassed *nirvāṇa* through the One Vehicle—such is the pure land in which the Tathāgata attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Seventh, the sentient beings in that Buddha-land will ultimately be able to perfect the superior vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), free from all other characteristics—such is the pure land in which the Tathāgata attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Eighth, the sentient beings in that Buddha-land will ultimately be able to perfect the True Teaching of the Tathāgata, with no trace of any heterodox paths or false doctrines—such is the pure land in which the Tathāgata attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Ninth, the sentient beings in that Buddha-land will ultimately be able to achieve a straightforward mind and a correct mind, free from flattery and crookedness; in such a pure land, the Tathāgata attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Tenth, the sentient beings in that Buddha-land will ultimately be able to achieve stainless merit and accomplish all pure, wholesome dharmas; in such a pure land, the Tathāgata attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Eleventh, all sentient beings in that Buddha-land will ultimately be able to accomplish the dharmas of the various sages, and there will always be a multitude of supreme fields of merit therein; in such a pure land, the Tathāgata attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Twelfth, all sentient beings in that Buddha-land will ultimately be able to establish a supreme and wondrous site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); it is within such a pure land that past Buddhas have attained the Way, and it is within such a pure land that the Tathāgata has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Mañjuśrī! These are called the twelve kinds of supreme merits that can purify a buddha-field.
In such a purified field, the Tathāgata attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Mañjuśrī! In my buddha-field, there is no teaching of distinctions such as śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Why is this?
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are free from the faults of various conceptualizations and attachments. Mañjuśrī!

If the Tathāgata were to preach the Mahāyāna for one class of beings, the Pratyekabuddhayāna for another class of beings, and the Śrāvakayāna for yet another class of beings—if he were to speak in such a manner—it would mean that the Tathāgata has failed to achieve a pure mind.
This would mean that the Tathāgata possesses a mind of partiality;
this would mean that the Tathāgata possesses a mind characterized by the fault of contention;
this would mean that the Tathāgata lacks a mind of impartial compassion.
This is the Tathāgata’s mind that has transcended all marks;
this is the Tathāgata’s mind that gives rise to no stinginess regarding any phenomena. Mañjuśrī!

Whatever various dharmas I teach for the sake of sentient beings, all those dharmas accord with bodhi and accord with the Mahāyāna; they grasp at omniscience and, being ultimately and definitively able to reach a single destination—that is, they are able to reach the state of omniscience.
“Mañjuśrī! For this reason, there is no differentiation of vehicles in my land.
At that time, the noble Mañjuśrī, Prince of the Dharma, the Bodhisattva, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there were no differentiation among the three vehicles, for what reason does the Tathāgata teach the Dharma of the three vehicles for the sake of all sentient beings, saying, ‘This is the vehicle of training for śrāvakas,’ saying, ‘This is the vehicle of training for pratyekabuddhas,’ and saying, ‘This is the vehicle of training for bodhisattvas’?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “When the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, speak of the three vehicles, they indicate differences in stages, not differences in vehicles;
when the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, speak of the three vehicles, they indicate differences in the characteristics of dharmas, not differences in vehicles.”
When the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, speak of the three vehicles, they are speaking of the distinctions among persons, not of distinctions among vehicles;
