when the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, speak of the three vehicles, they are demonstrating how those with few merits may come to know great merit, for within the Buddha-dharma there are no distinctions among vehicles.
Why is this? Because the nature of the dharma-realm is without differentiation. Mañjuśrī!

When the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, speak of the three vehicles, it is to cause all sentient beings to enter the Dharma-gates of the Tathāgata’s various teachings, and to cause all sentient beings to gradually enter the Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s Mahāyāna, just as one learns various arts by practicing them in successive stages.

“Mañjuśrī! It is, for example, like a master archer who, within the wisdom of archery, has reached the ultimate perfection of the foremost shore; he is able to teach his disciples through various immeasurable skillful means, such that they realize everything to its ultimate conclusion, just as he himself knows and sees.”

Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata, the master archer, is also like this. Having reached the ultimate further shore in all dharmas, he uses the discernment of the Tathāgata’s omniscient wisdom to teach and reveal the distinctions of the three vehicles to all sentient beings, just as a worldly master archer instructs his disciples.
“Mañjuśrī! Just as a small fire, with its initial sparks and flames, gradually increases until it can pervade the entire world, even becoming the great conflagration that burns at the end of an eon.”

Mañjuśrī! The fire of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is also like this: from the very nature of that single light of wisdom, it gradually increases and perfects the great light of wisdom—the Tathāgata’s all-knowing vision—capable of incinerating all defiled afflictions.
“Mañjuśrī! For example, the great Sumeru Kings of Mountains have no discriminating mind; when sentient beings arrive there, they all become one color, namely, the color of gold.
Mañjuśrī! In the same way, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, the King of Mountains Sumeru of unsurpassed great wisdom, likewise makes no distinctions among all sentient beings.
“If there are sentient beings who enter the Buddha-dharma, all those sentient beings shall become of one color, namely, the wondrous color of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā). Mañjuśrī!

For example, suppose a pure, exquisite, and clear-colored maṇi jewel of Indra were placed within the entire vessel-world (bhājana-loka). Within the sphere of that maṇi jewel, all colors and various marks throughout that sphere would, through the power of the maṇi jewel, become a single color—namely, blue.

Mañjuśrī! It is the same with the unsurpassed blue-colored maṇi-jewel of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One: when its light of wisdom illuminates sentient beings, they all become one color—namely, the color of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).

“Mañjuśrī! It is like the great ocean, into which immeasurable hundreds of thousands of river and stream waters flow; once they have entered, they all become of one single taste, namely the taste of salt, because it abides eternally.”
Mañjuśrī! The waters of the great ocean are called the all-encompassing wisdom of the Tathāgata;
the various waters of rivers and streams that flow into it are called the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.
That which, having entered [the ocean], all becomes of the same salty taste is called the One Vehicle;
that which is eternally abiding is called non-discriminative omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Mañjuśrī!
Based on this meaning, you should know that there is no distinction between vehicles.
Mañjuśrī! Therefore, when the Buddha speaks of the distinctions between the stages, he demonstrates to all sentient beings the gradual entry into the activities of the three vehicles.
Regarding the distinctions among the characteristics of the teaching of the Dharma: it demonstrates how the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes leads sentient beings into it through gradual stages;

and by speaking of small merits while knowing great merits, it shows the distinctions between the three types of persons among all sentient beings, demonstrating the Tathāgata’s unimpeded eloquence and the skillful means of his majestic display.
Mañjuśrī! When the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, speak of the three vehicles, they do so in reliance upon conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). Mañjuśrī!
When the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, speak of the One Vehicle, they do so in reliance upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This ultimate truth is exclusively the One Vehicle, for there is no second.

“Mañjuśrī! All those who are non-Buddhists in my Buddha-land—such as the Sāṃkhyas, the Vaiśeṣikas, the Cārvākas, and the Nirgranthas—are all the skillful means of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas; they are all sustained by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, such that the world is able to see them.”
Why is this? Because all Tathāgatas have skillfully eliminated all adverse conditions. Mañjuśrī!
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are called Sugatas; it is impossible for them to have any adversaries or enemies. Mañjuśrī!

For example, although a worldly Wheel-Turning King has accomplished some small portion of the merit of roots of goodness, he is one who has severed his roots of goodness, whose dharmas are not ultimate, who is fully possessed of all fetters and afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion, who does not leave the three realms of existence, who does not leave behind any latent tendencies or afflictions, and who does not leave behind any defiled afflictions.
That wheel-turning king ultimately has no enemies whatsoever, and ultimately has no adversaries whatsoever.
Why is this? Mañjuśrī!
Because a Wheel-Turning King has no thorns of enmity. Mañjuśrī!

How much less could there be thorns of Mara, thorns of enmity, or hostile adversaries among the non-Buddhists for a Tathāgata—who has accomplished all merit and wisdom, attained an uninterrupted great heart of compassion, traverses the untainted realm of empty dharma, fulfills the seven factors of enlightenment and all virtuous merits, ultimately achieves the quality of non-forgetfulness, is able to turn the unsurpassed, supreme, and wondrous wheel of Dharma, and has ultimately realized unsurpassed Bodhi? Such a thing is impossible.
Mañjuśrī! All those who are Sāṃkhyas, Vaiśeṣikas, Carakas, Nirgranthas, and so forth in my buddha-field are all manifested through skillful means by the power of the Tathāgata’s sustaining presence.

Mañjuśrī! Although these sons of good family from among the various non-Buddhist paths practice the characteristics of diverse heterodox teachings, they are all identical to the Buddha-dharma; for there is but one bridge for crossing over, and no other means of salvation.
“Mañjuśrī! Among all birds and beasts, there is none capable of standing before the lion king and uttering a sound. Mañjuśrī!”

The Tathāgata, the Lion, the Great Man, the King, is fully endowed with the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses. Among all the heterodox followers, such as the Nirgranthas, there is not one who dares to dispute the Dharma or its rightness and wrongness within the domain of the Tathāgata, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and utter a lion’s roar; such a thing is impossible, except for those Tathāgatas who employ the power of skillful means.

“Mañjuśrī! For example, when the solar disc rises and emits a great net of light, the radiance of all insects and fireflies is completely extinguished, and even the light of all mani-jewels and fires cannot manifest.”

Mañjuśrī! When the Tathāgata appears in the world, he radiates the brilliant light of the great sun-disk of wisdom; all the lights of the various non-Buddhist Nirgranthas, which are like the wisdom of insects or fireflies, are entirely eclipsed and unable to manifest.
“Mañjuśrī! For example, there is a king of iron named Akṣayantaka; wherever he is located, no ordinary iron dares to remain.
Why is this? Because it possesses a unique characteristic, it does not coexist in the same place as ordinary iron. Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgata, the Iron King, is also like this: wherever he appears in any land, all ordinary iron and the various non-Buddhists cannot come into being.
Why is this? Because the Buddha, the Tathāgata, has appeared in the world as a unique manifestation. "Mañjuśrī!
For example, Mañjuśrī, wherever the sovereign wish-fulfilling maṇi-jewel appears, there no counterfeit lapis lazuli beads can arise. Mañjuśrī!
Wherever the Tathāgata, the Great Wisdom Jewel King who fulfills all wishes, appears in the world, there none of the various non-Buddhist practitioners can arise.
“Mañjuśrī! For example, from within which kind of precious ore does Jāmbūnada gold emerge, yet copper, iron, and the like do not emerge from that same place? Mañjuśrī!”
The precious nature of the Tathāgata is likewise: in whatever land he appears in the world, there no followers of external paths shall arise. Mañjuśrī!
Based on this meaning, you should know that in whatever land a Tathāgata appears in the world, there no heterodox teachers (tīrthikas) shall arise. Why is this?

Mañjuśrī! In my buddha-field there are various non-Buddhist practitioners, such as the Nirgranthas and others; these exist entirely through the sustaining power of the Tathāgata, for the purpose of manifesting inconceivable realms of skillful means.

Why is this? Because all these various non-Buddhists dwell within the gate of inconceivable liberation; because they have all attained the gate of ultimate Prajñāpāramitā of great wisdom; because they have all attained the powerful, vigorous mastery of great skillful means; because they have all attained the mindfulness that never abandons the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; because they have all reached the foremost other shore and transform sentient beings through great spiritual power; and because they have all attained the empowerment of the Tathāgata to transform sentient beings.

When this gateway of the One Vehicle was being taught, eight thousand devaputras who had followed the practices of śrāvakas, having heard of the One Vehicle, resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Five hundred bhikṣus attained the samādhi of the Lamp of Equal Great Wisdom of the One Vehicle,
and twelve million bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

This trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and all the devas dwelling within the realm of space rained down *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers, as well as powdered sandalwood incense and other fragrances, which completely filled the area beneath the Tathāgata’s feet.

Countless hundreds of thousands of devaputras, dwelling in the midst of the sky, performed hundreds of thousands of various kinds of music, all producing wondrous sounds as an offering to the Tathāgata. They rained down celestial garments, struck divine drums, and spoke these words:
"In this world, we have never before heard such a rare, sublime, and most excellent Dharma-gate."
Again, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
May this Dharma-gate ultimately abide within Jambudvīpa, bringing great benefit to all sentient beings.”
Then eight thousand bhikṣuṇīs each removed the upper garment they were wearing and offered it to the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Mañjuśrī, you should know: The supreme skillful means of all Buddhas.”
When I appeared in this world of existence, I skillfully manifested the turbidity of the age.
Although all phenomena exist at all times as ultimately and eternally pure,
they appear as the turbidity of sentient beings because sentient beings receive the Dharma according to their own dispositions.
The Buddhas, those of supreme wisdom, appear within sublime eons;
their lands are eternally pure, and for this reason they are said to be free from turbidity.
Throughout immeasurable eons, I have fully practiced ascetic austerities.
Having purified all karmic obstructions and attained the merit of supreme wisdom,
one’s lifespan remains forever inexhaustible throughout immeasurable eons;
except for the power of the Buddha’s skillful means, there is thus no turbidity of life.
Because sentient beings give rise to the notion of permanence, I manifest impermanence;
though my life spans countless eons, I manifest the appearance of a short lifespan.
The Tathāgata’s supreme merits have been cultivated throughout immeasurable kalpas.
Beings of meager merit and timid nature, upon hearing this, give rise to a heart of alarm and fear;
for the sake of these beings, I have explained the distinctions through various classifications.
Ultimately, all shall attain Buddhahood; there is no other vehicle whatsoever.
For the sake of transforming sentient beings, I have distinguished and taught various other paths;
by gradually transforming them so they enter into the One, there is no differentiation into three.
It is like a skilled archer who is well able to distinguish between the sword and the arrow.
Just as one teaches various arts to one's disciples by explaining them in diverse ways,
so too does the Tathāgata, for the sake of bringing sentient beings to fulfillment,
explain a single Dharma through various distinctions.
Toward all sentient beings, I have no mind of discrimination;
yet because their capacities differ, what I teach has distinctions.
If I lacked a mind of equanimity, people would say that I am stingy and jealous.
One takes for oneself the Supreme Vehicle, while bestowing lower dharmas upon sentient beings.
Like the supreme Indra-jewel, which everywhere emits a blue-green light that universally illuminates all things alike, yet the jewel itself remains without discrimination.
The Buddha’s unsurpassed jewel of wisdom shines its radiance upon the world;
it is of the same hue as bodhi and is free from all conceptualizing minds.
Just as a tiny spark of fire grows and becomes a great light, so too does this wisdom expand.
All Arhats with limited wisdom increase and attain the Buddha-wisdom.
All sentient beings, having gone to the place of Mount Sumeru,
by the power of Sumeru’s radiance, all become one and the same color.
In this way, all these sentient beings, dwelling upon the Dharma-Sumeru of the Buddha,
by virtue of the Tathāgata’s power of Dharma, become one with the Buddha’s form-body (rūpakāya).
Just as a honeybee collects various kinds of substances, [so do they gather the qualities of the Buddha].
Placed within a single vessel, they are blended into one flavor.
So too does the Buddha teach the Three [Vehicles]: to ripen the faculties of sentient beings, he expounds various diverse dharmas, which result in the flavor of the Bodhi of a Buddha.
Just as when a Wheel-Turning King appears, there are no rival enemies;
so too, when my Dharma-King appears, there are no thorns of external paths.
Just as when the solar orb rises, all other lights are eclipsed.
Once the sun-disk of the Buddha has emerged, the heretics vanish of their own accord.
Just as where the king of iron is produced, no other common iron can arise;
so wherever the Buddha is born, no heretics can exist.
Wherever exquisite gold is produced, other copper and iron do not grow;
wherever a Buddha attains enlightenment, non-Buddhists naturally do not exist.
Just as a mani jewel does not dwell together with impurities, so it is here.
Therefore, in the place of its birth, there is no counterfeit lapis lazuli bead.
The same is true for the source from which the Tathāgata-maṇi jewel emerges:
it does not mix with those of other paths within a single land at the same time.
The great supernatural powers of the non-Buddhists are all the mastery of Bodhisattvas;
you should know that they manifest such signs through skillful means.
When all the Bodhisattvas hear of these non-Buddhists and others, [they understand this].
Endowed with the power of skillful means, they all gave rise to hearts of joy;
each developed a sense of reverence and offered respectful intentions.
They scattered flowers as an offering to the Buddha and perfumed him with various exquisite incenses.
While he was preaching the Dharma there, the great earth shook in six ways, and a voice resounded from the void, saying: "How rare! Such has never been heard before!
Immeasurable sons of the gods joined their palms in the sky and offered praise.
In unison they exclaimed, “Excellent! Excellent, Sugata! Chapter Four:

Visiting King Ugratejas *The Mahāsāṃghika-saṃnipāta Sūtra Spoken by the Nirgrantha Mahāsāṃghika* At that time, in the southern region, the Nirgrantha Mahāsāṃghika, together with eighty-eight million Nirgranthas, was traveling through various kingdoms to teach and transform sentient beings. In due course, he arrived at the city of Ujjayanī.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of followers who sang and danced, whistled and shrieked, performing hundreds of thousands of various kinds of music as they attended upon the great Śākyan ascetic Sañjayin from the front and rear as he proceeded toward the city of Ujjayinī.
At that time, the sovereign King Ugratejas heard that the great Sañjayin Nirgrantha and his assembly had come from the great southern kingdom with an immeasurable multitude to the city of Ujjayinī.
Having heard this, he immediately conceived a heart of profound respect for the great Nirgrantha Mahāsatya.

Having conceived a heart of reverence, desiring to welcome the great Śākyan son Sañjayin, he employed the power of the Great King, the supernatural power of the king, and the sovereign power of the king, together with his various ministers and princes, his teachers from whom he had studied, his entire family and retinue, the great elders of the kingdom, the lords of the various small towns, cities, and villages, and the fourfold host of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, who preceded and followed him in respectful circumambulation. They struck bells and beat drums, performed hundreds of thousands of kinds of immeasurable music, sounded hundreds of thousands of kinds of exquisite sounding drums, blew hundreds of thousands of kinds of exquisite sounding conchs, raised hundreds of thousands of millions of various colored silk canopies, banners, and streamers, and scattered hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of exquisite flowers.

Utpala flowers, padma flowers, kumuda flowers, puṇḍarīka flowers, aśoka flowers, bakula flowers, vīrakā flowers, and atimuktaka flowers were strewn all along the road. Golden and silver vases filled with hundreds of thousands of varieties of diverse, exquisite flowers, and hundreds of thousands of precious incense burners emitting priceless incense, were placed before him as he proceeded toward the place where the Nirgrantha Saccaka was.

At that time, the great Nirgrantha Saccaka saw King Ugratejas approaching with his great assembly from afar; having seen him, Saccaka the Nirgrantha stepped off the path and sat down upon a seat spread beneath a tree.

At that time, King Ugratejas saw Saccaka sitting beneath a tree from afar; he immediately descended from his elephant carriage and approached Saccaka the Nirgrantha on foot, where he sat upon a wish-fulfilling couch adorned with hundreds of thousands of exquisite, priceless mani-jewels.
At that time, the great Śākyan Nirgrantha went to inquire after the king’s welfare and spoke these words: “Welcome, Great King!
You have now sown the seeds of unsurpassed, most supreme, and rare merit; your blessings are many and not few.”
Why is this? Because the King was able to subdue his celestial, noble, and sovereign mind, humbling himself to approach the śramaṇa to inquire after his well-being.
"Great King!
Within the realm over which you rule, are there no thieves, bandits, or groups of fugitives who bring disorder to the people?
Are there no officials who are cruel and violent, plundering and devouring the people?"
Are there no people of various divergent karmas who are treacherous, hypocritical, arrogant, deceitful, or who deceive the people of the world?
Are there no rebels who disturb and bring chaos to the land and its people?
Is there no occurrence of robbery, plunder, or secret theft?
In the various border regions, do the officials and law-enforcers not deceive Your Majesty, nor fail to carry out Your Majesty’s commands? Great King!
Are all the śramaṇas and practitioners of purity within the realm you govern dwelling in peace and happiness?
Are their requirements for livelihood—clothing, food and drink, dwellings, bedding, and medicinal decoctions for illness—all such necessary items provided in abundance, without lack or deficiency?
Do the people of your kingdom all possess virtuous minds, and do they respect and make offerings to the various śramaṇas and pure practitioners?
Great King!

Within the realm you now govern, are there no hunters or trappers, no nets set upon rivers and mountains, no burning of forests or marshes, no releasing of hawks or running of dogs, no hooking of fish or turtles, no shooting of birds or beasts with crossbows, and no digging of pits or use of poisoned arrows and mechanical traps to carry out slaughter?
"Great King!
You are now the sovereign of this nation, possessing absolute authority over life and death; your commands regarding good and evil are such that none dare disobey them.
Since you ascended the throne, have there been any commands you have issued that were not virtuous?"
Do you know all the good and evil deeds performed by the people within the realm?
Do you encourage those who are able to practice virtue to advance further?
And do you exhort those who practice what is unwholesome to abandon it?
"Great King!
Does your body not give rise to evil thoughts to harm any sentient beings—whether two-legged, four-legged, many-legged, or legless?
For what reason?"
"Great King!

You should know that among all sentient beings who possess consciousness, they cherish their bodies and lives; there are none who do not fear death. When it comes to the karmic retribution of reaching the end of a hundred-year lifespan, regardless of whether one is old or young, not a single person can claim even a fraction of a share by saying, 'I ought to go.'"

Why is this? Because life is cherished and held dear; how much more so would one feel distress at being harmed? After death, they will again harbor mutual resentment and jealousy, seeking retribution against their enemies without end.
Therefore, Great King!
You should distance yourself from the transgression of taking life; lay aside the sword and staff, and let no harmful intent arise.
Great King!
You should now distance yourself from the transgression of stealing; relinquish your own means of livelihood, cultivate contentment, and harbor no desire for the possessions of others.
"Great King!
You should now distance yourself from the transgression of sexual misconduct; be content with your own wife, seek nothing from the wives of others, and do not give rise to improper thoughts.
Great King!"
You should now distance yourself from the fault of false speech; always speak the truth, let your words accord with the Dharma, and never utter empty talk.
Great King!

You should now distance yourself from the fault of divisive speech; do not use words that cause estrangement, but rather contemplate reconciliation for those who have been divided, and harbor no intent to create further discord.
"Great King!
You should now distance yourself from the fault of harsh speech; you should always employ endearing words, gentle and sublime speech, and never give rise to coarse language.
Great King!"
You should now distance yourself from the fault of frivolous speech; you should always speak with certainty and mindfulness, never engaging in improper speech.
Great King!

You should now distance yourself from the fault of covetousness; you should have no desire for the enjoyments of others, no intent to seize what is protected by others, and instead give rise to a heart of joy.
"Great King!
You should now distance yourself from the fault of anger; always give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, purify your mental karma, and do not harbor resentment.
"Great King! [he continued.]

You should now distance yourself from the fault of wrong views; seeing the fruits of your own karma, you should follow the noble ones and give rise to right view, without conceiving any divergent views.
Why is this? The sin of killing causes sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, a short lifespan; [second, much illness].
Second, one suffers from many illnesses.
The sin of stealing also causes sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, poverty; [second, illness].
Second, regarding shared property, one lacks autonomy.
The sin of sexual misconduct also causes sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retributive fruits:
first, their wife does not heed their words; [second, they are separated from their children].
Second, one's own wife is seized and stolen by another.
The sin of lying also causes sentient beings to fall into the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts; if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, they are constantly slandered by others.
Second, one is constantly deceived by others.
The sin of divisive speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts; if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, they suffer the destruction of their kin and retinue.
Second, one obtains evil associates.
The sin of harsh speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts; if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, they do not hear their good reputation.
Second, they constantly engage in quarrels and disputes.
The transgression of frivolous speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts; if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, their speech is not respected.
Second, their speech lacks certainty and truth, and they do not act for the benefit of others.
The transgression of greed also causes sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts; if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retributive fruits:
first, a lack of contentment; [and second, being deceived by others].
Second, they constantly give rise to a greedy mind.
The transgression of anger also causes sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts; if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, a lack of peace and security of mind; [second, a lack of respect from others].

Second, those who constantly harbor thoughts of harm and lack a compassionate heart—the sin of such wrong views also causes sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, they are always born into families that hold wrong views.
Second, their minds are constantly crooked and deceitful.
"Great King, you should know that such immeasurable and boundless masses of suffering all arise from the causal conditions accumulated through the ten unwholesome karmas."

Therefore, Great King! Do not be negligent or commit evil deeds lightly. You should contemplate that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; nothing in the entire world can be relied upon. Human life does not abide for long, lasting but a brief moment; do not give rise to the notion of permanence.
"Great King, you should observe this!

Since the beginning of the kalpa, the celestial thrones of the World-Honored Ones, royal positions, lands, and subjects have all succumbed to impermanence; not a single one remains. You should know that this body is exceedingly fragile and precarious—like a flame, like an echo, like a shadow, like lightning, like the moon reflected in water, like an image in a mirror, like a mass of foam, like a bubble on the water, like the core of a plantain tree, like fire struck from flint, like what is seen in a dream, or like a torrential waterfall suddenly rising in a mountain valley that fills the ravines and gullies only to pass away in an instant and return to exhaustion."
"Great King, you should know!
The body and life are not real; impermanence is likewise such that they fall away in an instant, and one cannot escape them in the future world.
Therefore, Great King!"
Do not rely on the present; you must fear the future.

Great King, you should know that the retributions of good and evil pursue one another like an echo following a sound or a shadow following a form; no one can escape them. They are also like an iron chain that cannot be severed. Do not treat your actions lightly, lest you invite heavy suffering for yourself.
At that time, the great Nirgrantha Satyaka spoke again in verse:
"O Great King, you should now Not engage in heedless conduct;
If you do not abandon all evils, Upon death you will surely enter hell."
Because those who commit evil deeds will certainly enter hell,
one should restrain the mind and be heedful, so as to be born in the realm of Śakra, Lord of Devas.
Among all sentient beings, there are none who do not cherish their own life.
If the King seeks long life, he should not practice killing.
Great King, you know that worldly people toil to amass wealth and treasures, always fearing they will not survive;
you should not give rise to thoughts of plundering them.
Because one does not encroach upon or seize what belongs to others, one will always be born into a place of abundance;
if one intentionally encroaches upon or harms others, one will always be born into a poor household.
Restrain oneself and do not lust after others; be content with one’s own wife.
Therefore, a wife loves her husband and will not allow others to violate him.
Do not speak false words; always mindfully rely on truthful speech.
Truthful speech leads to rebirth as Śakra, while false speech leads to rebirth as a hungry ghost.
Constantly mindful of avoiding double-tongued speech, one reconciles those who are divided;
with family and kin always in harmonious accord, one leaves this life to be born in the Brahma Heaven.
When speaking, do not be coarse or harsh, but speak words that others delight to hear.
Those who speak well are born in the heavens, where they constantly hear exquisite sounds.
By reflecting on the abandonment of all frivolous speech and contemplating beautiful words,
one is reborn as Śakra, Lord of the Devas, whose teachings all the gods revere and receive.
If you wish to benefit yourself, do not cause harm or affliction to others;
for the retribution of greed born in future lives, wealth shall be shared among the five families.
If you do not cultivate loving-kindness and compassion, yet practice a mind of anger and malice, [you will suffer].
Though one may practice various virtuous deeds, If one dies and enters the hells,
O Great King, you should now Abandon anger and delusion;
always maintain loving-kindness toward sentient beings, And do not engage in any acts of wrath or harm.
The King should abandon wrong views and firmly establish a mind of right view;
always upholding the pure Dharma, he shall receive a body that enjoys bliss among the devas.
You should constantly provide offerings to the bhikṣus who cultivate the brahma-faring.
"Therefore, abandon the evil realms and receive joy in the heavens.

At that time, after Mahāsatyaka Nirgrantha had inquired after the King's welfare and taught King Ugratejas the Dharma associated with the ten paths of wholesome action and heedfulness, he remained silent.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Great Śākyan Nirgrantha, Volume Two.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Great Śākyan Nirgrantha, Volume Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.

Chapter Five: On Kings, Part One. At that time, King Ugratejas, the sovereign of the land, having heard the True Dharma spoken by the great Śākyan son Mahāsatyaka, received it with joy and faith. He immediately inquired after the great Śākyan son, saying:

"Great Master, you are compassionate and have traveled far to wander and transform sentient beings. The roads are full of hardships; I wonder if your four elements are in harmony and if your strength is secure?"
"Are the sentient beings easy to transform?
Do the assembly of disciples practice according to what they have been taught?

It is my great fortune that the Great Master has not shunned our land; now that I am able to behold you and hear the preaching of the True Dharma, my heart is filled with joy. It is as if I were seeing a compassionate mother, as if a hungry person had obtained food, as if a thirsty person had found water, as if a naked person had gained clothing, as if a poor person had acquired treasure, as if a hot person had found coolness, as if a cold person had found fire, as if a blind person had regained sight, as if a deaf person had regained hearing, as if a prisoner had received amnesty, as if a lowly person had attained nobility, as if a lost person had returned home, and as if a student had encountered a teacher—my heart’s joy is just like this."
He further spoke these words:
"O Great Master, you should know!
From the time I first set out, I have been reflecting within my own mind:"

"The True Dharma is difficult to hear; a virtuous teacher is difficult to encounter; a human body is difficult to obtain; the sense faculties are difficult to possess in full; right view is difficult to give rise to; faith is difficult to engender; the coming together of favorable conditions is difficult; sovereign freedom is difficult to meet; and a time of great peace is difficult to find. I have now escaped all such difficulties."
"Now that I have encountered the Great Master, it is as if one who has entered the great ocean seeking precious jewels has reached an island of great treasures.
I have certain doubts that I wish to inquire about; I only pray that the Great Master will grant me a resolution regarding my doubts!"
Then the great Śākyeya Nirgrantha-putra said to King Udayana:
"Whatever you may doubt, you may now ask all at once; I shall analyze and explain it for you, resolving your doubts and causing you to attain understanding."
At that time, King Ugratejas, seeing that Mahāsāṃghika Nirgrantha had granted him permission to ask questions, felt great joy in his heart and addressed him, saying:
"O Great Master!..."
What is the phenomenon that arises?
What is its maintenance? Upon what phenomena do these names depend?
Saccaka the Nirgrantha said:
"Great King, you should know that what is called 'birth' refers to all sentient beings."
What is called the "receptacle world" refers to the vessel-world (bhājana-loka);
what is called "sentient beings" refers to the collection of the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha), which is termed "sentient beings.
By what dharma are these five aggregates of clinging defined?
That is to say:
the aggregate of form-clinging, the aggregate of feeling-clinging, the aggregate of perception-clinging, the aggregate of formations-clinging, and the aggregate of consciousness-clinging.
Great King, you should know this!
Based on these five dharmas, one speaks of "sentient beings" and the "receptacle world.
Regarding the explanation of sentient beings, it refers to the inclusion of the four modes of birth:
birth from eggs, birth from a womb, birth from moisture, and birth by transformation.
"To speak of the vessel-world (bhājana-loka) means to include space, earth, water, fire,
and wind. The King said,
"Great Master!"
"Who is able to protect all these sentient beings?
Who is able to sustain this receptacle world? He replied:
"Great King! All this is the karmic retribution of sentient beings themselves, as well as the sovereign power of Your Majesty’s kingdom to provide protection.
The king asked again:
“Great Teacher!
How can the retribution of one’s own karma protect sentient beings? He replied:
"Great King! There are sentient beings who, by the power of the superior karmic fruit of their own actions, are born in an exalted place.

Those beings harbor no sense of stinginess or possessiveness toward any object; they give rise to no notions of 'mine' or 'yours,' nor of 'self' or 'other. All necessities for life appear to them spontaneously and without effort, exactly as they think of them. They dwell throughout their lives in peace and happiness, free from the pains of coarse illness, cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and various afflictions. They have no malicious intent to harm one another, nor do they harbor deceitful or false thoughts. Their villages and cities are adorned with the seven treasures, and they constantly experience the sublime realm of excellent pleasures and exquisite tactile sensations. When their thousand-year lifespan is fulfilled and they cast off their bodies, they are reborn in the heavenly realms, the good paths, where they enjoy bliss."
Thus, it is said that in the northern continent of Uttarakuru, sentient beings are protected by their karma.

Great King, you should know that there are further sentient beings who, by the power of the retribution of their own karma, are born in a superior and sublime place; they possess bodily radiance, soar through the void, dwell in the bliss of meditative joy as their food, do not enter a womb for birth, have immeasurable lifespans, and remain in the world for a vast duration—these are what are called the sentient beings of the beginning of the eon.

Great King, you should know that there are further sentient beings who, by virtue of the power of their past merit as a superior cause for their own karmic retribution, are born into this world. They possess a heart of reverence and respect for their parents, family elders, and all śramaṇas and practitioners of purity whom they regard as fields of merit. They constantly practice wholesome deeds, perform what ought to be done, and fear unwholesome conduct. They always properly observe the five precepts and the eight precepts, and they practice giving to accumulate various merits.
This refers to the beings of virtuous roots during the second period at the beginning of the kalpa.

Great King, you should know that at that time, the roots of virtue of sentient beings were fully matured and they did not give rise to any evils; therefore, no royal laws had yet been established in the world. This is what is meant by saying that the retribution of one's own karma is able to protect sentient beings.
The King said: "Great Master!
I have now fully understood how such karma protects me."
"What is meant by saying that the sovereign power of a national king is able to protect sentient beings?
He replied, "Great King!"
"Various kings are lords of sentient beings, and by their power they are able to protect sentient beings.
The King said, "Great Master!"
"For what reason are those various kings called 'kings'? He replied, "Great King!"
A king is the parent of the people; because he is able to gather and protect sentient beings in accordance with the Dharma, bringing them peace and happiness, he is called a king.
Great King, you should know this!
A king’s nourishing of the people should be like that toward an infant; he should provide dryness and remove dampness without waiting for their words. Why is this?
Great King, you should know!
A ruler who succeeds in establishing his reign does so by taking the people as his state;
if the hearts of the people are not at peace, the state will fall into peril.
Therefore, a ruler must always cherish the people with the same concern he has for an infant, never allowing them to depart from his mind.

One should know the suffering and happiness of the people within the realm, and act with timely composure; one should know of floods and droughts, know of winds and rains, know of harvests and failures, know of abundance and scarcity, know of presence and absence, know of sorrow and joy, know of the old and the young, know of the sick and the healthy, know of various lawsuits, know of the guilty and the innocent, and know of the light and the heavy [offenses]; likewise, among the princes, ministers, and officials, one should know those who have merit and those who have none—one who knows in this manner is said to be "not separated from the mind."
"Great King, you should know this!
Having understood these matters within your kingdom, you should protect them with your power; that which ought to be given, provide it in a timely manner;
and that which ought to be taken, you should reflect upon and deliberate before doing so."
Employing laborers at the proper time so as not to deprive the people of their interests;
strictly prohibiting greed and violence so that the people may attain peace and happiness—this is called protection, and such a person is termed a king.
"Great King, you should know that there are four kinds of kings:
first, the Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin);..."
Second, the minor king; third, the next-minor king;
fourth, the frontier king.

Regarding the Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin): there is a kind of Wheel-Turning King known as the consecrated Kṣatriya who governs the four frontiers; he is uniquely honored, most excellent, and a Dharma-King who protects the Dharma. That Wheel-Turning King is endowed with the seven treasures.
What are the seven treasures?
First, the treasure of the queen;
second, the treasure of the mani-jewel;
Third, the wheel-treasure;
fourth, the elephant-treasure;
fifth, the horse-treasure;
Sixth is the minister-treasure;
seventh is the steward-treasure.
Thus, that wheel-turning king is fully endowed with these seven treasures; as he traverses the great earth, there is no opposition, no enmity or malice, no afflictions, and no weapons of war.
"Relying upon the True Dharma, you are impartial and without bias, providing consolation and subduing [the wicked].
The King said: "Great Master!"
"What is meant by a Wheel-Turning Sage King governing the four frontiers?
He replied, "Great King!"
"Because you have attained mastery over the four continents as their king.
The King said, "Great Master!"
"What is meant by being 'solely honored and most supreme'? He replied, "Great King!
"Because the commands issued do not encounter opposition.
The King said: "Great Master!"
"What is the protection of the Dharma? He replied, "Great King!"
"To cultivate the ten wholesome dharmas and not allow unwholesome dharmas such as killing to destroy them is called 'protecting the Dharma.
The King said, "Great Master!"
"What is a Dharma King? He replied, "Great King!"

The Wheel-Turning Sage King transforms the four continents by means of the ten paths of wholesome action, causing all beings to receive and uphold them, to abandon the ten unwholesome actions, and to practice the ten paths of wholesome action until they are fully perfected; thus he is called a Dharma King.
The king said: "Great Master!
By what cause does that wheel-turning monarch obtain the first jewel, the queen?"
"How is it accomplished? He replied, "Great King!"

Because the Wheel-Turning Sage King relies on his departure from the unwholesome karma of a hateful mind, he obtains a Queen-Jewel who stands in relation to him, experiencing the most supreme bliss; this is called "accomplishment."
“What is meant by ‘experiencing the most supreme bliss’?

Great King, you should know that from the body of the Cakravartin’s queen, there constantly issues the wondrous fragrance of priceless sandalwood; from her mouth, there constantly issues the priceless fragrance of the *utpala* lotus; and her body is as soft and supple as that of the *kalaviṅka* bird. When the *kalaviṅka* dwells on the islands of the great ocean, if any sentient beings touch that *kalaviṅka*, they immediately become free from all physical fatigue, as well as hunger, thirst, and all sorrows and afflictions, experiencing the foremost and unsurpassed bliss. The bliss experienced by the Cakravartin Queen upon seeing him is likewise so.”
"Great King, you should know this!
When that lady’s body is cold, it can provide warmth; when it is hot, it can provide coolness. There is no one in the world whose hand can touch that lady’s body."

Why is this? Because, having abandoned unwholesome paths of action through a mind free from greed and relying on the cause of wholesome roots, all sentient beings observe and revere her as they would a mother, a daughter, or a sister. Furthermore, that lady gives rise to three kinds of thoughts toward the wheel-turning king. What are these three?
First, her mind constantly honors and serves the king, never giving rise to any other thought.
Second, his mind is always respectful toward the king;
third, his mind is constantly mindful of the wheel-turning monarch. Why is this?
This is because the King is able to remain free from the defilement of a greedy mind. "Furthermore, Great King,
the Woman-Jewel of the Wheel-Turning Sage King is free from the five kinds of evil qualities of women."
What are the five?
First, to be free from the mind of fickle frivolity that lacks resolve regarding women;
second, to be free from the mind of craving for other men.
Third, they are free from the mind of stinginess, envy, and jealousy;
fourth, they are free from the perverted mind that gives rise to craving for improper objects;
fifth, when the life of the Wheel-Turning Sage King comes to an end, they likewise come to an end together with him.
"Furthermore, Great King,
that Jewel of a Consort possesses five kinds of merit. What are these five?
First, her thoughts shall never conflict with the King's mind;
second, she shall give birth to a thousand sons endowed with all perfections;
third, her lineage shall naturally be noble and illustrious.
Fourth, he is able to cause his dwelling place to be fully provided with all necessities of life;
fifth, when the king enjoys sensual pleasures with various women, he does not give rise to jealousy, malice, or evil thoughts.
"Furthermore, Great King,
the queen of that Wheel-turning King is endowed with three kinds of merit.
What are these three?
First, to be free from harsh speech;
second, to be free from wrong views;
third, even if a king engages in other activities within the realm of the five desires, they are unable to disturb his mind.
"Great King, you should know that when the wife of a Wheel-Turning Sage King relinquishes her body, she is reborn in the heavens. Why is this?"
"Because she is free from greed and envy, these are called the meritorious qualities of the wife of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, which cause the king to experience the most supreme and sublime bliss.
The king said, "Great Master!"
“By what cause does a Wheel-Turning Sage King obtain that maṇi jewel?
He replied, “Great King!”

Because the Wheel-Turning Sage King relies on his departure from the unwholesome karma of a hateful mind, he obtains that second maṇi-jewel, whereby he receives the most excellent light and the unsurpassed joy of the necessities of life.
“What is most excellent?
“Great King, you should know that the maṇi-jewel of a wheel-turning sage king possesses eight kinds of merit.”
What are the eight? First, as for its merit:

that mani-jewel emits great radiance in the darkness of night, like the full moon in autumn; its light can illuminate a hundred yojanas. Furthermore, when sentient beings suffer from the heat during the summer days, they obtain coolness when the light emitted by the mani-jewel touches their bodies.

Regarding the second merit: when a wheel-turning sage king travels through a wilderness devoid of water and sentient beings suffer from hunger and thirst, the maṇi jewel emits water endowed with the eight kinds of flavor and all virtues, thereby satisfying their hunger and thirst.
The third merit is that whatever the Wheel-Turning Sage King requires, all of it emerges from the maṇi jewel.
The fourth merit is that this maṇi jewel has eight facets; from each facet emerge various kinds of light, namely blue, yellow, red, white, crystal, crimson, and purple.

The fifth merit is that wherever this mani jewel is located, it can cause all sentient beings within a hundred yojanas to be free from the suffering of illness and to constantly attain a concentrated mind, ensuring that no wholesome karma they perform goes to waste.

Regarding the sixth merit: within the sphere where that maṇi-jewel resides, there are no malevolent nāgas capable of emitting poisonous vapors, nor hail, wind, or malicious rain to harm sentient beings.

The seventh merit is that all mountains, rivers, valleys, gullies, streams, and springs that have dried up are made to flow again; forests, grasses, trees, flowers, and fruits that have withered are made to flourish; and lotus ponds and their flowers and groves are all made complete.
The eighth merit is that wherever that mani-jewel is located, the people will have no epidemics, poisons, or untimely deaths;
even as for the animals—tigers, wolves, lions, snakes, rats, cats, wildcats, weasels, hawks, and falcons—that prey upon one another, they will not give rise to harmful intentions.

"Furthermore, Great King, the Wheel-Turning Sage King possesses a full thousand sons who are physically robust, courageous, and heroic; they subdue the world, obey the king’s commands, are able to protect the Great Dharma, and act in accordance with the practice of the Dharma. Their hearts are filled with compassion for all sentient beings. This is called the function of the wheel-turning sage king’s maṇi jewel, which enables the king to experience the most supreme and excellent bliss."
The king said: "Great Master!
By what cause does a Wheel-Turning Sage King obtain the third treasure, the wheel?"
He replied, "Great King!

Because the Wheel-Turning Sage King relies on his departure from the unwholesome karma of a hateful mind, he obtains that wheel-treasure; wherever he dwells, all are naturally subdued, and he attains great, supreme bliss."
The king said: "Great Master!
What is meant by 'attaining great and supreme bliss'?"
“Great King, you should know that the wheel-treasure possessed by a Wheel-Turning Sage King is fully endowed with five kinds of meritorious qualities.
What are these five?
Regarding the first merit: the substance of that wheel-treasure is pure Jambūnada gold; it possesses a thousand spokes and is five yojanas in width, appearing in the world like a second sun.
The second merit is that when the wheel-treasure flies through the void, nothing can obstruct it, and it can travel eight thousand *yojanas* in a single day.

The third merit is that it accords with the King’s mental inclinations; whenever the Wheel-turning King desires to go to the four continents of the Four Heavenly Kings—namely, Jambudvīpa in the south, Aparagoyānī in the west, Uttarakuru in the north, and Pūrvavideha in the east—the wheel-treasure immediately flies through the void and proceeds ahead according to the King’s thoughts. By the power of that wheel, the fourfold army—elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—all likewise fly up and follow along.

Regarding the fourth merit: as for those who do not submit to the Wheel-Turning King, if the king forms a thought in his mind, that wheel-treasure flies to the place he intends and brings them all into submission.

Regarding the five merits: the power of that wheel-treasure is without rival; all minor kings who behold it are subdued. Because the Universal Monarch practices according to the Dharma and is free from a mind of anger, this is called the function of the wheel-treasure of the Wheel-turning Sage King, which causes the king to experience the most supreme great bliss.
The king said: "Great Master!
By what cause does a Wheel-Turning Sage King obtain the fourth treasure, the elephant?"
He replied: "Great King!

Because the Wheel-Turning Sage King relies upon his departure from the unwholesome karma of a hateful mind, he obtains the elephant-treasure and experiences the bliss of the foremost and most excellent vehicle."
The King said: "Great Master!
What is meant by the bliss of the supreme vehicle?"
“Great King, you should know that this Great Elephant Treasure is like a fine horse— tamed, gentle, and compliant with one’s will— to subjugate other kingdoms.”

Its seven limbs are well-established—namely, the four feet, the head, the trunk, and the tail—and these seven parts possess great power, capable of withstanding a thousand ordinary elephants; it is as white as solidified snow.
For example, O Great King, among all ordinary elephants, none can come forward to sniff the scent of Śakra’s elephant, Airāvaṇa.
That elephant possesses sovereign mastery in three places: namely, in the sky, in water, and on land.
"Great King!
That elephant can travel with great speed, circling Jambudvīpa three times in a single day.
Great King, you should know this!"

As for that elephant king ridden by the Wheel-Turning King, at that time the elephant king was of one mind with the king; wherever the king directed his thoughts, the elephant would immediately follow. Its gait was level and upright like that of a king of geese—neither too fast nor too slow, neither crooked nor perverse. When walking among ordinary people, it did not cause them alarm or fear; even when women touched it, its heart felt no anger or agitation.
When it comes time for battle, it can manifest extremely fierce and harmful forms that cannot be approached.

Whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, eating, or being bound, it can be pulled, led, or drawn by even a single thread; it follows commands without fail. This is called the function of the elephant-treasure of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, which enables the king to experience the bliss of the most supreme vehicle.
The king said: "Great Master!
By what cause does a Wheel-Turning Sage King obtain the fifth treasure, the horse-treasure?"
He replied: "Great King!
Because the Wheel-Turning Sage King relies on his departure from the unwholesome karma of a hateful mind, he obtains that Horse Treasure and experiences the supreme joy of the swiftest vehicle."
The king said, "Great Master!
In what way is it swift?"
"Great King, you should know!

As for that horse-treasure, its color is white like the *kumuda* flower, and its body is covered with the patterns of celestial wheels. It is neither too large nor too small, neither too tall nor too short; its physical form is perfectly proportioned, its nature is gentle, and it is well-trained. Like the horse Vaḍavā of King Śakra, it goes and stays according to its will, traversing Jambudvīpa three times in a single day without any sense of fatigue."

"Great King, you should know that such is the utility of the horse-treasure of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, which enables the King to experience the supreme bliss of the most swift and excellent vehicle."
The king said, "Great Master!
By what cause does a Wheel-Turning Sage King obtain the sixth treasure, the minister-treasure?"
He replied: "Great King!

The Wheel-Turning Sage King, by relying on the abandonment of a mind of anger, obtains the treasure of the minister, which allows the king to travel at ease and enjoy the supreme bliss of being free from affairs."
The king said: "Great Master!
What is this supreme bliss of non-action?"

"Great King, you should know! That minister governs affairs on behalf of the King exactly according to the King’s own mind. He is concerned for the state and forgets his own person; he does not attend to private matters, but cherishes and protects the common people as if nurturing his own two eyes. Following whatever the King intends, he accomplishes it immediately; he is neither obstructed nor attached. He practices the Right Path, remains far from what is contrary to the Dharma, and at all times and in all places, he does not commit harm or injury. Relying correctly upon the King’s commands, he practices the ten wholesome dharmas (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*), never deviating from virtuous conduct, never deviating from that which accords with the Dharma, and never deviating from the meaning of that which accords with the Dharma—able to fulfill them all."
"Great King, you should know that this is what is called the function of the wheel-turning sage king’s precious minister; it enables the king to experience the foremost, supreme bliss.
The king said:
“Great Master!
By what cause does a Wheel-Turning Sage King obtain the seventh treasure, the Lord of the Treasury? He replied:

"Great King! Because the Wheel-Turning Sage King relies on his departure from the unwholesome karma of a hateful mind, he obtains the treasure of the steward, which fulfills the king's wishes and allows him to receive peace and happiness."
The king said: "Great Master!
How does one fulfill and experience peaceful happiness?"

“Great King, you should know that the Treasure of the Steward possesses great merit. All mountains, deep gullies, secluded valleys, wildernesses, marshes, hills, mounds, pits, and uneven places—high and low—he is able to fill with all kinds of rare treasures, such as vajra-jewels, indra-nīla jewels, mārakata jewels, and agate jewels; yet these jewels are never exhausted, let alone gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, which are not even counted among them.”

That Lord of the Treasure Store is always joyful at heart; he is free from the mark of crookedness and free from the mark of duplicity; he does not give rise to affliction in others, and all who see him find their hearts filled with joy.
"Great King, you should know!
This is what is called the function of the Wheel-Turning Sage-King’s Treasure of the Steward, which causes the king to fulfill all his wishes and enjoyments.
Great King, you should know!"

Because the Wheel-Turning Sage King is endowed with these seven treasures, he rules over the four continents as well as the various dragon kings and the two kinds of celestial kings—namely, those of the four continents and the Heaven of the Thirty-three—together with Śakra, the Lord of Devas, sharing his seat. By relying on his departure from even a single instance of resentment, malice, or unwholesome path of action, he has attained such a complete set of the seven treasures and enjoys supreme bliss; how much more so, then, for one who fully practices the ten paths of wholesome action!
“Great King, you should know!
A Wheel-Turning Sage King further possesses seven kinds of so-called ‘soft jewels,’ whose merits are slightly inferior to those of the previous seven jewels.
What are these seven?
First, the sword treasure;
second, the leather treasure;
third, the bed treasure.
Fourth, the treasure of gardens;
fifth, the treasure of dwellings;
sixth, the treasure of garments.
"Seventh, there is the jewel for the feet.
The King said, "Great Master!"
"What is the first sword-treasure of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, and what is its function?
"Great King, you should know!

As for that sword-treasure, within the realm ruled by the Wheel-Turning Sage King, if there is anyone who thinks of disobeying the King’s command, the sword-treasure will immediately fly through the air to that person's location. Upon seeing it, those minor kings will submit and prostrate themselves before the sword-treasure to inquire after it. Yet, that sword-treasure does not give rise to a murderous intent nor harm a single sentient being; this is called the merit of the Wheel-Turning Sage King’s sword-treasure, whereby no weapons or blades are employed throughout all the lands, and all naturally comply."
“Great Teacher! What is the second precious hide of a Wheel-Turning Sage King?
“Great King, you should know this!”

As for the leather-treasure possessed by that wheel-turning king, it is the skin of the ocean dragon king produced from within the great ocean, which is brought forth and offered to the noble wheel-turning king by a maritime merchant leader.

That skin-treasure is five *yojanas* wide and ten *yojanas* long; its substance is pure and bright, shining as brightly as the sun. Fire cannot burn it, and water cannot rot it. Even when fierce winds topple mountains, they cannot move it. Its body contains both warmth and coolness, capable of warding off cold and heat. Wherever the King goes, the skin-treasure follows. Covering the entire retinue of the Wheel-turning King for ten *yojanas*, it serves as dwellings, providing sufficient housing for all the people. Each person obtains a separate house without obstructing one another; such are the meritorious functions of the skin-treasure.
“Great Teacher! What is the third precious bed of a Wheel-Turning Sage King?
“Great King, you should know this!”

The bed-jewel belonging to that wheel-turning king, when set up, stands level, upright, stable, and immovable; it is neither high nor low, neither broad nor narrow, neither long nor short, neither sunken nor mounded, neither hard nor soft, neither rough nor slippery, being supple and perfectly suited.
If the king enters meditative absorption while seated upon that precious throne, he immediately enters the samādhi of liberation;
if the king wishes to give rise to thoughts of greed, hatred, or delusion, these are instantly extinguished as soon as he sits upon that precious throne.
When women see the king seated upon the precious throne, they all become free from thoughts of greed, hatred, and delusion. This is called the functional efficacy of the merit of the precious throne.
“Great Teacher! What is the fourth jewel-garden of a Wheel-Turning Sage King?
“Great King, you should know this!”
When that Wheel-Turning King wishes to enter meditative concentration, as soon as he enters that garden, he attains a concentrated mind.

If the king wishes to enjoy the pleasures of the five senses, upon entering that garden, by virtue of the merit of the wholesome deeds performed by the king, all the delightful things found in the celestial realms—flowers, fruits, birds, springs, flowing streams, ponds, rivers, music, song, dance, and instruments of play—all naturally vanish from those heavens and appear before the king.
"At that time, the Wheel-Turning King likewise enjoys various sensual pleasures just like the devas; this is called the functional efficacy of the merit of the Jewel of the Garden. "Great Teacher!
What is the fifth jewel of the noble Wheel-Turning King, the Jewel of the Palace?"
"Great King, you should know this!
If that Wheel-Turning King enters that house and wishes to see the sun, the moon, and those various constellations, he sees them all within that very house;
he sees all the various and extraordinary precious curiosities of those celestial palaces without any obstruction."
The music performed by those gods within their palaces is heard everywhere;
immediately freed from sorrow, affliction, and all fatigue, they experience supreme bliss even in their sleep.
During his sleep, he saw various wondrous and auspicious signs in a dream:
in the cold season there was a warm breeze, soft, fragrant, and beautiful;
in the hot season there was a cool breeze, refreshing and pleasant, providing the joy of delightful touch.

During the second watch of the night one sleeps; during the third watch one rises, distancing oneself from sleep and arising to experience the joy of the Dharma; during the fourth watch one preaches the Dharma to teach and transform others—this is called the functional utility of the merit of the jewel of the householder.
“Great Teacher! What is the sixth treasure of the Wheel-Turning Sage King, the robe-treasure?
“Great King, you should know this!”

As for the clothing-jewel possessed by that wheel-turning king, it is unlike any silk cloth or thread in the world; its patterns run both lengthwise and crosswise, it is the most supple of all things, and no dust or grime can stain it. Upon wearing that precious garment, one immediately becomes free from cold and heat, hunger and thirst, illness and emaciation, grief and affliction, and extreme exhaustion.
"Great King, you should know that this precious garment cannot be burned by fire, cannot be cut by a blade, and cannot be rotted by water; such are the functional merits of this precious garment."
“Great Teacher! What is the precious jewel used for the feet of a Wheel-Turning Sage King?
“Great King, you should know this!”

The jewels used for the feet of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin) refer to items such as boots; if the king wears them, he does not sink when wading through water, as if walking upon dry land, nor is he burned when entering fire, as if in a cool, refreshing pool.

When the king wishes to travel abroad to enjoy the pleasures of walking, even though he journeys for hundreds of thousands of yojanas, he does not feel exhausted; this is called the functional merit of the foot-jewel.

"Great King! These are called the seven kinds of soft jewels of a Wheel-Turning Sage King; they are the fruit and retribution of a small portion of the habitual tendencies from the ten wholesome deeds, not yet the full perfection of the ten paths of wholesome karma."
The King said: "Great Master!
What is meant by 'wandering everywhere across the great earth without any rival'?"
What is meant by "being without thorns"?
What is meant by "being without afflictions"?
What is meant by "being without weapons"?
What is meant by relying on the True Dharma?
What is equanimity?
And what is meant by comforting and subduing?
He replied: "Great King!
He who traverses the entire earth has no rival, for he has attained mastery over the whole earth."
"Free from thorns" means being without the thorns of adversaries and enemies who act with malice.
"Free from afflictions" means not coercing or intimidating others through the use of forceful power.
"Free from weapons" means remaining apart from weapons and not inflicting harm.
To rely on the True Dharma means to depart from unrighteous greed, hatred, and delusion, thereby causing one to practice the True Dharma and transforming ignorance and darkness.
Equanimity means to bestow equal compassion upon all sentient beings, like thinking of them as one's only child, without partiality or favoritism.
He comforts and subdues others because he causes other kings and sentient beings to dwell peacefully in their respective abodes, neither displaced nor deprived. Why is this?
Great King, you should know!
When a Wheel-Turning Sage King rules over the four continents, there are various minor kings in all the cities and towns throughout those lands and regions.
Those minor kings go out to welcome the Wheel-Turning King and speak these words:
"Great King, you should know!"

This great earth is thus secure, thus fulfilled, thus abundant, thus blissful, and thus free from disease; clothing and food are obtained spontaneously, and there is no suffering or affliction. It is filled with many sentient beings, people, elephants, and horses, all of whom are fully satisfied. All of this belongs to the Great Heavenly Holy King, who enjoys it according to his will.
"We shall follow the Great King's commands and dare not disobey.
Then the Wheel-Turning King addressed the kings, saying:
"You kings, each of you should establish peace in your own kingdoms; I have come for your sake, not for the sake of territories."
"You all should conduct your governance in accordance with the True Dharma and not rely on false teachings; rely on an impartial mind and do not rely on a biased one.
If within your kingdom any false teachings arise, you must swiftly eliminate them; this would be compliance with my command, and it shall be considered that you have truly received your kingdom.
If you do not eliminate them, I shall inflict upon you the most severe and grievous punishment."
"Great King, you should know that this is what is called the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) protecting all sentient beings.
As for the minor kings— namely the regional kings, the subordinate regional kings, and the frontier kings— those two types of kings comply with the commands and edicts of the Universal Monarch."
"Great King, you should know that this is what is called a great king, the ruler of the land, transforming sentient beings. The King said:
“Great Master!
By what dharma do other minor kings govern their countries and nourish their people so as to act in accordance with the Dharma? He replied:

“Great King! As for the various minor kings, they rely on the principles of royal treatises to govern their nations through the Way and protect all sentient beings—with the exception of the Wheel-Turning Kings. Why is this?

When a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, at that time sentient beings are free from all unwholesome and evil desires, free from perverted craving, and free from minds of false views; in each of those various kingdoms, there are no unlawful hunters or the like.

Why is this? Because by relying on the Dharma-king’s law, they clearly discern transgression and merit; their minds are neither deluded nor distressed, and they harbor no doubt regarding the Dharma. Thus, their actions accord with principle, and they do not give rise to faults or errors.

"Great King, you should know that this is what is called a Wheel-Turning Sage King protecting that world through the power of his own karma and merit; at such a time, the various minor kings cease all their deliberations and do not act.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Great Śākyeya Nirgrantha-putra, Fascicle Three.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Great Śākyeya Nirgrantha-putra, Fascicle Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Five, Part Two: Discourse on the Two Kings.
The two kings said: “Great Master!
"At what time do the various minor kings practice the dharma of royal discourse?
He replied, "Great King!"

In the final age, when the Wheel-Turning Sage Kings have vanished and no longer appear, when the True Dharma is not practiced and false dharmas flourish in competition, sentient beings give rise to three kinds of faults from their evil minds:
first, a greedy mind that delights in what is contrary to the Dharma;
second, a perverted greedy mind; [and third, a greedy mind that covets the property of others].
Third, their minds are entangled in the net of false teachings.

Those minor kings themselves lack wisdom and have lost their clear understanding; therefore, the sages have expounded the treatises on statecraft for minor kings so that they may practice the True Dharma and protect the sentient beings of the world.
The King said: "Great Master!
What is meant by 'a mind that delights in unrighteous greed'?"
He replied: "Great King!
To give rise to a mind of pleasure within the ten unwholesome paths of action—this is called delighting in a mind of greed for what is contrary to the Dharma."
“What is called a perverted mind of greed?

When one has obtained various means of livelihood through the strength of one’s own hands, acquired them according to the proper seasons, acquired them through the True Dharma, and acquired them in accordance with the Dharma, yet one does not give rise to a sense of contentment and further seeks the wealth of others—this is called a perverted mind of greed.”
The king said: "Great Master!
What is meant by 'the mind being entangled by the net of false dharmas'?"
He replied: "Great King!
You have conceived the notion that there is meaningful discourse within the non-meaningful discourses of the various external paths."
To conceive the notion of benefit regarding useless discourse;
to conceive the notion that what is not the Dharma is the Dharma;

and in this degenerate age, to regard treatises composed by those who are not wise as authentic scriptures, to give rise to faith in them, and to cultivate wrong views while considering them to be merit—this is called being entangled in the net of false dharmas.
The King said: "Great Master!

By what dharma is the 'Discourse on Kings' (Rājanīti) defined, such that all minor kings may rely upon that discourse to govern their countries and manage their people, thereby being called those who are able to protect sentient beings in accordance with the Dharma?"
He replied, “Great King!
It is by being free from all perverted thoughts of craving.”
One is free from all inverted states of mind characterized by hatred;
one is free from all inverted states of mind characterized by delusion, by relying on the antidote, the essential nature, the distinctions, and the benefit.

Regarding the basis of the antidote and the basis of the essential substance: with respect to the factors to be countered, these are called the wholesome roots of non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
How can the factors to be remedied and the remedial factors be brought forth? The factors to be remedied are:
a heedless mind and a lack of compassion.

As for the factors that serve as remedies, they are as follows: a king who practices the Dharma possesses a mind of non-negligence and great compassion; he knows that the body is impermanent and that the necessities of life are impermanent. He skillfully observes his own body, perceives its various faults, and understands them as they truly are. Thus, he remains detached from the enjoyment of material resources. Although this king who practices the Dharma has attained sovereign power, he does not engage in unrighteousness; this is what is called a "mind of non-negligence."
"Great King, you should know!
According to the principles of the treatises on kingship, one should not accept what ought not to be obtained; even if it is obtained, one should not take it.
As for that which ought to be obtained, one must not dare to take it at an improper time."
If one obtains items that are rightfully due according to the season, one should take them from the poor without causing them distress.

When faced with times of famine, banditry, rebellion, or mutual conflict—during such times of calamity—one should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and, without avoiding personal danger, protect all sentient beings.
To bestow clothing and food upon the poor, and to instruct those who act wickedly in the wholesome Dharma—this is called a compassionate mind.

Great King, you should know that by relying on these two dharmas, one is termed a king who practices the Dharma; such a king rightly protects sentient beings with a mind free from negligence and a heart of great compassion.
The king said: "Great Master!
A king who practices the Dharma possesses a heart of compassion; how, then, can he govern those sentient beings who engage in evil conduct?"
He replied: "Great King!

If that Dharma-practicing king wishes to govern those beings of evil conduct, he must first give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, observe with wisdom, and contemplate five dharmas; only then should he govern them."
What are the five? First, relying on what is real rather than what is unreal;
second, relying on the proper time rather than the improper time.
Third, relying on the meaning rather than what is meaningless;
fourth, relying on gentle speech rather than harsh speech;
fifth, relying on a mind of loving-kindness rather than a mind of anger.
The king said: "Great Master!
How is it that one relies on what is real and not on what is unreal?"
He replied: "Great King!

To interrogate according to the Dharma, to elicit their own words, and to punish them based on actual transgressions rather than on what is untrue—this is called relying on the real and not on the unreal."
The king said: "Great Master!
In what way does one rely on the proper time and not on the improper time?"
He replied, “Great King!
When the King possesses power, if one disobeys his command, that person should be punished for their crime.”
"If the king lacks the power, one should desist and not treat him; this is called acting at the proper time, not at an improper time.
The king said, "Great Master!"
"What is meant by 'relying on the meaning and not on what is meaningless'? He replied, "Great King!"
One should question the person as to what state of mind gave rise to the offense.
If it arose from an evil mind, they should be punished according to the law;
if it did not arise from an evil mind, they should not be punished for the offense. This is called relying on the meaning rather than the literal expression.
The King said: "Great Master!
What is speech that is gentle and not harsh?"
He replied: "Great King!

You know that these sentient beings have committed offenses against the royal law; they should merely be rebuked and not subjected to other punishments. You should speak of their transgressions truthfully without concealment, and address them with well-spoken words of admonition."
"To reprimand in this manner is not a failure to reprimand; it is called gentle speech, not coarse or harsh speech.
The King said, "Great Master!"
"What is meant by a mind of loving-kindness and not a mind of anger? He replied, "Great King!"

The wise know that this is not merely for the sake of reprimand, but to sever such transgressions. Apart from depriving one of life, one must not cut off the hands, feet, eyes, ears, nose, or tongue. Relying upon a mind of great loving-kindness and great compassion, one may permit imprisonment, shackling, binding, various forms of reprimand, the confiscation of livelihoods, or banishment to another region; however, these are done to induce repentance and reform, never out of a malicious intent to abandon sentient beings. This is called a compassionate mind, not a mind of anger.
The king said, "Great Master!

How can a king who practices the Dharma thus cause suffering to other sentient beings— imprisoning, beating, binding, and banishing them to other regions— and yet still claim to possess a heart of compassion?"
"These two dharmas are contradictory.
How, then, can one be called a king who practices the Dharma?
At that time, Mahāsatyaka Nirgrantha replied:
"Great King! Regarding this matter, I shall now provide you with a parable.
Great King, you should know this!"

For example, when parents deal with a child who has committed evil deeds, because they cherish their child, they wish to cause them to repent and reform. They employ skillful means to discipline the child through hardship, provided that they do not deprive the child of life nor destroy their sense faculties. Beyond this, they may subject the child to various forms of suffering according to their judgment, such as beating or scolding; yet this is not called a heart of abandonment, nor a heart of malice, nor a heart of vexation. This is because their regard for their child is profound, and they act in order to cause the child to repent and never commit such acts again.
Furthermore, those parents are not said to be acting contrary to the Dharma; rather, they are said to be mindful of their child and do not lose their heart of loving-kindness.
"Great King, you should know this!"

The King who practices the Dharma likewise governs all sentient beings of evil conduct in this same way. Because his compassionate heart is profound, he acts to cause them to repent and reform; he does not deprive them of life nor destroy their sense faculties.
