"Excessive heedlessness can obstruct the dharmas of śamatha and vipaśyanā; this fault of frivolous laughter is a cause for rebirth in the evil realms.
Then he spoke in verse:
"When the mind is defiled by frivolous laughter, The mind does not abide in samādhi."
Rebuked by the wise, one who practices virtue does not attain liberation.
If you wish to obtain swift benefit, you should abandon all negligence;
for in this present life there will be no peace, and you will lose your reputation and merit.
The King said: "Great Master!
Are there any other sentient beings in the world who are exceptionally intelligent, possessed of great wisdom, keen faculties, and sagacity, yet still have faults and transgressions?"
He replied: "Great King! There are such sentient beings, and they do indeed have transgressions."
The king said: "Great Master!
Who, among these sentient beings, is such a one?"
He replied, “Great King!
This King Prasenajit of the kingdom of Kośala is intelligent and of great wisdom, keen-witted and sagacious, yet he possesses faults.”
The King said, "Great Master!
What were the transgressions of that King Prasenajit?"
He replied, “Great King! This King Prasenajit has eaten to excess.”
"Great King, you should know that a wise person should not eat to excess. Why is this?"
Great King, you should know this:

one who eats to excess finds the body difficult to move; they become lazy and indolent, and what they have eaten is hard to digest. Such a person is far removed from the benefits of wholesome dharmas in both the present and future lives.
And he spoke in verse:
"One who eats to excess Becomes heavy-bodied and full of indolence;
In both the present and future lives, They lose great benefit for their own person."
"Sleeping brings suffering upon oneself and also troubles others;
one becomes dazed and finds it difficult to wake from it. Therefore, one should measure one's food according to the occasion.
The King said:
“Great Master!
Are there perhaps other sentient beings in the world who are clever, possessed of great wisdom, of sharp faculties, and sagacious, yet still have faults? He replied:
“Great King! There are such sentient beings who also possess transgressions.
The king said:
“Great Master!
Who among these sentient beings is such a one? He replied:

“Great King! This sentient being is none other than your own self. Great King, you too are exceedingly clever and possessed of great wisdom; you have sharp faculties and discernment, great power, and a mind free from cowardice. You delight in giving and are fully endowed with majestic virtue, yet you also possess faults.”
The king said, "Great Master! What are my transgressions?"
He replied: “Great King!
Your Majesty’s transgression is exceedingly violent and evil; Your Majesty is too severe, Your Majesty is too negligent, Your Majesty is too harsh, and Your Majesty is too precipitate.”
"Great King, you should know that a wise person ought not to be excessively wicked. Why is this?"
"Great King, you should know this!

If a king or a prince is by nature too wicked, he will be disapproved of by many people, unloved by many people, and disliked by many people; even his own parents will not take pleasure in seeing him, let alone others such as ministers, princes, elders, and householders. Therefore, Great King, a wise person should not be too wicked."
"Great King, you should know that when a wise person intends to perform an action, they should proceed with composure and not in too great a hurry.
And he spoke this verse:
"If a king practices evil deeds, his mind clouded by anger,
he terrifies all living beings with every movement; even his parents fear him,
let alone others who are not kin— how could they ever feel affection for him?"
"Great King, you should know that the wise abandon anger.

At that time, King Ugratejas sat facing him; hearing the Great Śākyan Nirgrantha disparage himself, he felt intolerance, anger, resentment, and vexation in his heart. Deprived of joy, he conceived a mind of malice and spoke these words:
"Śākyan Nirgrantha!..."
Why do you now speak of my faults and evils before this great assembly and revile me?
Since time immemorial, no one has dared to look directly upon my face; for you to revile me now, your crime deserves the death penalty.
Having spoken these words, with a mind of malice, he addressed his ministers, saying:
"You must seize this foolish śramaṇa who utters such unpleasant speech and take his life."
At that time, Satyaka the Nirgrantha was struck with such terror that his hair stood on end.
He said to King Ugratejas:
"Great King!..."
Do not now hastily commit such an evil deed, which will bring me no benefit!
I have wholesome words to offer; I pray that Your Majesty will grant me safety for a moment and listen to what I have to say.
The king said, "Śramaṇa!
I grant you fearlessness; whatever you wish to say, you should speak it quickly."
Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha said:
"Great King, you should know that I, too, am guilty."
The king said, "Śramaṇa! What is your offense?"
Saccaka the Nirgrantha said:
"Great King, you should know this:

my fault lies in speaking words that are too true, words that are not false, and words that accord with reality; for I spoke such truthful words before one such as myself—an evil person, a terrifying person, a person of quick temper, a person devoid of compassion, a person who acts impulsively, and a person of such wicked conduct."
"Great King, you should know that a wise person should not always speak truthful words at all times and in all places. Why is this?"
Because it would not be beneficial.
Your Majesty, you should know this!

A wise person should carefully observe who is a fit person to speak with and who is not; they should skillfully discern the proper time to speak and the improper time; and they should skillfully discern the appropriate place to speak and the inappropriate place, and only then utter their words.
Why is this? Great King,
you should know that those who speak the truth are not loved by the world, are not liked by the world, are not praised by the wise, and are resented by the foolish people of the world.
And he spoke in verse:
"The wise man who, not knowing the proper time, suddenly speaks the truth according to his own will, is censured even by the wise; how much more so by those who lack wisdom!"
"Even in all circumstances, the wise do not always speak the truth;
for it is true, Kauśika, that one who speaks the truth has entered an evil path.

At that time, King Ugratejas, having heard the Nirgrantha Saccaka speak thus of his own faults, was immediately enlightened and his heart was filled with joy. He addressed the Nirgrantha Saccaka, saying:
“Great Master! It was not the Master’s fault, but my own extreme rashness.
Now that I have heard the Master’s instruction, it is like one who has found a lamp in the darkness, or as if a blind person has gained sight; I shall always receive and uphold it.”
"I now repent; I pray that you, Master, will not abandon me of your truthful word.
He then spoke in verse:
"I am truly foolish and ignorant, Failing to recognize the words of my spiritual friend."
Therefore, having given rise to an evil mind, I uttered such wicked words.
Now, before these holy ones, I repent of such transgressions;
may you have compassion for all sentient beings and cause my sins to be extinguished.
The Sūtra Spoken by Mahāsatyanirgrantha-putra, Scroll Five.
The Sūtra Spoken by Mahāsatyanirgrantha-putra, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Eight: The Tathāgata’s Merit of Being Without Fault, Part One.
At that time, King Ugratejas, having heard what Saccaka the Nirgrantha had said and having attained great joy, further questioned him regarding his doubts, saying:
"O Great Master!..."

Now, within this realm of sentient beings and among this assembly of beings, is there perhaps anyone else who is intelligent and of great wisdom, possessing sharp faculties and discernment, who knows what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, and is free from fault?
He replied: "Great King! There are such sentient beings who are free from all faults."
The king said, "Great Master! Who is it now?"
He replied, “Great King,
this is the ascetic Gautama, a son of the Śākya clan.”
"Born into the family of the Śākyas, he left the household life to pursue the Way.
Great King, you should know that according to what is taught in the four Vedas, there is no fault whatsoever in that Śākya śramaṇa Gautama."
It is said that being born into a great family makes one beyond reproach. Why is this?
Because he was born into the house of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
His lineage is noble and honorable, beyond reproach or disparagement. Why is this?
Because he was born into the family of the Ikṣvāku clan.
The adornment of merit and virtue is beyond reproach. Why is this?
Because the body is adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
He is endowed with actual reality and is beyond reproach. Why is this?
Because he has fully accomplished the possession of the precepts, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique dharmas.
Therefore, it is known that the śramaṇa Gautama is free from fault.
"Great King, you should know!

If that Śākya son, the śramaṇa Gautama, had not abandoned his home to leave the household life and pursue the Way, he would have become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin) ruling over the four continents, practicing the Dharma and acting as a Dharma King."

He was endowed with the seven treasures—the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the wish-fulfilling jewel treasure, the queen treasure, the minister treasure, and the steward treasure—and possessed a full thousand sons who were brave, heroic, and possessed the marks of a great man; their physical majesty was beyond reproach, and their strength was capable of subduing all other armies. Having fully accomplished the marks of a Wheel-Turning King, he attained sovereignty over the four continents, and there was no one equal to him.

Upon this great earth, there shall be no thorns of enmity, no afflictions or harms, and no swords or staves; having subdued all according to the Dharma, they shall dwell in sovereignty, practicing equanimity.
Yet that prince, the śramaṇa Gautama, did not delight in such worldly pleasures; he left home for the homeless life and, with courageous diligence, practiced great asceticism.

For six years he practiced austerities with a mind free from indolence, eating but one sesame seed or one grain of rice per day, until he attained perfect enlightenment while seated at the site of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa).
Beneath the tree, having subdued all demonic powers, he focused his mind on the wisdom of correspondence;
regarding all that is to be known, all that is to be attained, all that is to be seen, all that is to be realized, and all that is to be personally verified—
all those dharmas that ought to be attained— he was able to realize through his own wisdom without learning them from a teacher.

Having realized this as it truly is, I therefore know that among all those in the world—gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—there is no one who is his equal, let alone anyone who surpasses him.
That śramaṇa Gautama is unequaled and unsurpassed; therefore, he has none at all.
There is no fault. Why is this?
Because that śramaṇa Gautama is peerless in his family lineage, peerless in his physical form, and peerless in his wisdom; therefore, there is no fault.
He spoke again in verse:
"Superior in family, appearance, birth, and lineage; With the excellence of the various marks and a hundred blessings;
Adorned with the eighty minor marks— Thus is the Buddha’s own body adorned."
Having practiced asceticism for six years, sitting beneath the Bodhi tree,
he subdued the hosts of Māras and attained all-encompassing wisdom.
As the Teacher of gods and humans, he constantly keeps in mind the benefit of the world.
With a mind of impartial compassion, he saves those in suffering without distinction between enemy and kin.
At the city of Vārāṇasī, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the Four Noble Truths—that there is no self, no life-principle, and no sentient being; therefore, there is no fault.
At that time, King Ugratejas said to the great Nirgrantha Saccaka: "Great Master!

You should explain what constitutes the thirty-two marks of a Great Man of the Tathāgata; by being adorned with these thirty-two marks upon his body, how does he obtain the name 'Great Man, Lion-King'?"
At that time, Mahāsatyaka Nirgrantha addressed King Ugratejas, saying: "Great King!
Now you should listen with single-minded attention; I shall speak for your sake."
The king said: "Great Master!
I wish most earnestly to hear it."
Saccaka the Nirgrantha said:
"Great King, you should know that the thirty-two marks of the Śramaṇa Gautama are as follows:"
First, the soles of the śramaṇa Gautama’s feet are level and full, and he stands firmly upon the ground;
second, the soles of the śramaṇa Gautama’s feet are endowed with the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel;
third, the hands and feet of the śramaṇa Gautama are soft and supple, like celestial *karpāsa* cotton.
Fourth, the fingers of the śramaṇa Gautama are slender and long;
fifth, the fingers of the śramaṇa Gautama are all webbed;
sixth, the heels of the śramaṇa Gautama are full and rounded.
Seventh, the feet and ankles of the śramaṇa Gautama are high and prominent;
eighth, the śramaṇa Gautama has calves like those of the king of deer;
ninth, the physical form of the śramaṇa Gautama is upright and majestic.
Tenth, the śramaṇa Gautama has the male organ concealed within a sheath like that of a horse king;
eleventh, each hair of the śramaṇa Gautama grows from a single pore and they do not grow in confusion;
twelfth, the hair of the śramaṇa Gautama is as exquisite and pure as the color of blue lapis lazuli.
Thirteenth, the body hairs of the śramaṇa Gautama curl upward;
fourteenth, the skin of the śramaṇa Gautama is like the color of gold;
fifteenth, the skin of the śramaṇa Gautama is fine and soft.
Sixteenth, the śramaṇa Gautama has seven parts that are level and full;
seventeenth, the śramaṇa Gautama’s two shoulders are rounded and thick;
eighteenth, the śramaṇa Gautama’s two shoulders are high, prominent, and as perfectly round as a mountain of gold.
Nineteenth, the body of the śramaṇa Gautama is broad and long;
twentieth, the body of the śramaṇa Gautama is perfectly round and upright like the king of nyagrodha trees;
twenty-first, the cheeks of the śramaṇa Gautama are like those of a lion.
Twenty-second, the śramaṇa Gautama has a full forty teeth;
twenty-third, the śramaṇa Gautama’s teeth are bright and closely set;
twenty-fourth, the śramaṇa Gautama’s teeth are square, even, and level.
Twenty-fifth, the śramaṇa Gautama’s teeth are as white as snow;
twenty-sixth, the śramaṇa Gautama’s tongue attains supreme flavors;
twenty-seventh, the śramaṇa Gautama’s tongue can cover his face.
Twenty-eighth, the voice of the śramaṇa Gautama is like the voice of Brahmā;
twenty-ninth, the eyes of the śramaṇa Gautama blink both upward and downward like those of a bull-king;
thirtieth, the appearance of the śramaṇa Gautama’s eyes is as bright and clear as the petals of a blue lotus.
Thirty-first, the śramaṇa Gautama is perfected in the merit of the tuft of hair between his eyebrows;
thirty-second, the śramaṇa Gautama has a head so lofty and prominent that its crown cannot be seen.
"Great King, you should know that this śramaṇa Gautama possesses the thirty-two marks. Because the śramaṇa Gautama adorns his body with these thirty-two marks, he is called a Great Man, a Lion-King."
And he spoke in verse:
"The mark of the lofty crown is subtle and wondrous; The most supreme body is magnificently adorned.
His hair is like blue lapis lazuli, Pure in color, with whorls turning to the right."
His eyes blink like those of a bull-king, shaped like the petals of a blue lotus;
therefore, all praise the body of Gautama as being beyond reproach.
Gautama’s subtle and wondrous voice surpasses the sounds of all the Brahma worlds.
Just as the kalaviṅka bird is peerless among all other birds,
so too his tongue can cover his face; pure as a lotus petal,
this wondrous mark surpasses all living beings, and for this reason, none in the world can equal him.
The faculty of his tongue attains supreme flavors, and all tastes are indistinguishable to him;
he has swiftly perfected the marks of excellence, and thus the Buddha is without fault.
Regarding the merit of Gautama’s teeth, none can equal them.
Brilliantly pure like white jade or snow, they are level and uniform without deviation.
The cheeks are well-proportioned and broad above, square like those of the lion king;
the color of the lips is praised by all, resembling the *bimba* fruit.
The two shoulders are high and prominent, both front and back perfectly rounded;
divine light dazzles the eyes of the multitude, as majestic and beautiful as a mountain of gold.
Among all the marks upon Gautama’s body, he is adorned with the thirty-two signs of excellence.
The upper and lower parts of his body are perfectly symmetrical, like the king of *nyagrodha* trees.
Gautama’s body is broad and tall; he stands with such sublime composure that one can never tire of him.
The wise always thirst for him in longing admiration, gazing upon him with a heart that never grows weary.
The body of the Guṭama’s merit is fully perfected in seven places;
its skin is always radiant and fresh, like Jāmbūnada gold.
The hairs on his body are fine and soft, such that dust and grime cannot defile them.
When born, his hair whirled to the right; the strands were closely joined, all curling upward.
His hair was pure, blue-black, and beautiful; thick, full, and not unevenly distributed.
Thus, the marks of Gautama surpass the appearances of all the world.
Gautama’s body is upright; whether sitting or standing, he is free from crookedness.
His private parts are concealed like those of a horse-king, and he is also like a great dragon king.
His calves are like those of the deer-king, with their thickness and girth being even from top to bottom.
Therefore, when the wise observe this, they feel no weariness or fatigue.
His fingers and toes are joined by webbing, which is always bright and clear both inside and out;
his nails are like leaves of red copper, and his fingers are shaped like copper ladles.
The insteps are full and high; the body is well-fleshed like a perfect conch-shell.
The heels are majestic and well-proportioned, being perfectly round without any unevenness.
All the toes are slender and long, and their joints are supple and flexible.
May your feet remain healthy and at ease, treading upon the earth ever in peace and security.
This is the merit of Gautama; a mountain of various marks of virtue.
Relying upon this accumulation of merit, the body of Gautama is manifested and perfected.
Such a body of merit transcends the worlds of gods and humans;
like that pure, full moon, it shines forth among the multitude of stars.
The marks of a Great Man, O Gautama, adorn this body of merit.
The Sovereign of Great Compassion manifests, Able to benefit all worlds.
The Dharma-body is pure and stainless, Possessing immeasurable virtues;
Such wondrous marks as these Are the domain of Gautama alone.
The king said: "Great Master!
What are the eighty secondary marks of a Tathāgata?"
Because his body is adorned with the marks and signs through these merits of a hundred blessings, he is called the Tathāgata whose body possesses the marks of merit adorned by a hundred blessings.
He replied, “Great King!
I shall now provide an analogy to establish this point.
Great King, you should know:
suppose all sentient beings included within the three-thousandfold world system, born by the four modes of birth—namely:

Whether born from eggs, from a womb, from moisture, or by transformation—should all such sentient beings at once obtain a human body, and having obtained a human body, each and every one of those beings were to practice the ten wholesome actions and achieve the merit of a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin).

If one were to take the mass of merit cultivated and accomplished by all those sentient beings who have become universal monarchs (cakravartin), and increase each individual portion of that merit a hundredfold, only then would it suffice to accomplish the merit of a single minor mark (anuvyañjana) within a single pore of the Śramaṇa Gautama;
likewise, the merit contained within each of his remaining pores is exactly the same.
"Great King, you should know this!
If all these merits of the pores were increased a hundredfold, one would then achieve a single secondary mark (*anuvyañjana*) among all those possessed by the body of the śramaṇa Gautama.
Just as it is with this one secondary mark, so it is with each and every other secondary mark."
"Great King, you should know!
If all these excellent merits were increased a hundredfold, one would then achieve the merit of a single mark among all the marks of a Great Man possessed by the body of the Śramaṇa Gautama.
In this same way, the merit of each and every other mark is likewise."

"Great King, you should know that when the merit of these thirty-two marks is increased a hundredfold, one then achieves the merit of a single mark: the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows of the śramaṇa Gautama."

If the merit of such a white tuft of hair between the eyebrows were increased a hundredfold, one would then achieve the merit of a single mark among the marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa), namely the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of the head, belonging to the śramaṇa Gautama.
"Great King, you should know!

If the merit of such a crown-protrusion (*uṣṇīṣa*) were increased a hundred thousand million times over, one would then achieve a single quality among the marks of a Great Man belonging to the Śramaṇa Gautama: the quality of the conch-like voice (*śaṅkha-svara*). Because the Śramaṇa Gautama possesses this quality of the conch-like voice, even if every single sentient being included within the realm of sentient beings were to simultaneously pose hundreds of thousands of various different questions—each asking about matters that no other had previously asked—he is able, with wisdom corresponding in a single thought-moment, to answer all those sentient beings with a single sound, enabling each of them at once to attain understanding."
"Great King, you should know!

Because the śramaṇa Gautama adorns his body with these merits, he is said to have accomplished the marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa). For this reason, Gautama has accomplished the bodily marks of a hundredfold merit; for this reason, Gautama has accomplished the wondrous voice of a Brahmā conch."
And he spoke in verse:
“The body of Gautama is endowed with merit, Sustained by the marks of a hundred blessings;
He guides and delivers all living beings, Therefore he is called the Teacher of Gods and Humans.”
Seeing, hearing, and receiving [his] gifts— the merit thereof is immeasurable.
Gautama has appeared in the world to bring benefit to all sentient beings.
According to the distinctions within the realm of sentient beings, each asks differently according to their kind.
Gautama, with his wisdom of a single thought-moment, answers with a single voice so that all may understand.
Gautama appears in the world and, with his Brahma-voice,
turns the supreme wheel of Dharma, causing the suffering of gods and humans to end.
At that time, King Ugratejas questioned Saccaka the Nirgrantha, speaking in verse:
“Great Teacher, you have just described the names Of the Tathāgata’s minor marks;
I pray that for the sake of all sentient beings, And for my own benefit, you will explain them in detail.”
At that time, Saccaka the Nirgrantha replied to King Udayana: "Great King!

You have performed a great service for all sentient beings by manifesting even a small portion of the Tathāgata’s merits; this will bring much benefit. Listen attentively now, and I shall explain in detail each of the eighty secondary marks of the śramaṇa Gautama."
Based on those various marks of excellence, he extensively proclaimed the various meritorious physical characteristics of Gautama, like the full autumn moon appearing amidst the multitude of stars.
What are these eighty?
First, the śramaṇa Gautama’s head is dignified and majestic, with the upper and lower parts in perfect proportion.
Second, the head of the śramaṇa Gautama is full and beautiful like the fruit of the madhūka tree;
third, the hair of the śramaṇa Gautama is long, soft, and beautiful like fine black silk;
fourth, the strands of the śramaṇa Gautama’s hair are orderly and not disheveled.
Fifth, the hair and body hairs of the śramaṇa Gautama curl gracefully, spiraling to the right like a conch shell;
sixth, the color of the śramaṇa Gautama’s hair is lustrous, like blue lapis lazuli;
seventh, the eyebrows of the śramaṇa Gautama are long and pure white, like the crescent moon at its first appearance.
Eighth, the śramaṇa Gautama’s eyes are long and wide, like the petals of a blue lotus;
ninth, the śramaṇa Gautama’s earlobes are well-rounded like hanging dewdrops;
tenth, the śramaṇa Gautama’s nose is long, high, and straight, with the nostrils not visible.
Eleventh, the breath of the śramaṇa Gautama is fragrant and pure, such that those who smell it never tire of it;
twelfth, the color of the śramaṇa Gautama’s tongue is a radiant red, like a sheet of red copper;
thirteenth, the mark of the śramaṇa Gautama’s tongue is fine, smooth, thin, sharp, and soft.
Fourteenth, the lips of the śramaṇa Gautama are crimson-red like the *bimba* fruit;
fifteenth, the śramaṇa Gautama’s teeth are white, fine, and sharp, shining brilliantly upon his face;
sixteenth, the complexion of the śramaṇa Gautama is radiant and beautiful, shining like a clear mirror.
Seventeenth, the face of the śramaṇa Gautama is well-proportioned, with its upper and lower parts being neither too broad nor too narrow;
eighteenth, the face of the śramaṇa Gautama is full and beautiful like the full moon;
nineteenth, the face of the śramaṇa Gautama is upright and handsome, exceptionally distinguished and lovely.
Twentieth, the body of the śramaṇa Gautama is constantly pure, unstained by dust or grime;
twenty-first, the body of the śramaṇa Gautama is pure and supple like a spring flower in full bloom;
twenty-second, the tall body of the śramaṇa Gautama is upright like the banner of Śakra.
Twenty-third, the śramaṇa Gautama’s bodily marks and signs of merit are transcendent;
twenty-fourth, the śramaṇa Gautama’s body is supple and lustrous, as if anointed with oil;
twenty-fifth, the proportions of the śramaṇa Gautama’s body, whether thick or thin, are perfectly rounded like those of the king of nyagrodha trees.
Twenty-sixth, none can find fault with the various marks and signs of the body of the śramaṇa Gautama;
twenty-seventh, the physical strength of the śramaṇa Gautama is unrivaled, like that of Nārāyaṇa;
twenty-eighth, the deportment and conduct of the śramaṇa Gautama, including his advancing and retreating, are governed by the Dharma.
Twenty-ninth: The various marks and signs of the body of the śramaṇa Gautama are such that all sentient beings delight in beholding them without ever wearying.
Thirtieth: The various physical forms of the body of the śramaṇa Gautama cause even evil sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy upon seeing them.
Thirty-first: The gait and deportment of the śramaṇa Gautama are such that sentient beings who behold them never tire of observing them.
Thirty-second: The śramaṇa Gautama turns his body to look back like a great elephant king;
thirty-third: the śramaṇa Gautama’s bodily movements possess a majestic air like that of a lion king;
thirty-fourth: the śramaṇa Gautama’s physical appearance is grave and dignified, lacking any sign of levity.
Thirty-fifth, the physical marks of the śramaṇa Gautama are vast and immeasurable;
thirty-sixth, the physical marks of the śramaṇa Gautama are broad and long, lacking any sign of shortness or smallness;
thirty-seventh, the halo of light surrounding the body of the śramaṇa Gautama extends one zhang in every direction.
Thirty-eighth, the various radiant marks on the body of the śramaṇa Gautama illuminate the ten directions;
thirty-ninth, the physical marks of the śramaṇa Gautama are so dignified that all who see him submit and take refuge;
fortieth, the skin of the śramaṇa Gautama is fine and dense, always possessing a lustrous sheen.
Forty-first, the skin of the śramaṇa Gautama is smooth and full, without the signs of aging or wrinkling;
forty-second, the body and complexion of the śramaṇa Gautama are radiant with light such that the eyes of sentient beings cannot gaze upon them directly;
forty-third, the radiance of the body and complexion of the śramaṇa Gautama is no different by day or night.
Forty-fourth, from all the pores of the śramaṇa Gautama’s body, a wondrous fragrance constantly issues forth;
forty-fifth, the śramaṇa Gautama’s physical appearance and majestic virtue surpass those of all the world;
forty-sixth, the various sinews and veins of the śramaṇa Gautama’s body are deeply hidden and do not appear.
Forty-seventh, the bones and joints of the śramaṇa Gautama are interconnected like a chain of hooks;
forty-eighth, the body hairs of the śramaṇa Gautama are fine, soft, and each curls to the right;
forty-ninth, the color of the śramaṇa Gautama’s body hair is radiant, like Jāmbūnada gold.
Fifty: The hands and feet of the śramaṇa Gautama are reddish-white like the color of the *utpala* flower;
fifty-one: the hands and feet of the śramaṇa Gautama are fresh and pure, always possessing a lustrous moisture;
fifty-two: the ten fingers of the śramaṇa Gautama are slender, long, well-rounded, and beautiful.
Fifty-third: The ankles of the śramaṇa Gautama are inconspicuous, being level and without unevenness;
fifty-fourth: the shanks of the śramaṇa Gautama are firm and long, with the upper and lower parts full and well-proportioned;
fifty-fifth: the hands and feet of the śramaṇa Gautama are perfectly rounded, without any unevenness.
Fifty-sixth, the fingers of the śramaṇa Gautama are soft and supple, with both the inner and outer surfaces being pleasant to grasp;
fifty-seventh, the lines upon the hands of the śramaṇa Gautama are fine, clearly visible, deep, and well-defined;
fifty-eighth, the lines upon the hands of the śramaṇa Gautama are straight and distinct.
Fifty-ninth: The lines on the palms of the Śramaṇa Gautama’s hands are unbroken; sixtieth:
The nails of the Śramaṇa Gautama are thin, glossy, and the color of red copper; sixty-first:
When the Śramaṇa Gautama stands, he does not lean, but remains perfectly upright and balanced.
Sixty-second: The śramaṇa Gautama abides in peace and stability, such that no one can move him;
sixty-third: the movement and majestic power of the śramaṇa Gautama’s body are like those of a lion king;
sixty-fourth: when the śramaṇa Gautama turns his body to look back, he does so like a great elephant king.
Sixty-fifth, the śramaṇa Gautama walks with even and upright steps, free from any tilting or crookedness;
sixty-sixth, the śramaṇa Gautama walks with a calm and dignified gait like that of an elephant king;
sixty-seventh, the śramaṇa Gautama moves his feet and takes his steps like a king of white geese.
Sixty-eighth: When the śramaṇa Gautama walks, his feet do not touch the ground, and the marks [on his soles] are brilliantly manifest;
sixty-ninth: the śramaṇa Gautama possesses the fullness of all nine apertures;
seventieth: the śramaṇa Gautama’s abdomen is small and does not protrude.
Seventy-first, the navel of the śramaṇa Gautama is deep and round;
seventy-second, the voice of the śramaṇa Gautama is harmonious, beautiful whether coarse or fine;
seventy-third, the exquisite voice of the śramaṇa Gautama reaches afar, being heard without obstruction wherever one listens.
Seventy-fourth, all the sounds and voices of the śramaṇa Gautama accord with the inclinations of sentient beings, and all who hear them find harmony and joy;
seventy-fifth, the speech of the śramaṇa Gautama adapts to local dialects without addition or subtraction;
seventy-sixth, the Dharma taught by the śramaṇa Gautama accords with the capacities of his audience and is free from error.
Seventy-seventh: The śramaṇa Gautama is able to preach by conforming to the local dialects and accents of the world;
seventy-eighth: The śramaṇa Gautama preaches the Dharma with a single voice, causing all different species to understand it simultaneously;
seventy-ninth: The śramaṇa Gautama preaches the Dharma in successive order according to the presence of causes and conditions.
Eightieth: On the chest of the śramaṇa Gautama there is the sign of the *śrīvatsa*, manifesting the marks of merit.

Great King, you should know that this is called the body adorned with the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) of the śramaṇa Gautama, which has fully accomplished the signs of merit. None among all the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, devas, māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or various non-Buddhists are able to possess them; therefore, I say that he is without fault.
And he spoke in verse:
"O Lord of the Earth, listen to my words: the Tathāgata possesses eighty secondary marks;
by means of these various marks and signs, the body of Gautama is adorned."
Gautama’s fingernails are rounded and beautiful; their shape is like that of half a bamboo tube.
They possess a lovely, deep red-copper hue, with a luster as if smeared with oil.
The flesh between his fingers is smooth and full, arranged in perfect, even symmetry without any discrepancy.
The lines on his palms are even and straight, deep and fine with distinct markings.
His veins are deep and show no irregularity; the color of his lips is like that of the *bimba* fruit.
His feet stand well and without deviation; therefore, he is always peaceful and secure.
The ankle bones are hidden and do not appear, their high and low points difficult to distinguish;
the marks upon his hands are clearly manifest, revealing all manner of virtues.
His tongue is wondrously soft and supple, like fresh celestial cotton-wool.
Thin as a leaf of red copper, its radiant color is ever brilliant and fresh.
All the joints are deeply concealed, and its wondrous marks are exceedingly difficult to see;
his two hands extend beyond his knees, and all devas and humans offer praise.
His wondrous voice is profound and far-reaching, like that of a great nāga king;
it is like the thunder amidst rain from the heavens, its sound subtle, exquisite, and most supreme.
Gautama’s body is like the full moon, perfectly corresponding with the purity of the true mark (dharmatā).
His wondrous form is well-proportioned and beautiful, with both upper and lower parts perfectly rounded.
Having forever exhausted all unwholesome physical marks, he is replete with every merit;
his chest is full like that of a lion, and each of his secondary characteristics is distinct.
The hands and feet possess a fine luster, and the skin is as fresh as gold;
such merits as these cannot be faulted in the slightest.
The physical marks are well-proportioned in sequence, free from all coarse or rough textures.
The navel wheel is perfectly round, its cavity deep and free from depressions or curves.
All parts of the body are formed through the accumulation of merit;
all conditioned phenomena are utterly pure, and its radiance is free from darkness and turbidity.
Such a body of merit is perfectly prepared and beyond reproach;
therefore, all the worlds gaze upon it with delight, never wearying of the sight.
Arising like a great dragon king, he stirs the depths of the profound ocean with his majestic power.
His gait is like that of a bull-king, his majesty like the stride of a lion.
His physical form is exceedingly supple, with bones and joints perfectly aligned;
he moves like a king of geese, neither too fast nor too slow.
The abdomen is small and unobtrusive; the flanks are soft and the ribs are level.
The body hair curls to the right with a brilliant luster, its radiant color like a flash of lightning.
Whether walking or coming and going, all his features are exceedingly dignified and beautiful.
Free from the pursuit of hatred and attachment, he has perfected all causes of excellence.
Gautama is devoid of all evils; his myriad marks manifest auspiciousness.
Free from yellowish or dark complexions, he is without any unseemly moles or blemishes.
His eyebrows are like the newly risen moon; their color is as black as refined gold.
His pure eyes are free from envy; his broad eyes shine like stars.
The gateway of his face is square and well-proportioned; from it he emits a wondrous voice of harmony.
His various marks transcend all living beings, free from the entanglements of all afflictions.
His brow-mark is exceedingly beautiful; his nose is high like a suspended tube;
his two eyes are broad and long, like the petals of a blue lotus.
The eyebrows are even and do not part; their fullness is as perfect as a compass-drawn circle.
The teeth are high, orderly, and sharp; the two canine fangs illuminate the face.
The body hairs are without irregularity; the throat and neck are free from unevenness.
Therefore, O Gautama, your marks are such that no being among gods or humans is your equal.
Your head is rounded like a parasol; the fontanelle is flat and even;
the skin of your forehead is entirely free of wrinkles; and your body is firm and round like a conch shell.
Gautama’s body hairs are fine and smooth, neither disordered nor scattered;
they curl to the right in whorls and constantly emit sublime sounds.
Gautama’s body hairs are fresh and pure, such that dust and grime cannot stain them.
Like that pure lapis lazuli, unstained by mud;
the body-hairs of Gautama are complete, each standing in its proper place.
Like many *tṛṇa-lambaja* grasses, they are uniform, fine, and do not entwine one another.
Gautama’s body hairs are fine and soft, like the hair on the abdomen of a bumblebee king;
free from the signs of illness and old age, his hair and nails do not turn white.
Gautama’s chest is full and rounded, and he sits like a lion.
Like a fish, like a tall banner, and also like a vajra-hook;
like a golden jar standing upright, like a painting that turns back upon itself;
like a padma flower, and like the goddess Śrī with her conch-shell.
As he sits cross-legged, within each and every joint his strength is like that of Nārāyaṇa; for this reason, he transcends the world.
On Gautama’s chest is the sign of the thousand-spoked wheel, complete with its ten thousand spokes.
The hands and feet are not unlike one another; the thousand-spoked wheels are without flaw.
O Lord of Men, this is precisely so: among the minor marks of Gautama, neither the followers of the Two Vehicles nor the non-Buddhists, nor any among gods or humans, possess their equal.

“Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has accomplished such a body endowed with these marks and signs; among all sentient beings, there is no one like him. For this reason, I say that the śramaṇa Gautama is without fault.”
"Great King, you should know this!

The śramaṇa Gautama has fully accomplished the power of the mind of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and is able to bring great benefit to all sentient beings without any harmful intent. Because that mind of great loving-kindness is unimpeded, unobstructed, constantly practiced, and naturally illuminating, it reaches everywhere throughout the spheres of all worlds and enters into the afflictions and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of all sentient beings."
"Great King, you should know!
It is like the maṇi-jewel of pure water: because its own substance is pure, it is able to purify all turbid water.
Great King, you should know!"

The water of the great compassionate mind of the śramaṇa Gautama is likewise: while his own body is pure, he is further able to purify the mire of afflictions and the turbid waters of various views of all sentient beings.
"Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished such great loving-kindness; therefore, what I have said is without fault.
He then spoke in verse:
“Gautama possesses great compassion; he surveys the realms of the ten directions and the minds of all sentient beings, never for a moment able to abandon them.
Therefore he is named the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who has perfected the mind of great loving-kindness.”
Therefore, the Omniscient One is free from all faults.
Just as that wish-fulfilling maṇi jewel can purify water,
because its nature is luminously pure, it is able to clear all turbid waters.
Gautama is likewise: his own nature is free from all defilements, and he is able to purify the turbid minds of sentient beings with the water of a compassionate heart.
"Great King, you should know this!"
The śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately perfected thirty-two kinds of contemplative minds of great compassion toward all sentient beings.
What are these thirty-two?
First, because the śramaṇa Gautama sees that sentient beings have fallen into the great darkness of the abyss of ignorance, he gives rise to a mind of great compassion.
Second, the śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion because he sees all sentient beings fallen into and entangled within the cave of ignorance;
third, the śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion because he sees all sentient beings fallen into the great perilous places of the world;
fourth, the śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion because he sees all sentient beings departing from the place of tranquility and falling into the world.
Fifth, the śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion because he sees all sentient beings fallen into the great torrent of water and being carried away by its current;
sixth, the śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion because he sees all sentient beings fallen into the perilous and difficult place of great suffering characterized by perversion;
seventh, the śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion because he sees all sentient beings fallen into the evil realms and separated from the noble path.

Eighth, the śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion because he sees that all sentient beings are bound by great afflictions as those who are bound and those to whom they are bound, being constantly enveloped by the various nets of affliction;
ninth, the śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion because he sees that all sentient beings are never satisfied and can never be filled with respect to their sensory objects;
tenth, the śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion because he sees that all sentient beings are subject to the masters of craving and lack self-mastery.

Eleventh, the śramaṇa Gautama perceives that all sentient beings are constantly afflicted by the great suffering of old age and death and yet do not give rise to revulsion; therefore, he gives rise to great compassion.

Twelfth, the śramaṇa Gautama perceives that all sentient beings are never free from various ailments and are oppressed and tormented by all manner of diverse sufferings of illness; therefore, he gives rise to great compassion.

Thirteenth, the śramaṇa Gautama perceives that the three fires of all sentient beings are constantly burning, scorching them day and night without ever being extinguished; therefore, he gives rise to great compassion.

Fourteenth, the śramaṇa Gautama perceives that sentient beings are entangled in inferior karma and thereby increase the various sufferings and afflictions of the world; for this reason, he gives rise to great compassion.
Fifteenth, the śramaṇa Gautama perceives that sentient beings constantly harbor fear and dread, lacking a mind of peace and security; for this reason, he gives rise to great compassion.
Sixteenth, the śramaṇa Gautama perceives that sentient beings are entangled by minor gains and thus forget their great transgressions; for this reason, he gives rise to great compassion.

Seventeenth, the śramaṇa Gautama perceives that all sentient beings are intoxicated by various forms of negligence; that the serpent of beginningless sleep constantly slumbers within their hearts; and that on the path through the wilderness, they are perpetually pursued by the enemies of the five aggregates; therefore, he gives rise to great compassion.
Eighteenth, the śramaṇa Gautama perceives that all sentient beings are constantly robbed of their wealth of goodness by the hindrances; therefore, he gives rise to great compassion.

Nineteenth, the śramaṇa Gautama perceives that the eyes of all sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance, perpetually obscured so that they do not see the spiritual friends; therefore, he gives rise to great compassion.

Twenty: The śramaṇa Gautama perceives that all sentient beings are constantly distracted in their minds by various affairs, like tangled threads for which no one provides order; therefore, he gives rise to great compassion. Twenty-one:
The śramaṇa Gautama perceives that all sentient beings are always amidst clamor and lack tranquility; therefore, he gives rise to great compassion. Twenty-two:
The śramaṇa Gautama perceives that all sentient beings are always in difficult circumstances and lack security; therefore, he gives rise to great compassion.
Twenty-third: The śramaṇa Gautama, seeing that sentient beings are entangled in various wrong views, gives rise to great compassion;
twenty-fourth: the śramaṇa Gautama, seeing that sentient beings pursue the bait of craving and rely upon various latent tendencies of wrong view, gives rise to great compassion;

twenty-fifth: the śramaṇa Gautama, seeing that sentient beings throughout the long night cling to perversions of perception and perversions of mind—conceiving the notion of permanence in impermanent phenomena, the notion of pleasure in suffering phenomena, the notion of purity in impure phenomena, and the notion of self in selfless phenomena—gives rise to great compassion.

Twenty-sixth, the śramaṇa Gautama perceives that all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have constantly borne the heavy burden of the evils of birth and death, yet undergo great suffering and affliction without weariness or distaste;

therefore, he gives rise to great compassion. Twenty-seventh, the śramaṇa Gautama perceives that all sentient beings rely upon the world, being weak, meager, and lacking strength, mistaking what is not firm for firmness;

therefore, he gives rise to great compassion. Twenty-eighth, the śramaṇa Gautama perceives that all sentient beings are defiled by taints, always remaining amidst immeasurable impurities; therefore, he gives rise to great compassion.
Twenty-ninth, the śramaṇa Gautama perceives that sentient beings are bound by craving and do not feel weary of or abandon it; therefore, he gives rise to great compassion.

Thirtieth, the śramaṇa Gautama perceives that sentient beings are subdued by various offerings and honors, and constantly seek the requisites for life and such offerings; therefore, he gives rise to great compassion.

Thirty-first, the śramaṇa Gautama perceives that sentient beings are constantly entangled by various sense objects, causing their minds to give rise to distress and affliction; therefore, he gives rise to great compassion.
Thirty-second: The śramaṇa Gautama perceives that sentient beings have fallen into the ground of arrogance and self-conceit; therefore, he gives rise to great compassion.
Great King, you should know this!
This is called the Śramaṇa Gautama’s ultimate accomplishment of thirty-two kinds of contemplative minds of great compassion toward all sentient beings; therefore, what I have said is without fault.
And he spoke in verse:
“Gautama sees sentient beings confined within the prison of the world,
transmigrating through all realms of existence and constantly undergoing every kind of suffering.”
Their minds shrouded by the darkness of delusion, they do not know how to give rise to weary detachment;
for this reason, the Unsurpassed Honored One constantly gives rise to a heart of great compassion.
When Gautama sees sentient beings who delight in and cling to the various worlds, [he feels pity].
Drifting upon the rivers of the four currents, they follow along and cannot turn back;
constantly submerged in the ocean of birth and death, they do not know how to seek liberation.
For this reason, the One Possessing the Ten Powers always gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
Gautama beholds sentient beings fallen into great peril,
having entered upon an unrighteous path where no savior exists;
therefore Gautama contemplates them and gives rise to a heart of great compassion.
He establishes them in the Buddha’s bodhi, the most supreme state of fearlessness.
Seeing sentient beings bound within the prison,
serving as slaves to craving and driven by the various sense objects, Gautama [liberates them].
Wallowing in the ocean of old age and death, They neither perceive nor understand;
Therefore, the One of Ten Powers Constantly gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
Gautama beholds sentient beings Blazing with the three fires.
Constantly dwelling in the various evil realms, Harassed by all manner of sufferings,
Terrified of the miserable paths, And having no place of refuge— Therefore,
the One Possessed of Ten Powers Constantly gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
Gautama sees sentient beings who delight in and are attached to the various realms of existence;
with their minds unrestrained by heedlessness, they greedily cling to all sensory objects and are constantly afflicted by manifold harms, yet they give rise to no fear.
Therefore, the One Possessing the Ten Powers constantly gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
Gautama beholds sentient beings shrouded by the darkness of ignorance and obstructed by various veils, never free from all hindrances.
The various views are as tangled as silk; there is no one capable of unraveling them.
For this reason, the One of Ten Powers constantly gives rise to a heart of great compassion.
Gautama beholds sentient beings fallen into the eight heterodox views.
Because craving causes one to dwell long, it constantly binds the mind;
thus, amidst all such hardships, one finds no joy in renunciation.
For this reason, the One of Ten Powers always gives rise to great compassion.
Gautama observes sentient beings who give rise to perverted minds;
amidst suffering and impurity, they conceive notions of pleasure and purity;
amidst impermanence and non-self, they conversely hold to self, permanence, and reality.
Therefore, the One Possessing the Ten Powers always gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
Seeing sentient beings, Gautama observes that they rely on frail and meager strength, constantly oppressed by heavy burdens;
yet he never conceives a thought of weariness or detachment.
Giving rise to the notion of solidity, they are stained by attachment and cannot let it go;
for this reason, the One of Ten Powers constantly gives rise to a heart of great compassion.
Gautama beholds sentient beings within the ocean of craving and existence.
Because their minds are shrouded by gain and honor, they constantly seek after objects of desire;
their greed is like a wild fire, burning fiercely and never satisfied.
For this reason, the One Possessed of Ten Powers always gives rise to great compassion.
Gautama beholds sentient beings who have fully created various karmas of suffering,
constantly beset by sorrows and grief, and oppressed by afflictions;
for the sake of uprooting those beings from their manifold harms and vexations, [he acts].
Therefore, the One Possessing the Ten Powers always gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
Gautama constantly contemplates that entire realm of sentient beings;
because he always gives rise to the mind of great compassion, he is free from all faults.
"Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished the three foundations of mindfulness.
The king said:
“Great Teacher! What are the three applications of mindfulness of the Tathāgata? He replied:
"Great King! First, there is no mind of joy;
second, there is no mind of anger."
"Third, there is a mind free from both anger and joy.
The King said, "Great Master!"
"What is meant by 'a mind without joy'? He replied, "Great King!"

Regarding those who lack a joyful heart: when the śramaṇa Gautama preaches the Dharma in the assembly, if there are sentient beings whose bodies are upright and respectful, who lend an attentive ear without distraction, who receive the teaching with compliance, and who practice according to what has been taught.
The śramaṇa Gautama does not take joy in this; he does not give rise to elation or exultation.
Why is this? Because the śramaṇa Gautama has abandoned all partiality, maintaining equanimity, and dwells securely in a single-minded concentration.
The king said, "Great Master!
What is meant by a mind free from anger?"
He replied, "Great King!

When the śramaṇa Gautama preaches the Dharma to the assembly, if there are sentient beings who do not show physical reverence, do not listen attentively with their ears, oppose the holy teachings, and do not act according to what has been taught."
The śramaṇa Gautama does not give rise to a mind of anger, nor does he arouse a mind of intolerance; he does not produce a lack of faith, nor does he harbor a mind that opposes my teaching.
"Why is this? Because the śramaṇa Gautama has abandoned all partiality with an equanimous mind and dwells securely in one-pointed concentration.
The king said:
“Great Teacher!
What is the mind that is neither joyful nor angry? He replied:

“Great King! When the śramaṇa Gautama teaches the Dharma to the assembly, within that assembly there are some who maintain upright bodies with reverence, lending their ears without distraction, receiving the instructions accordingly, and practicing as taught;
while others lack reverence, fail to attend to the sphere of his teaching, oppose the noble instruction, and do not practice as taught.”
Regarding these two individuals, the śramaṇa Gautama does not give rise to a mind of joy, a mind of exultation, or a mind of elation;

he does not give rise to a mind of anger, nor does he arouse a mind of intolerance, nor does he give rise to a mind of lack of faith, nor does he harbor thoughts that they have transgressed his instructions.
Why is this? Because the śramaṇa Gautama has abandoned all partiality and dwells in equanimity, abiding securely in a single mind.
Your Majesty, you should know this!
"The śramaṇa Gautama dwells with a mind unstained by relying on the three foundations of mindfulness;
therefore, I say there is no fault. And he spoke in verse:
"In the Dharma taught by Gautama, those who possess single-minded right reception..."
Because he dwells constantly in right mindfulness, he does not give rise to a mind of joy.
Within the Dharma taught by Gautama, he does not receive it with an improper mind;
because he dwells constantly in right mindfulness, he likewise does not give rise to a mind of anger.
Within the Dharma taught by Gautama, there are two parts: acceptance and non-acceptance.
Because he abides eternally in equanimity, he neither feels anger nor joy.
"Great King, you should know this!"
"The śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished the three acts that require no protection.
The king said, "Great Master!"
"What is the Tathāgata’s karma of the three things that need no protection? He replied, "Great King!
First, failure to guard the bodily action;
second, failure to guard the verbal action;
third, failure to guard the mental action.
The King said: "Great Master!
What is meant by 'not guarding bodily action'?"
He replied: “Great King!
The Śramaṇa Gautama’s bodily conduct is pure.”
The śramaṇa Gautama has no unwholesome conduct; therefore, the śramaṇa Gautama does not form the thought:
"My bodily karma is unwholesome; fearing that others might know it, I shall guard my mind."
"Why is this? Because the śramaṇa Gautama has no impure conduct of body; this is called the first instance of non-protection of bodily action.
The king said:
“Great Teacher!
What is meant by ‘not guarding verbal karma’? He replied:
“Great King! The śramaṇa Gautama is pure in his verbal karma.
There is no impurity in the verbal karma of the śramaṇa Gautama; therefore, the śramaṇa Gautama does not form a mental thought [of concern]:”
"I shall guard my mind, fearing that others might know of the impurity of my verbal karma.
Why is this? Because the śramaṇa Gautama possesses no impurity of verbal karma; this is called the second failure to guard verbal karma.
The king asked, "Great Master!
What is meant by 'not guarding mental karma'?"
He replied, "Great King,
the mental karma of the śramaṇa Gautama is pure."
The śramaṇa Gautama has no impurity in his mental karma; therefore, the śramaṇa Gautama does not form the thought:
"My mental karma is impure; fearing that others might know it, I shall guard my mind."
Why is this? Because the śramaṇa Gautama has no impurity in his mental karma; this is called the third failure to guard mental karma.
Great King, you should know this!
"The śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished the three types of karma that require no protection; therefore, I say he is without fault.
And he spoke in verse:
"Gautama’s three kinds of karma Are free from falsehood and indeterminate."
Therefore, ever pure, he transcends all protective realms.
For the sake of the assembly of disciples, he preaches the Dharma with an impartial mind;
those with faults he is able to eliminate, while those without faults he gathers under his care.
“Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished the purity of all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
The king said:
“Great Teacher!
What is the purity of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes? He replied:
"Great King! The purity of the Śramaṇa Gautama’s knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) is fourfold:
first, the purity of his body’s knowledge of all modes;..."
Second, the purity of the observation of all-knowledge;
third, the purity of the mind of all-knowledge;
fourth, the purity of the wisdom of all-knowledge.
The King said: "Great Master!
In what way is the body of the Tathāgata pure through all modes of knowledge?"
He replied: "Great King!

As for the Śramaṇa Gautama’s purity of the body in all its aspects: he is free from all afflictions, and all residual habitual tendencies have been extinguished without remainder; he takes up or discards birth and death according to his will, and his body attains mastery in all places—this is called the purity of the body in all its aspects."
The king said: "Great Master!
How does the Tathāgata perceive the purity of all-knowledge?"
He replied: "Great King!

When the śramaṇa Gautama contemplates the purity of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), he is free from all afflictions (*kleśa*) and the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of those afflictions within his response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*); these are all extinguished without remainder. He manifests and then vanishes at will, attaining mastery among all forms of contemplation; this is called contemplating the purity of the knowledge of all modes."
The king said: "Great Master!
How is it that the Tathāgata’s mind and omniscience (sarvākārajñatā) are pure?"
He replied: "Great King!

As for the Śramaṇa Gautama’s mind being pure in all aspects of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), he has completely distanced himself from all afflictions (*kleśa*), the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of those afflictions, and all mental defilements; his mind has attained mastery, and he has gathered and fulfilled all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). This is called the mind being pure in all aspects of omniscience."
The king said: "Great Master!
How is the Tathāgata’s wisdom—the knowledge of all modes—pure?"
He replied, “Great King!

As for the Śramaṇa Gautama’s purity of knowledge and omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna-viśuddhi*): all portions of ignorance, as well as all afflictions (*kleśa*) and the residual impressions (*vāsanā*) of those afflictions, have been extinguished without remainder; he has attained unobstructed mastery over all phenomena (*dharma*). This is called the purity of knowledge and omniscience.”
"Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished such purity of all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna). Therefore, what I have said is without fault."
And he spoke in verse:
"Gautama, the All-Knowing One, Relies upon the four dharmas of purity;
Therefore his vision is stainless, And his body of wisdom is sovereign."
"Gautama possesses pure wisdom And is fully endowed with the fourfold knowledge;
The afflictions and their habitual tendencies are extinguished, Therefore, he is without fault.
*Sāṃkhyāyanaprakaraṇa-sūtra*, Scroll Six.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Great Śākyan Nirgrantha, Scroll Seven,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty,
Part Two: Chapter Eight, Part Two— The Tathāgata’s Faultless Merits.
The King said:
"Great Master! What is the sovereign mastery of the Tathāgata?"
He replied: "Great King!
The śramaṇa Gautama possesses ten kinds of mastery:
First, mastery over life;
second, mastery over the mind;
third, mastery over material things;
Fourth, mastery over karma;
fifth, mastery over birth;
sixth, mastery over the fulfillment of wishes;
Seventh, mastery over faith;
eighth, mastery over vows;
ninth, mastery over wisdom;
Tenth is mastery over phenomena (*dharmavaśitā*).
"Great King, you should know that attaining the supreme nectar is called mastery over life (*āyurvaśitā*); [mastery over phenomena is as follows:]"
To know that all things are but this one mind is called mastery over the mind;
to gather precious jewels from within empty space is called mastery over objects;
to be far removed from all afflictions, habitual tendencies, ignorance, and the latent proclivities is called mastery over karma.
To turn at will within profound meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and samāpattis is called mastery over birth;
to proceed spontaneously in all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*) is called mastery over the wish-fulfilling gem;
to attain the contemplation of mastery regarding the sense bases (*āyatana*) is called mastery over faith.
The immediate accomplishment of all matters as soon as the mind arises is called mastery over vows (*praṇidhāna-vaśitā*);
the fact that the actions of body, speech, and mind have wisdom as their foundation is called mastery over knowledge (*jñāna-vaśitā*);
and the manifest abiding in the equal *dharmadhātu*, true suchness (*tathatā*), and the stainless limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is called mastery over phenomena (*dharma-vaśitā*).
"Great King, you should know this!
To be far removed from taking life and to be free from thoughts of anger or harm is the cause for mastery over life.

To possess unimpeded great loving-kindness toward sentient beings experiencing pleasure, and unimpeded great compassion toward sentient beings experiencing suffering, is the cause for mastery over the mind."
Relinquishing all material things with an impartial mind in order to seek great enlightenment is the cause for mastery over objects;
the purity and non-defilement of the actions of the three karmas is the cause for mastery over karma;
and gathering all roots of goodness through the bodhicitta is the cause for mastery over birth.
Relinquishing all forms of offerings, reverence, prostrations, and praises, and bestowing elephants, horses, and carriages upon sentient beings, is the cause for mastery over sovereignty;
constantly proclaiming the Triple Gem to teach and transform sentient beings is the cause for mastery over faith;
responding to the requests of all sentient beings by providing what they seek at the appropriate time is the cause for mastery over aspiration.
Constantly practicing the gift of Dharma without seeking gain, fame, or honor is the cause for mastery over wisdom;

constantly teaching sentient beings that all Tathāgatas and all sentient beings are equal in true suchness (tathatā), having the Dharma-body as their essence rather than a body sustained by food and drink, is the cause for mastery over phenomena.
"Great King, you should know this!
Because they have attained mastery over life, they counteract all fears of birth and death;
because they have attained mastery over the mind, they counteract all fears of afflictions."
Because they have attained mastery over objects, they counteract all fear of poverty;
because they have attained mastery over karma, they counteract all fear of the evil realms;
because they have attained mastery over birth, they counteract all fear of the bonds of rebirth.
Because they have attained mastery over the fulfillment of wishes, they counteract all fears of seeking;
because they have attained mastery over faith, they counteract all fears of slandering the Dharma;
because they have attained mastery over vows, they counteract all fears of being bound by mental conceptions.
By attaining mastery over wisdom, one counteracts all fears caused by the thorns of doubt;
by attaining mastery over the Dharma, one counteracts all fears regarding the great assembly.
"Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately achieved such mastery; therefore, what I have said is without fault.
He then spoke in verse:
"Gautama practices right conduct for the benefit of all sentient beings;
therefore, among all phenomena, he has attained mastery over them all.
Mindful of protecting all living beings, he harbors no intent to kill or steal."
Therefore, regarding wealth and life, one will always possess mastery over one's place of birth.
By constantly practicing the Dharma-gift of meditation, one forever severs all causes of evil;
with no obstructions in the karma of the mind, one will always possess mastery over one's place of birth.
Constantly mindful of the root of Bodhi, Not disturbing the minds of sentient beings,
Praising the merit of the Triple Gem, One brings vast benefit to all beings.
The three karmas proceed in reliance upon wisdom, And the mind dwells eternally within the Dharma-realm.
"Born with intention, faith, and aspiration, He possesses constant mastery over wisdom and the Dharma.
'Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharmas), namely:'"
The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.
The śramaṇa Gautama has accomplished such pure dharmas of the path; therefore, I say that there is no fault in him.
The king said:
"Great Master! What are the Tathāgata’s four foundations of mindfulness?"
He replied: "Great King!
As for the four foundations of mindfulness of the śramaṇa Gautama:..."
First, the foundation of mindfulness of the body;
second, the foundation of mindfulness of feelings;
third, the foundation of mindfulness of the mind;
The fourth is the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).

"Great King, you should know that regarding the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), the śramaṇa Gautama contemplates the internal body, the external body, and both the internal and external body; within this body, he performs two kinds of contemplation."
First is the contemplation of impurity;
second is the contemplation of purity.
As for the contemplation of impurity, it is the observation that the body is impure and filled with foulness, for it deceives all ordinary worldlings.
The practitioner of pure contemplation reflects thus:
"By means of this impure body of mine, I shall now attain the pure body of a Buddha, the pure Dharma-body, the body of pure merit, and the body that all sentient beings delight to behold."
Having made this contemplation, one is able to purify two practices:
first, impermanence; second, permanence.
What is impermanence?

One contemplates the body as impermanent, certain to die; having contemplated thus, one does not commit various evil deeds or live by wrong livelihood for the sake of the body. Instead, for the sake of this body, one should cultivate the three firm dharmas:
first, the firmness of the body; second, the firmness of life; and third, the firmness of wealth.
Having observed in this way, one distances oneself from all crookedness of body, speech, and mind, and practices with an upright heart.
What is meant by "the permanent"?
Having contemplated impermanence, one attains the permanent body; because of impermanence, one attains the body of merit.
Because of impermanence, one does not sever the lineage of the Buddha, the lineage of the Dharma, or the lineage of the Sangha. Why is this?

By cultivating the application of mindfulness to the body and observing the bodies of all sentient beings, one ultimately accomplishes the Dharma-body of all Buddhas. Because there is the Dharma-body, by making such an observation, one attains a mind of equality and a non-discriminative mind, and does not give rise to the outflows—namely, the outflow of desire, the outflow of existence, and the outflow of ignorance. One does not perceive a self or what belongs to a self, dwells in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and achieves all-knowledge; this is called the application of mindfulness to the body.
"Great King, you should know this!

Regarding the śramaṇa Gautama’s practice of the foundations of mindfulness of sensation (vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna): he contemplates internal sensations, external sensations, and both internal and external sensations.

Within these sensations, he performs two kinds of contemplation—namely, that they are permanent or impermanent—and he arouses a mind of loving-kindness and compassion while contemplating all sentient beings."
When experiencing pleasant feeling, greed arises;
when experiencing painful feeling, hatred arises;
and when experiencing neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, delusion arises.
He reflects thus: "All sensation is suffering.
That which is ultimate bliss is the cessation of all sensation; this is eternal bliss."
"In accordance with where one is born, one shall constantly give rise to all hearts of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion (*karuṇā*).
Whether experiencing pleasant sensations oneself or in others, one remains free from defiled thoughts and gives rise to a heart of loving-kindness;
when experiencing painful sensations, one contemplates the three evil realms, remains free from hateful thoughts, and gives rise to a heart of compassion."
When experiencing neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one leaves behind the mind of ignorance and gives rise to a mind of equanimity.
One contemplates all feelings as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
Seeing one who experiences pleasant feeling, one knows it is suffering;
seeing one who experiences painful feeling, one views it as a boil or a wound;
seeing one who experiences neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one sees it as a lack of tranquility.
Contemplating pleasant feelings, one knows they are impermanent;
contemplating painful feelings, one knows they are empty;
contemplating neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings, one knows they are non-self.
One who contemplates in this manner is said to practice the foundation of mindfulness of feeling.

"Great King, you should know that for the śramaṇa Gautama, the foundation of mindfulness of mind consists of contemplating the internal mind, the external mind, and both the internal and external mind; within this mind, he performs two kinds of contemplation."
That is to say: permanence and impermanence. Regarding the contemplation of permanence:

one contemplates the nature of bodhi within one's own body, neither forgetting nor losing it, with right mindfulness undisturbed. Contemplating the mind in this way, one further contemplates the bodhicitta that has been generated. This nature of the mind, having arisen, immediately ceases; it does not abide from moment to moment. It is not found in the internal sense bases, nor in the external sense bases, nor in both the internal and external sense bases. It is not found among the aggregates (*skandha*), nor among the elements (*dhātu*). One reflects thus: "Are such mental objects identical to or different [from the mind]?"
If the mind were distinct from its object, then there would be two minds existing at one time;
if the mind were identical to its object, it could not observe itself, just as the tip of a finger cannot touch itself—the same applies to the mind.

Having made this contemplation, one sees that the mind has no abiding place and is impermanent and subject to change; one then knows that this mind is neither born from conditions nor not born from conditions, neither eternal nor annihilated, neither internal nor external, neither existent nor non-existent.
The Bodhicitta is likewise: this mind is not form and cannot be seen; it is like an illusion and like a transformation, free from all obstructions.

Having observed one's own mind, one observes the nature and characteristics of the minds of all sentient beings; as is the nature and characteristics of one's own mind, so too are the nature and characteristics of the minds of all sentient beings.
Knowing that one's own mind is empty, one knows that the emptiness of the minds of all sentient beings is likewise.
Observing the equality of one's own mind, one observes that the equality of the nature of the minds of all sentient beings is likewise.
This is called the foundation of mindfulness of the mind.

"Great King, you should know that regarding the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna) of the śramaṇa Gautama, it means observing internal phenomena, external phenomena, and both internal and external phenomena; within these phenomena, one performs two kinds of observation, namely: permanence and impermanence."
He constantly perceives all phenomena with the Buddha-eye, never failing for a moment until he sits at the site of enlightenment.
When contemplating all phenomena, he does not perceive a single dharma, nor even the most subtle of characteristics;
being detached from emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-action, non-arising, non-cessation, and non-substantiality, he does not perceive any phenomenon, even the most subtle of marks.
Those who do not enter into the twelve links of dependent origination perceive both phenomena and non-phenomena; there is nothing that is not a phenomenon.
What is meant by "phenomenon"?
It refers to the absence of self, the absence of sentient beings, the absence of life-span, and the absence of a person—this is called a phenomenon.
What is the unrighteous?

It refers to the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-force, the view of a person, the view of annihilation, the view of permanence, the view of existence, and the view of non-existence; these are called the unrighteous.
The śramaṇa Gautama views all dharmas as both dharmas and non-dharmas. Why is this?
Because viewing them as empty, signless, and wishless is called "all dharmas are dharmas."
Self-conceit, arrogance, the notions of "I" and "mine," and the grasping at various views—these are called all dharmas that are non-dharmas.

Having thus contemplated the nature of all dharmas, one does not perceive any dharma that is not a cause for bodhi or a cause for the path to transcendence; they are all dharmas of transcendence. If one does not seek all dharmas in this manner, it is called the extinction of dharmas.

That which arises does so from conditions; that which ceases does so from conditions. When observing in this way, one observes the three types of formations: namely, unwholesome formations, wholesome formations, and imperturbable formations.
Among the three types of conduct, one should constantly practice meritorious conduct and perform the ten wholesome dharmas to purify the three karmas:
to purify bodily karma is to seek the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics of all Buddhas, so that others cannot harm them;
to purify verbal karma is so that whatever Dharma one preaches is joyfully heard by sentient beings.
Regarding the karma of a pure mind: it is because one maintains an equanimous mind toward all sentient beings and constantly enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Through such skillful means, one contemplates the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), thereby abandoning all defilements that obstruct enlightenment; one does not cling to the view of eternalism, nor does one cling to the view of nihilism, but practices the vision of the Middle Way.

This Middle Way cannot be seen by worldly wisdom; it is ineffable and cannot be demonstrated. It has no characteristics, no form, no location, nothing to grasp, and nothing to abandon. It is pure and tranquil, invisible to the eye, and so forth, even intangible. It has no destination; it does not abide in the world, nor does it transcend the world. It is ineffable, neither many nor few, neither eternal nor annihilated, neither characterized nor uncharacterized, neither conscious nor unconscious, neither false nor real, neither this nor that, neither existent nor non-existent, neither conditioned nor unconditioned, neither active nor inactive, neither born nor dead, neither nirvana nor a produced phenomenon. This is called the Middle Way.
One does not contemplate the foundation of mindfulness of dharmas by means of the fleshly eye, the divine eye, or the wisdom eye.
Why is this? Because these three eyes are devoid of marks.
Therefore, observing phenomena with the Dharma-eye, the mind does not cling to them nor lose track of them; this is called the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena.
"Great King, you should know this!"
By practicing the four foundations of mindfulness, one attains four kinds of detachment:
by contemplating the impurity of the body, one becomes detached from the inversion of purity;
by contemplating that sensation is suffering, one becomes detached from the inversion of pleasure.
By contemplating the impermanence of the mind, one departs from the inversion of permanence;
by contemplating the selflessness of phenomena, one departs from the inversion of self.
Furthermore, by contemplating the foundation of mindfulness of the body, one becomes detached from edible food.
In the mindfulness of feeling, one is detached from the nutriment of contact;
in the mindfulness of mind, one is detached from the nutriment of consciousness;
in the mindfulness of phenomena, one is detached from the nutriment of volition.
"Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished such foundations of mindfulness; therefore, I say that he is without fault.
The king said:
“Great Master!
What are the Tathāgata’s four methods of right exertion? He replied:
"Great King! The four right efforts of the śramaṇa Gautama refer to four kinds of diligence:
preventing two kinds of unwholesome dharmas and gathering two kinds of wholesome dharmas."

The śramaṇa Gautama has accomplished a virtuous nature; his mind dwells in wholesome dharmas. He does not employ diligence to extinguish unarisen evil dharmas or those already arisen, nor does he employ diligence to give rise to unarisen wholesome dharmas or those already arisen.
