Why is this? Because the śramaṇa Gautama has constantly cultivated a virtuous nature throughout immeasurable lifetimes; thus, all unwholesome dharmas naturally do not arise, and all wholesome dharmas are naturally fulfilled.

Unwholesome states (*akuśala-dharma*) refer to those that are not associated with the aggregate of morality (*śīla-skandha*), not associated with the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*), and not associated with the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*). At the time of practicing the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), various states of indolence and the afflictions of the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) obscure the mind’s eye. Being separated from the five roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) such as faith, these unwholesome states that have not yet arisen do not arise, and those already arisen are immediately extinguished through diligent effort.

Wholesome states (*kuśala-dharma*) refer to the roots of goodness such as faith; through diligent effort, those not yet arisen are caused to arise, and those already arisen are increased and expanded. These are called the four right efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*).
"Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished these four dharmas of right effort; therefore, what I have said is without fault."
The King said: "Great Master!
What are the Tathāgata’s four bases of psychic power?"
He replied: "Great King!
The four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) of the śramaṇa Gautama are as follows:"
First, the fulfillment of desire;
second, the fulfillment of diligence;
third, the fulfillment of the mind.
Fourth is the contemplation of wish-fulfillment.
These four dharmas have loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity as their foundation.
One should constantly cultivate these four immeasurable minds; by constant cultivation, the mind becomes pliant and supple.
Because the mind is pliant and supple, one attains entry into the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna.
By entering these various dhyānas, the body becomes light and soft.
Having thus accomplished physical lightness and mental pliancy, one enters the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Having entered the bases of psychic power well, one immediately gives rise to supernormal powers—whether through desire, or diligence, or mind, or investigation.
Desire means being single-mindedly directed toward that dharma;
diligence means accomplishing that dharma;
and the mind means observing that dharma.
As for contemplation (*vitarka*), it is the accomplishment through skillful means regarding those phenomena.

Once the factor of mental pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) has been thus established, one is able to attain the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): desire serves as the adornment, diligence brings about accomplishment, the mind abides correctly, and contemplation is well able to perform discernment.

The śramaṇa Gautama has attained the four bases of psychic power; according to his understanding and as he acts, his mind attains mastery, proceeding wherever he wishes. He skillfully performs all karmas and ultimately accomplishes all fundamental practices, moving through them without obstruction, like the wind traveling through space.
They attain four masteries:
first, mastery over life;
second, mastery over the body;
Third is mastery over phenomena (*dharma-vaśitā*);
fourth is mastery over supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-vaśitā*).

Regarding mastery over life (*āyur-vaśitā*): in order to discipline sentient beings, wherever they are born—whether as gods or humans—one can manifest a long lifespan within a short lifespan, or manifest a short lifespan within a long lifespan; this is called mastery over life.

Regarding mastery over the body: because of this mastery, one creates a body according to the mind and creates physical form according to the mind, manifesting various modes of deportment for the sake of sentient beings; if one wishes to assume the same physical characteristics as all sentient beings, one is able to do so entirely—this is called mastery over the body.

Mastery over phenomena (*dharmeśvaratā*) means being able to know all supramundane dharmas and demonstrating mundane matters to all sentient beings; skillfully understanding the profound twelve links of dependent origination and attaining unimpeded eloquence, one is able to adapt to the speech of various sentient beings and cause them to abide in right faith—this is called mastery over phenomena.

Mastery of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-vaśitā*) means being able to cause the waters of the four great oceans to merge into a single sea, which neither comes nor goes and possesses no sign of movement;

being able to cause all the Mount Sumerus of the trichiliocosm to merge into a single mountain, which neither comes nor goes, undergoes no increase or decrease, and remains as it was without change, without obstructing the Four Heavenly Kings or the Heaven of the Thirty-three;

and being able to cause the entire trichiliocosm to be adorned with gold, silver, and the seven treasures, manifesting at will the fragrance of sandalwood flowers—this is called mastery of supernormal powers.
"Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished these four bases of psychic power; therefore, what I have said is without fault."

Great King, you should know that once the śramaṇa Gautama has accomplished these four bases of psychic power, he is able to enter all meditative concentrations, liberations, supernormal powers, unhindered knowledges, and the four immeasurable minds.
The king said:
"Great Master! What is the Tathāgata’s meditative concentration?"
He replied: "Great King!
The śramaṇa Gautama possesses the nine successive attainments and enters samāpatti."
First, the first dhyāna;
second, the second dhyāna;
third, the third dhyāna.
Fourth, the four dhyānas;
fifth, the sphere of infinite space;
sixth, the sphere of infinite consciousness;
Seventh, the sphere of nothingness;
eighth, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
ninth, the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
"Great King, you should know this:

the śramaṇa Gautama, having detached himself from all desires, unwholesome states, and evil dharmas, with directed thought and sustained evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters and dwells in the first dhyāna."
"Free from all desires and evils" refers to the various defiled phenomena that are the objects of the first dhyāna; to distance oneself from those phenomena is called "freedom from all desires.
"Free from all evil and unwholesome phenomena" refers to the ten unwholesome karmas, such as killing, which arise due to greed, hatred, and delusion; these are called unwholesome phenomena.
Being detached from those phenomena is called the first dhyāna.
"Possessing vitarka" means it is accompanied by vitarka. What is vitarka?
By relying on what object does one accord with the first dhyāna?
This "vitarka" (initial application) consists of many types, namely: knowing, perceiving, reflection, investigation, concentration, and so forth; this is what is called vitarka.
What is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*)?

It is the mental application that accords with the initial dhyāna, wherein one contemplates and reflects upon feeling, desiring concentration and knowing the awakening-factors; this is called contemplation.
Based on the practice of disenchantment, together with that initial dhyāna characterized by both applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), it is established.
Based on the practice of renunciation, one accomplishes the practice of the first dhyāna together with that joy and bliss; this is called "entering the first dhyāna with joy and bliss.
As for "practice," it refers to such things as receiving and maintaining, mindfulness and protection, joy and bliss, and knowledge; these are termed "practice."
"Great King, you should know this!

The śramaṇa Gautama dwells in the first dhyāna and has attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) with an intensified resolve. For this reason, he enters the first dhyāna to seek the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas."

In order to seek a further superior patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one conceives the notion of non-solidity within the first dhyāna; giving rise to a desire for the higher state, one abandons that first dhyāna to seek the second dhyāna.

Desiring to enter that second dhyāna, he distances himself from the mind of the first dhyāna characterized by directed thought and evaluation; he extinguishes that mind, detaches from that mind, purifies that mind, and brings that mind to stillness.

With internal clarity, one-pointedness of mind, and being without directed thought or sustained evaluation, one enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss.

Regarding "internal clarity": it refers to the counteraction of those factors that obstruct the second dhyāna; because those factors have been stilled and are purified and free from turbidity, it is called internal clarity.

"One-pointedness of mind" means that all initial and sustained application (vitarka-vicāra) of the first dhyāna has been extinguished, becoming tranquil and of a single flavor like the great ocean; just as all waters that enter it become of one taste, namely the taste of salt.

Entering the second dhyāna, one extinguishes all vitarka and vicāra of that first dhyāna; being tranquil, of a single flavor, and without vitarka or vicāra, this is called attaining the samādhi without vitarka or vicāra.
Based on that samādhi, joy arises; that is, one gives rise to a joyful mind toward the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
Based on that joyful mind, all wholesome merits are spontaneously fulfilled.

"Desiring to cause that patience toward the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) to become increasingly superior, increasingly radiant, increasingly sublime, and increasingly supple, and to attain a mind of higher aspiration, he does not dwell in nor take pleasure in that second dhyāna, but seeks further the practice of the even more excellent third dhyāna."

Giving rise to such a thought, he realizes that this mind of joy obstructs the third dhyāna and the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Therefore, he abandons joy, practices equanimity and mindfulness, and with clarity of wisdom, experiences pleasure with the body; this pleasure is what the noble ones describe as "equanimous. Relying on the superior aspiration for the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas within that second dhyāna, he leaves behind that joy and pleasure, enters the practice of the third dhyāna, and attains the bliss of samādhi.
"Becoming weary of that joy, he gives rise to this thought:
'This joyless pleasure is impermanent pleasure; it is a phenomenon subject to exhaustion and cessation; it is not eternal, not constant, not true pleasure, and not ultimate pleasure.'"
Having understood this, he further gives rise to an even more superior desire for the supreme patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Relying on that superior patience and superior desire, he takes no delight in suffering or pleasure, remains detached from suffering and pleasure, and—having previously stilled sorrow and joy—enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by purity of equanimity and mindfulness; thus he attains the samāpatti of the fourth dhyāna.

With a supple mind, a masterful mind, a tranquil mind, a luminous mind, and an upright mind, he relinquishes all those objects of pleasure to all sentient beings. When he bestows peace and happiness upon those beings, he immediately attains the manifestation of the light of that supreme, non-arising patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Because this light of supreme patience manifests before him, his practice becomes swift; even amidst the sublime bliss of the fourth dhyāna, he does not give rise to a mind of attachment to pleasure.

"Having become detached from that pleasure, with equanimity and mindfulness purified, one perceives only the manifestation of infinite space before oneself; transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing all perceptions of sensory resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, one knows infinite space and thus enters the sphere of infinite space."
Observing form in this way, there are briefly two kinds:
first, the four great elements;
second, that which depends upon the four great elements.
The four great elements refer to earth, water, fire, and wind;
that which depends on the four great elements refers to visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility.

Thus, there are extensively eight kinds of material characteristics (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*). To be free from those material characteristics, to be devoid of those material characteristics, and to extinguish all such material characteristics is called "transcending all material characteristics."

Whatever phenomena possess the characteristic of form, those phenomena necessarily possess the characteristic of resistance. By extinguishing all such characteristics of resistance, one does not attend to nor engage in various diverse characteristics; thus, one is able to transcend those various diverse characteristics. Because one does not attend to those various diverse characteristics, one perceives only the characteristic of empty space. Therefore, knowing infinite empty space, one enters the practice of infinite empty space.
Therefore, it is said: "Transcending all marks of form.
Having entered that samādhi of boundless space, one gives rise to this thought:

"Space is boundless, space is limitless, space is shoreless; according to whatever phenomena [are considered], because they are equal to the boundlessness [of space], those phenomena have no prior limit, no middle limit, and no subsequent limit."

Thus, observing that all phenomena have no beginning, middle, or end, one enters this samādhi; immediately, one gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings, relinquishes all phenomena, and attains the wisdom of equality which manifests before them.

“At that time, within that patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), for the first time the light of superior progress manifests before him. Transcending all marks of infinite space, he manifests the knowledge of the mark of infinite consciousness and enters the practice of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*)."
He gives rise to this thought:
"This characteristic of boundless space is merely the conceptualization and discrimination of consciousness.

Having attained such a mind, he knows that all phenomena are merely the characteristics of consciousness; this consciousness is immeasurable. Entering such a samādhi, he attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), yet it is not the ultimate accomplishment of the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.

Having transcended all signs of infinite consciousness, it manifests before one; knowing the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one enters the practice of the sphere of little-ness (*akiṃcanya*).

"Nothingness" means that there is no such thing as the conceptualizing mind of greed, hatred, and delusion, nor various conceptualizations and false discriminations. All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) of the world arise from the mind of false discrimination; because those things do not exist, it is called "nothingness."
"Little" refers to what was previously explained: within phenomena, the minor marks, subtle marks, and minute marks are called "marks of little.
Because those marks of little do not exist, it is said that there is "no little.
Because one has transcended all such coarse and subtle perceptions, it is said that there is "nothing whatsoever and nothing lacking."
Abiding in this samādhi, one attains the manifestation of the light of the increasingly superior *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*.

In order to attain that superior *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*, one does not delight in that samādhi of non-existence and non-substantiality, but gives rise to a heart of superior aspiration, further seeking the superior practice of the transcendent samādhi.
One gives rise to this thought:
"This is non-existent and lacks even the slightest characteristic of activity, for it is also a subtle mark born of false discrimination.
Next, one contemplates the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
What is meant by "neither-perception-nor-non-perception"?
That which is non-perception is emptiness; that which is non-non-perception arises from causes and conditions.

At that time, the samādhi of neither-perception-nor-non-perception manifests before one; having transcended all subtle marks of the sphere of nothingness, one enters the samādhi of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
While dwelling in that sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he gave rise to this thought:
"In this sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there is nothing to be delighted in; I shall distance myself from these phenomena.
Thereupon, he realized the samādhi of the non-arising and non-ceasing of all phenomena, which manifested before him.
Knowing that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing, and seeing that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is quiescent— neither proceeding nor abiding— at that time,
one is said to have attained the supreme, pure forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
This is called the ninefold sequential entry into samāpatti.
Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished such meditative dharmas; therefore, what I have said is without fault.
The king said:
"Great Master! What is the characteristic of the Tathāgata’s liberation?"
He replied: "Great King!
The śramaṇa Gautama has eight kinds of liberation: [text continues]"
First, possessing form, one sees forms;
second, having the internal perception of form, one sees external forms;
third, the purity of faith.

Fourth, transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing all perceptions of sensory resistance, and not attending to any perceptions of diversity, one knows infinite space and enters the practice of the sphere of infinite space;
fifth, transcending all perceptions of infinite space, one knows infinite consciousness and enters the practice of the sphere of infinite consciousness;
sixth, transcending all perceptions of infinite consciousness, one knows that there is nothing whatsoever and enters the practice of the sphere of nothingness.
Seventh, transcending all spheres of nothingness, knowing the peace of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters the practice of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
eighth, transcending all practices of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, extinguishing all sensation and perception, one enters the practice of the attainment of cessation.
These are called the eight liberations.
Regarding "one possessing form sees forms": that which possesses form consists entirely of dharmas produced by causes and conditions;
seeing them as empty and devoid of a life-principle (jīva), being able to see in this way, one attains liberation from bondage—this is termed "liberation."

Regarding those who perceive external forms while possessing internal perceptions of form, seeing that these are empty and devoid of a life-principle (*jīva*), and realizing that all are phenomena born of causes and conditions—to be able to see in this way is to attain liberation from bondage; this is called emancipation.

Regarding purity through faith: if one discriminates between the signs of purity and impurity, it is called wrong view; because of this purity through faith, one attains liberation from bondage, which is called deliverance.

Transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing all perceptions of sensory resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, one knows infinite space and enters the sphere of infinite space. Having immeasurable space and being able to know space in this way, one attains liberation from bondage; this is called emancipation.

Transcending all marks of the infinite nature of space, one knows infinite consciousness and enters the practice of infinite consciousness. This immeasurable consciousness and infinite consciousness—this very infinite consciousness is emptiness. One who can know it thus attains liberation from bondage; this is called emancipation.

Having transcended infinite consciousness and knowing that there is nothing whatsoever, one enters the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). Here, "that which exists" refers to the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion; by entering the sphere of nothingness, one extinguishes those afflictions. Being able to know in this way, one attains liberation from bondage, which is called "deliverance."

Having transcended nothingness, one knows that the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is peaceful; thus entering the practice of neither-perception-nor-non-perception: that which is "not with perception" is by nature empty and quiescent, and that which is "not without perception" exists dependent upon causes and conditions. To be able to see in this way is to attain liberation from bondage, which is called emancipation.

Having transcended all states of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and extinguished all sensation and perception, the practitioner who enters the meditative attainment of cessation perceives in this way:
perception is like a mirage, and sensation is like a bubble;
perception is itself sensation, and sensation is itself perception.
There is no self and no life-principle; one who can see in this way attains liberation from bondage, which is called emancipation.
Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished such liberation; therefore, what I have said is without fault.
The King said,
“Great Master! What is the Tathāgata’s practice of supernormal knowledge?”
He replied: "Great King!
The śramaṇa Gautama possesses six kinds of supernormal powers (ṛddhi):"
First, the supernormal power of the divine eye;
second, the supernormal power of the divine ear;
third, the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others.
Fourth is the supernormal power of recollecting past lives;
fifth is the supernormal power of mastery over the mind;
sixth is the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows.
"Great King, you should know this!"

The divine eye possessed by the śramaṇa Gautama surpasses that of all devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings, as well as that of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. He is able to clearly see everything accomplished through merit and wisdom throughout the ten directions; he sees all forms, colors, and luminous images within the ten directions—whether coarse or subtle, near or far—all of which he perceives with complete clarity and discernment. Furthermore, he knows without exception all the continuous cycles of birth and death among all sentient beings throughout the various realms of existence, including their karmic actions and their fruits, as well as the distinctions among their faculties. He also beholds the adorned, pure, and wondrous buddha-lands of all the Tathāgatas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and he sees without exception all the practices performed by the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and sentient beings of the five destinies therein.
Why is this? Because this eye is pure, seeing without obstruction;
because this eye is unstained, it does not cling to forms.
This eye is liberated, for it is far removed from the bonds of all views and afflictions;
this eye is pure, for its nature is luminous;
this eye is without dependence, for it is free from objects of perception.
This eye does not arise, for it has severed the afflictions;
this eye is stainless, for it has severed all evils;
this eye is free from cataracts, for it has severed the net of doubt.
This eye does not arise, because it has severed all obstructions;
this eye is free from greed, hatred, and delusion, because it can sever all fetters and latent tendencies;
this eye attains clarity, because it illuminates and comprehends all phenomena.
This eye is known through mindfulness, for it does not function as consciousness;
this eye is unsurpassed, for it is the ultimate holy path;
this eye is unobstructed, for it illuminates all sentient beings with equanimity.
This eye is unstained, for its nature is pure.
Why is this? Because the śramaṇa Gautama dwells in a mind of great compassion, skillfully discerns the meaning [of things], and is free from contention.
According to what they see, hear, or are told, they abandon all unwholesome deeds;
proceeding toward the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), their minds are free from hindrance.
Upon seeing those who are stingy and greedy, they are able to bestow wealth as a gift.
Seeing those who violate the precepts, he exhorts them to restrain their sense faculties;
seeing those who harbor anger, he exhorts them to practice patience and avoid contention;
seeing those who are indolent, he exhorts them to apply themselves with diligent vigor.
Seeing those who are distracted, he demonstrates the bliss of meditative concentration;
seeing those who are deluded, he teaches them to cultivate wisdom.
Thus, he attains the pure and unobstructed divine eye; this is called the supernormal knowledge of the divine eye.
"Great King, you should know!

The divine ear possessed by the śramaṇa Gautama reaches throughout the worlds of the ten directions; it can distinguish all sounds therein—the voices of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—and it likewise knows the voices of the Buddhas preaching the Dharma, as well as the voices of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas."
All sounds that can be perceived by the faculty of hearing, including those of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, and fleas—all such sounds he is able to hear.
Furthermore, whatever sounds are produced from the mental objects of sentient beings—whether virtuous, non-virtuous, or indeterminate—he understands them all.
He hears all sounds of the past and future, reaching back to the very limit of their origin.

Why is this? Because the śramaṇa Gautama dwells securely in great compassion and is able to hear all sounds without obstruction; because he has severed all afflictions and extinguished their habitual tendencies, this is called the supernormal knowledge of the divine ear.
“Great King, you should know this:

regarding the range of the Śramaṇa Gautama’s supernormal knowledge of others’ minds, he knows the thoughts of all sentient beings and those included within the category of sentient beings, exactly as they are in their minds.”

That is to say, he thoroughly discerns and knows the virtuous mind, the non-virtuous mind, the neutral mind; the mind that accords with afflictions, the mind that turns away from afflictions; the mind of a śrāvaka, the mind of a pratyekabuddha, the mind of a bodhisattva, and the mind of a buddha; the mind of a deva, the mind of a nāga, the mind of a yakṣa, the mind of a gandharva, the mind of an asura, the mind of a garuḍa, the mind of a kiṃnara, the mind of a mahoraga, the mind of a human and non-human, the mind of those in hell, the mind of animals, the mind of hungry ghosts, the mind of beings in the realm of Yama; and he thoroughly discerns and knows the past mind and the future mind.

Why is this? Because the Śramaṇa Gautama dwells securely in great compassion; he knows the minds of others without hindrance or obstruction, because he is free from all afflictions, because he has severed all habitual tendencies, and because he illuminates all phenomena. To be able to understand in such a way is called the supernormal knowledge of the mental faculties of others.
"Great King, you should know this!
Regarding the supernormal knowledge of past lives possessed by the śramaṇa Gautama, he recollects and knows one birth,
two births, and even ten births, a hundred births, a thousand births, immeasurable hundreds of births, and immeasurable..."
He knows a thousand births, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of births, as well as the formation and destruction of the heavens and earth,
the formation of immeasurable worlds, the destruction of immeasurable worlds, immeasurable worlds undergoing both formation and destruction,
and immeasurable kalpas of formation and destruction; he knows all sentient beings who were born therein, their respective lineages, and their respective names.
With such physical forms, such lifespans, such experiences of suffering, such experiences of pleasure,
such dwellings, and such clothing, food, and drink; dying here to be reborn here,
dying there to be reborn there, dying here to be born there, or dying there to be born here.
They know everything of the past limit without exception.

Furthermore, he knows all the Buddhas of the past who have reached the limit of the past, including their retinues, parents, wives, children, brothers, and sisters; from their initial resolve to leave home and seek the Way, through the cultivation and accumulation of vows and practices, their making offerings to the Buddhas, their teaching and taming of all sentient beings, and their sitting beneath the Bodhi tree to attain equal and perfect enlightenment—he can fully recollect and know their such names, such abodes, such sublime seats, such śrāvakas, such attendants, such devas, such humans, such assemblies, such non-Buddhists, such preaching of the Dharma, such deliverance of sentient beings, such lifespans, such parinirvāṇas, such duration of the True Dharma, and such duration of the Semblance Dharma.
Why is this? Because they abide in great compassion and are skillfully proficient in the performance of deeds;
because this wisdom is free from affliction and they abide in meditative concentration.
This wisdom is fearless because it skillfully encompasses all forms of wisdom;
this wisdom is spontaneous because it is attained through direct realization without seeking it from others;
this wisdom is right mindfulness because it is ultimately never lost.
This wisdom is a merit because it brings the Mahāyāna to ultimate fulfillment;
this wisdom is a root of goodness because, arising from the pāramitās, it reaches the further shore.
This is called the supernormal knowledge of the wisdom of recollecting past lives.
The Mahāsāṃghika-sātrāntika Sūtra Spoken by the Great Śākyan Nirgrantha-putra, Scroll Seven;
The Mahāsāṃghika-sātrāntika Sūtra Spoken by the Great Śākyan Nirgrantha-putra, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
The Third Part of Chapter Eight: The Merits Beyond Reproach of the Three Tathāgatas.
“Great King, you should know this:

As for the śramaṇa Gautama’s practice of the wisdom of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-vidyā*), it is because he wishes to subdue sentient beings who hold wrong views and are stubborn and difficult to transform, leading them to follow the True Dharma, that the śramaṇa Gautama is able to manifest various kinds of supernormal transformations for the sake of teaching and conversion—whether through physical forms, through power, or through emanations.”

Regarding "physical forms" (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*): this refers to manifesting the physical forms of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas; the physical forms of Śakra-devendra, Brahmā-rāja, and the Four Heavenly Kings; the physical form of a Cakravartin King; and various other forms, even down to those of animals. According to what sentient beings ought to see in order to receive transformation, he is able to manifest them all and preach the Dharma for them.

If there are sentient beings who, relying on their physical strength and power, give rise to arrogance, anger, and haughtiness, [the Buddha], desiring to subdue such beings, manifests great power like that of Nārāyaṇa; he places Mount Sumeru upon the tip of a single finger and hurls it to immeasurable worlds in other directions. Or, at times, he cuts out the entire trichiliocosm down to its watery foundations and lifts it with one hand high up to the Peak of Existence, remaining there for an eon. By manifesting such power, he causes the arrogant and haughty minds of those beings to subside, and then preaches the Dharma for them.

As for transformation, by the power of transformation one can change the great ocean into water like that in a cow’s footprint; yet the great ocean does not diminish and the cow’s footprint does not enlarge. Conversely, one can transform the water in a cow’s footprint so that it becomes the great ocean.
When the kalpa is about to end and the calamity of fire arises, those who should see water shall see it transformed into water, and those who should see wind shall see it transformed into wind;
when the calamity of water arises, those who should see fire shall see it transformed into fire, and those who should see wind shall see it transformed into wind;

when the calamity of wind arises, those who should see water shall see it transformed into water, and those who should see fire shall see it transformed into fire—manifesting such various transformations to inspire joy in all sentient beings and preaching the Dharma for them.

Why is this? Because these supernormal powers (abhijñā) are encompassed by the dharmas of faith-aspiration, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; they are characterized by subduing and gentleness, and because the mind has attained mastery through skillful cultivation and accumulation, they are called the supernormal power of psychic transformation (ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna).
“Great King, you should know!

As for the Śramaṇa Gautama’s practice of the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*), all his outflows have been exhausted, and he has distanced himself from all habitual tendencies of affliction (*vāsanā*). These are namely: the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), the outflow of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). This exhaustion of outflows is not like that which is attained by any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.”

Why is this? Because although all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others have attained the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya), they encounter obstacles in all places of birth and lack the sovereign power to teach and transform sentient beings; therefore, they possess hindrances.
The śramaṇa Gautama is without any such obstacles; this is called the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣayajñānābhijñā).
"Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished such supernormal knowledge and practice; therefore, what I have said is without fault."
The king said: "Great Master!
What are the Tathāgata’s four kinds of unimpeded knowledge?"
He replied: "Great King!
The four kinds of unimpeded knowledge are as follows:"
First, non-obstruction regarding phenomena;
second, non-obstruction regarding meaning;
third, non-obstruction regarding expression;
The fourth is the unimpeded eloquence of delight in teaching (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).

Great King, you should know that regarding the Śramaṇa Gautama’s unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), it means that he observes sentient beings’ initial resolve for practice, their mental dispositions of great desire, and their mental dispositions of few desires; as well as wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, worldly and world-transcending phenomena, conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, tainted and untainted phenomena, compounded and uncompounded phenomena, dark and bright phenomena, and the phenomena of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. He knows, in accordance with reality, that the nature of awakening is equal to the nature of all phenomena, and he expounds them for others according to what each should hear. This is called the wisdom of unimpeded knowledge of phenomena.

"Great King, you should know that the Śramaṇa Gautama’s unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*) consists in the knowledge of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*) among all phenomena. It is the knowledge of non-self, the knowledge of the absence of sentient beings, the knowledge of the absence of persons, and the knowledge of the absence of a life-span. It is the unobstructed knowledge regarding the past, the boundless knowledge regarding the future, and the knowledge of all modes regarding the present. It is the knowledge of the truths:

the knowledge of suffering as non-composition, the knowledge of origination as non-activity, the knowledge of cessation as intrinsic nature, and the knowledge of the path as the power to reach [liberation]. It is the knowledge that enters into the mental activities of all sentient beings, knowing them all as they truly are. According to what each should hear, he is able to preach for them; this is called the unimpeded knowledge of meaning."

"Great King, you should know! Regarding the Tathāgata Śramaṇa Gautama’s unimpeded knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*): he is fully able to comprehend all sounds and speech. That is to say, he can fully comprehend all the sounds, speech, and written characters of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth. According to the various distinctions among those who should hear, he is able to accord with each specific regional dialect to preach the Dharma and explain its meaning; this is called the unimpeded knowledge of language."

“Great King, you should know that the Śramaṇa Gautama’s unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) means that according to what should be heard and whatever questions are asked, he responds with straightforwardness regarding all speech and written characters as they are distinguished by his mouth; his mind never grows weary or indolent. That is to say, he expounds all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), attainments (*samāpatti*), and the eloquent teachings of the Three Vehicles, responding appropriately to the mental activities of all sentient beings. His words are exquisite and his speech is without obstruction, like flowing water that can never be exhausted; this is called the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence.”
"Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has accomplished these four kinds of unimpeded knowledge; therefore, what I have said is without fault.
The king said:
“Great Master! What are the Tathāgata’s four immeasurable minds? He replied:
“Great King! The four immeasurables are as follows: immeasurable loving-kindness, immeasurable compassion, immeasurable sympathetic joy, and immeasurable equanimity.”
"Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama possesses ten kinds of immeasurable great compassion:
first, impartial great compassion, because he does not discriminate among any sentient beings;..."
Second is the great compassion of benefit, which can open the way to the good realms of devas and humans and to nirvāṇa, while closing off all evil destinies;
third is the great compassion of rescue and protection, which ultimately enables the crossing of all sentient beings over the perilous difficulties of birth and death;
fourth is the great compassion of pity, which does not abandon any sentient being and nurtures their faculties.
Fifth is the great compassion of liberation, because it extinguishes the fever of afflictions of all sentient beings;
sixth is the great compassion that gives birth to bodhi, because it reveals to all sentient beings supreme nirvana and great bodhi;
seventh is the unimpeded great compassion toward all sentient beings, because it emits great radiance that universally illumines the entire realm of sentient beings.
Eighth is the great compassion equal to space, because it rescues and protects all sentient beings;
ninth is the great compassion with objective conditions, because it awakens all sentient beings to the knowledge of the true Dharma;
tenth is the great compassion without objective conditions, because it realizes the true nature of reality that is free from birth and death.
"Great King, you should know!
This is called the immeasurable state of loving-kindness.
Great King, you should know!"
The śramaṇa Gautama possesses ten kinds of immeasurable great compassion:
first, uncommon great compassion, because its nature is that of great compassion;
second, tireless great compassion, because he undergoes great suffering on behalf of all sentient beings.
Third is the great compassion that enters all evil realms, because it dwells within birth and death to deliver sentient beings;
fourth is the great compassion regarding taking birth among devas and humans, because it manifests that all phenomena are entirely impermanent;
fifth is the great compassion that does not abandon sentient beings fixed in wrong views, because it gives rise to the mind of great vows over immeasurable eons to achieve adornment and fulfillment.
Sixth is the great compassion that does not cling to one’s own happiness, because it seeks to bestow happiness upon all sentient beings;
seventh is the great compassion that does not seek recompense, because one’s own mind is pure;
eighth is the great compassion that eliminates the inverted minds of all sentient beings, because it teaches the true Dharma.
Ninth is the great compassion that teaches the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), because it knows that the self-nature of all *dharmadhātus* is intrinsically pure;
tenth is the great compassion that teaches emptiness within emptiness and non-existence, because it is not defiled by adventitious afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Great King, you should know!
This is called immeasurable compassion.
Great King, you should know!"
The śramaṇa Gautama possesses ten kinds of immeasurable great joy:
first, great joy because he celebrates all sentient beings who resolve to attain bodhicitta;
second, great joy because he contemplates all sentient beings relinquishing all modes of existence (bhava).
Third is great sympathetic joy, because one does not give rise to malice toward those who violate the precepts, but rather brings them to spiritual maturity through instruction;
fourth is great sympathetic joy, because one causes all sentient beings engaged in disputes and litigation to achieve reconciliation and attain unsurpassed wisdom;
fifth is great sympathetic joy, because one constantly protects the True Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
Sixth is great joy, because it is far removed from both the mundane and the supramundane;
seventh is great joy, because it causes all sentient beings not to cling to any means of livelihood and to always delight in the True Dharma;
eighth is great joy, because it is not shared with others and is difficult to subdue.

Ninth is great joy, which does not destroy the dharma-realm, causing all sentient beings to constantly delight in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimukti*), and samādhi, so that these may continue without interruption;

tenth is great joy, which causes all sentient beings to single-mindedly seek tranquility, extinguishing distracted minds to attain unsurpassed wisdom, remaining far removed from false views and fulfilling all their aspirations.
This is called the immeasurable mind of sympathetic joy.
"Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama possesses ten kinds of immeasurable minds of great equanimity:

First is great equanimity (*upekṣā*), because one does not add joy to the mind when all sentient beings show respect and make offerings, nor does one give rise to affliction when all sentient beings treat one with contempt or insult;
second is great equanimity, because though one constantly dwells in the world, one is not defiled by the eight worldly dharmas;
third is great equanimity, because knowing the vessel and knowing the time, one maintains a mind of equality toward those who are vessels and those who are not.
Fourth is great equanimity, because it does not bestow upon sentient beings the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, whether they be those in training or those beyond training;
fifth is great equanimity, because it is far removed from all afflictions and habitual tendencies;
sixth is great equanimity, because it does not praise the practice of the two vehicles' bodhi that involves wearying of birth and death.

Seventh is great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*), because it is far removed from speech concerning worldly existence or nirvāṇa, speech that does not lead to dispassion, frivolous speech, speech that afflicts others, and even all speech that obstructs bodhi;
eighth is great equanimity, because if there are sentient beings who must wait for the right time to be transformed, the Tathāgata temporarily relinquishes them therein;
ninth is great equanimity, because if there are sentient beings who should be transformed by the Buddha, he is able to manifest various forms and images according to what they ought to see.

Tenth is great equanimity (*upekṣā*): being far removed from dualistic phenomena, without superior or inferior, without grasping or abandoning, without falsehood or reality; observing with equality, dwelling securely in the truth, and attaining pure patience—this is called the immeasurable mind of equanimity.
"Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished these four immeasurable minds; therefore, what I have said is without fault."
The King said,
“Great Master! What are the characteristics of the five faculties of the Tathāgata?”
He replied: "Great King!
As for the characteristics of the five faculties, they are the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom."
"Great King, you should know that as for the śramaṇa Gautama’s faculty of faith, he has faith in four things.
What are these four things?
First, within the cycle of birth and death, they practice giving with right view and believe in the retribution of karma, such that they would never commit evil even at the cost of their own lives;
second, they believe in the bodhisattva path, do not follow various [wrong] views, and single-mindedly seek bodhi without seeking other vehicles;

third, they have faith and understanding that all phenomena are identical to emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, identical to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and identical to the profound dependent origination of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), being without self, without person, without sentient beings, and free from discrimination.
Fourth, to have faith in all Buddhas’ ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and eighteen unique qualities.
Having thus developed such faith, one eliminates the web of doubts and gathers all Buddha-dharmas; this is called the faculty of faith.
"Great King, you should know this:

regarding the faculty of energy (vīryendriya) of the śramaṇa Gautama, whatever dharma is subsumed under the faculty of faith (śraddhendriya), that dharma is cultivated as the faculty of energy; this is called the faculty of energy."
If a dharma is embraced by the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), that dharma is never forgotten; this is called the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*).

If a dharma is embraced by the faculty of mindfulness, that dharma is neither forgotten nor lost, and the mind is single-pointed and undistracted; this is called the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).

If a dharma is embraced by the faculty of concentration, it is that which is contemplated by wisdom, the very essence of wisdom, which internally illuminates itself, does not depend on others for knowledge, and abides in right practice; this is called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
"Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished these five faculties; therefore, I say there is no fault in my words.
The king said:
“Great Master! What are the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s five powers? He replied:
“Great King! As for the characteristics of the five powers, they are the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.
Great King, you should know this!”

Regarding the power of faith of the śramaṇa Gautama: this faith is single-minded and indestructible; even if a celestial Māra were to transform himself into the body of a Buddha and manifest entering and emerging from meditative concentration and liberation, he could not shake it—this is called the power of faith.

One attains the gateway of firmness regarding all wholesome dharmas; by cultivating various meditative concentrations according to the power thus attained, one cannot be destroyed by gods or humans, and all that was originally vowed is fully accomplished—this is called the power of diligence.
The various dharmas in which one dwells cannot be destroyed by afflictions. Why is this?
Because the power of right mindfulness is able to subdue them; such a power of mindfulness is indestructible, and this is what is called the power of mindfulness.
Staying far removed from clamor, he always delights in solitary wandering; though he speaks with words and sounds, these do not obstruct the first dhyāna.
He dwells skillfully in vitarka and vicāra, which do not obstruct the second dhyāna;
his mind gives rise to joy, which does not obstruct the third dhyāna.
Although he delights in teaching and transforming all sentient beings, he does not abandon the Buddha-dharma, nor is he hindered by the mind of the fourth dhyāna.

When practicing the four dhyānas, he encounters no obstacles from factors that impede meditative concentration; he neither abandons these concentrations nor is he bound by them, yet he is able to take birth freely in various places—this is called the power of concentration.

Knowing both mundane and supramundane dharmas, there is not a single dharma that can destroy this wisdom. In whatever place of birth one may be, all arts and skills are naturally known without being received from a teacher. All the ascetic practices of the world's non-Buddhists are able to be undertaken and practiced for the sake of transforming sentient beings; this supramundane dharma, which enables one to transcend the world, is accomplished through the power of wisdom, and is thus called the power of wisdom.
"Great King, you should know!
The śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished these five powers; therefore, I say that there is no fault in him.
The King said:
“Great Teacher!
What are the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s seven factors of awakening? He replied:

“Great King! The seven factors of enlightenment are as follows: the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment of energy, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.”

"Great King, you should know that as for the awakening factor of mindfulness of the śramaṇa Gautama, it is able to contemplate all phenomena, to discern phenomena, and also to observe the specific characteristics of all phenomena."
What is their specific characteristic?
To contemplate that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, and to maintain mindfulness of such thorough awakening, is called the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

If one can discern and clearly understand the eighty-four thousand aggregates of teachings—just as those understood phenomena are: understanding what is of definitive meaning as being of definitive meaning, what is not of definitive meaning as being not of definitive meaning, conventional truth as being conventional truth, ultimate truth as being ultimate truth, and provisional designations as being provisional designations—and if one correctly understands them without doubt, discerning and selecting such phenomena, this is called the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

If one contemplates the dharma, discriminates the dharma, rejoices in the dharma, relies upon the dharma, concentrates on the dharma, and relinquishes attachment to the dharma; if one embraces these with wisdom, exerts courageous diligence, desires non-retrogression, and zealously practices advancement, not abandoning the original intention while walking the right path—this is called the awakening factor of diligence (*vīrya-sambodhyaṅga*).

Within the immeasurable, pure, and supreme dharma of bliss practiced in cultivation, the mind gives rise to joy and delight without indolence; this exultant joy can eliminate all afflictions of body and mind, and is thus called the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

If one removes the defilements of afflictions from body and mind, leaves behind the hindrances, enters the sphere of meditative concentration, and causes the mind to abide correctly, this is called the awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
One is able to fully awaken to and comprehend whatever meditative absorption one enters; it is not the case that one awakens to the Dharma without entering absorption.

Furthermore, one comprehends all views, afflictions, fetters, and bonds, such that the mind is equanimous and all phenomena are seen as having no distinct characteristics. To be able to awaken in this way is called the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

If, regarding phenomena that cause sorrow or joy, one’s mind does not sink, nor is it led astray by worldly dharmas; if there is neither high nor low, but one abides upright and immovable; if there are no outflows (*āsrava*), no joy, and no attachment, and one is free from all obstructions, conforming to the ultimate truth and following the straight path—this is called the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
"Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished these seven factors of enlightenment; therefore, I say that he is without fault.
The king said:
“Great Master! What are the eight factors of the noble path of the Tathāgata? He replied:
"Great King! The eight factors of the noble path are as follows: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration."
Great King, you should know this:

as for the right view of the śramaṇa Gautama, if one perceives the supramundane, one does not give rise to views of a self, a person, a sentient being, a life-span, a nourisher, a soul, nor of nihilism, eternalism, existence, or non-existence; furthermore, one does not give rise to views of the wholesome, the unwholesome, or the indeterminate, nor even give rise to the dualistic view of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa—this is called right view.

If one gives rise to those afflictions such as greed, anger, and delusion, this is called improper; if one does not give rise to these things but contemplates only morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, being able to contemplate thus and abide within the aggregate of morality, it is called right reflection.
Whatever one says, it shall not cause harm or affliction to oneself or others; by accomplishing such wholesome speech and giving rise to the right path, this is called Right Speech.
If an action is black with a black retribution, or white with a white retribution;
or if an action is both black and white with a black-and-white retribution—one must never dare to commit such acts.
However, as for an action that is neither black nor white, which has a retribution that is neither black nor white—[one may perform it].
If an action can exhaust other actions, that action must be performed; this is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*).

Practicing the noble lineages, the dhūta ascetic practices, and the proper deportment—remaining unshakable and unwavering, free from all guile and flattery, and not being led astray by worldly gain and offerings—one does not feel feverish envy upon seeing others obtain profit, and one always knows contentment regarding one’s own gains. Such right conduct is praised by the Noble Ones; this is called right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*).
If diligence is directed toward what is wrong, it is not praised by the Noble Ones—namely, the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion—and such right diligence is never applied to them;
however, if a practice can lead one into the Noble Path of the True Realities and toward the tranquility of Nirvana, that is right diligence.

If mindfulness is not lost, one remains unmoved within the Dharma; being upright and without crookedness, one perceives the faults of birth and death and advances to seek nirvana. Binding the mind so as not to forget, one does not lose the right path—this is called right mindfulness.
If one is concentrated and undistracted, dwelling in this concentration regarding all phenomena, one achieves right determination; this is called right concentration.
Great King, you should know that those who dwell in this samādhi achieve right determination for the sake of bringing liberation to all sentient beings; this is called right concentration.
This Eightfold Noble Path is that which has been practiced by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present; it is therefore called the Noble Path.
Great King, you should know this!

The śramaṇa Gautama is fully endowed with these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; because he relies upon these dharmas, the śramaṇa Gautama is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Therefore, what I have said is without fault.
And he spoke in verse:
“Gautama has attained mastery Over the four foundations of mindfulness, The four right efforts,
And all the meditative concentrations and samādhis.”
Gautama alone has reached the ultimate; there is no second person.
Therefore it is said that Gautama is free from all faults.
Gautama’s path of supernormal power is most supreme and beyond compare.
Having cultivated the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and fully reached the other shore,
the Great Sage is able to skillfully understand the differences among those who are vessels for liberation;
therefore, knowing them as they truly are, he is able to purify all sentient beings.
Having attained mastery in the holy life (brahmacarya), and having attained right view, tranquility, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, one is therefore free from fault.
The water of the Eightfold Noble Path is pure and free from turbidity.
He washes all sinful beings and clothes them in the precious raiment of the seven factors of enlightenment.
He leads them to that immovable state, the fearless realm of nirvāṇa;
therefore, it is said of Gautama that he is free from all faults.
Gautama is like a bull-king, alone surpassing all the herds;
all the sages revere and look up to him, for there is none in the world equal to him.
Free from all evils, he is fully endowed with every merit.
"Constantly mindful of benefiting the world, he is therefore free from fault.
Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished ten kinds of powers of knowledge!"
The King said: "Great Master!
What are the ten kinds of powers of knowledge of the Tathāgata?"

He replied: “Great King, the ten powers are as follows: the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible; the power of knowing the ripening of karma; the power of knowing the various dispositions of beings; the power of knowing the inclinations of others; the power of knowing the degrees of the faculties of others; the power of knowing the paths leading to all destinations; the power of knowing meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and equanimities; the power of knowing past lives; the power of knowing the divine eye; and the power of knowing the exhaustion of the outflows.”
"Great King, you should know this!

As for the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), it is the wisdom that definitively understands cause and effect; it knows that from this cause such a fruit will arise, and that such a fruit will not arise;
it knows that practicing unwholesome conduct will certainly result in a painful retribution and will never produce a pleasant retribution."
Practicing wholesome causes will certainly yield pleasant fruits and never produce bitter fruits;
where there is such a principle, there is this retribution, and where there is not, there is no such retribution.
This is called the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*).
"Great King, you should know!

Regarding the Tathāgata’s power of knowing the accumulation of karma through wisdom: he is able to know, as it truly is, the fruits and retributions obtained from all karmas of the past, future, and present; he knows the locations and the specific matters, and he knows the causes and the effects. While some may claim that past events have ceased and are entirely non-existent, the Śramaṇa Gautama teaches that although the past lacks manifest characteristics, this karma is capable of obtaining retribution in a future life."

If there are karmic actions that are the cause for śrāvakas, the cause for pratyekabuddhas, the cause for bodhisattvas, or the cause for tathāgatas, the śramaṇa Gautama is able to fully know them all; this is called the power of knowing the accumulation of karma.

"Great King, you should know! Regarding the power of knowing desires, the śramaṇa Gautama is able to know, as they truly are, the various inclinations and pleasures of all sentient beings. He knows which sentient beings delight in the five desires; he knows which sentient beings delight in cultivating the path; he knows which sentient beings abide in the group of those fixed in error; he knows which sentient beings abide in the group of those fixed in correctness; he knows which sentient beings abide in the group of those not yet fixed; he knows which sentient beings delight in the path of the śrāvaka; he knows which sentient beings delight in the path of the pratyekabuddha; and he knows which sentient beings delight in the unsurpassed path."
Having understood this, he teaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate, extensively delivering all sentient beings.
This is called the power of knowing the inclinations [of others].
"Great King, you should know!"
As for the power of knowing dispositions possessed by the Śramaṇa Gautama, he is able to know, according to reality, the immeasurable varieties of the dispositions of all sentient beings:

the tainted disposition, the untainted disposition, the mundane disposition, the supramundane disposition, the permanent disposition, the impermanent disposition, the disposition of the dharma-realm, and the non-differentiated disposition. Furthermore, he knows the dispositions that sentient beings delight in practicing and which have become difficult to change; he knows the desires arising from those dispositions and the inclinations they take up. He knows their wholesome and unwholesome dispositions, as well as the arising of the disposition of a śrāvaka, the disposition of a pratyekabuddha, and the disposition for unsurpassed bodhi—all of which he knows as they truly are, and accordingly preaches the Dharma to them.
This is called the power of knowing the faculties.

"Great King, you should know that as for the śramaṇa Gautama’s power of knowing the faculties, he is able to know, according to reality, the differences among the faculties of all sentient beings. He knows the outflow-tainted faculties and the outflow-free faculties; he knows the sharp faculties and the dull faculties; he knows their increase and decrease. He is able to know greed, anger, and delusion, and their immeasurable varieties, each with its own degree of lightness or heaviness—all of which he knows exactly as they are."
He knows the faculties that can increase birth and death; he knows the faculties that can diminish birth and death;
he knows the wholesome faculties and the unwholesome faculties; he knows the faculties that are neither wholesome nor unwholesome;

and he knows the faculty of the eye, the faculty of the ear, the faculty of the nose, the faculty of the tongue, the faculty of the body, the faculty of the mind, the male faculty, the female faculty, and the life-faculty.
The faculties: the faculty of suffering, the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of grief, the faculty of joy, the faculty of equanimity;

the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom; the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of knowing, and the faculty of one who has known.
One knows the cause of the eye-faculty up to the cause of the mind-faculty, and one knows the cause of the ear-faculty.

Taking the eye-faculty as a condition, one knows the nose-faculty as its cause; taking the nose-faculty as a condition, one knows the tongue-faculty as its cause; taking the tongue-faculty as a condition, one knows the body-faculty as its cause.
One knows that the adornment of precepts enables the cultivation of giving, and that the adornment of giving enables the cultivation of precepts.
One knows who may be taught giving and who may be taught the precepts; this applies likewise even to wisdom.

He is able to know who may be taught the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; he knows who may be taught the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the unsurpassed Buddha-vehicle. He knows those with the faculties of a pratyekabuddha who study the vehicle of the śrāvakas;
he knows those with the faculties of a perfectly awakened one who study the vehicles of the śrāvakas or the pratyekabuddhas;
and he knows how a person of inferior faculties can cultivate superior faculties, and how a person of superior faculties cultivates inferior faculties.

Knowing that the faculties of sentient beings are not yet ready to be tamed, he gives rise to a mind of equanimity; toward those who can be subdued, he preaches the True Dharma. He knows the signs of faculties being mature or immature, the signs of immaturity becoming maturity, the signs of neither immaturity nor maturity, and the signs of maturity within maturity. Knowing the faculty of birth and death, knowing the faculty of liberation, knowing the faculty of adornment, and knowing the faculty of fulfillment—having known them thus, he preaches the Dharma for them.
This is called the power of knowledge regarding the faculties (*indriya-jñāna-bala*). "Great King,

you should know that as for the Śramaṇa Gautama’s power of knowledge regarding the path leading to various destinations (*gati-gāminī-pratipad-jñāna-bala*), he is able to know, according to reality, that those who practice this path will fall [into such-and-such a state]."
From the hells up to birth in the heavens, those who practice this path attain nirvāṇa. All such karma arises from the roots, desires, and dispositions;

by knowing that tainted (*sāsrava*) karma leads to birth in the five destinies, while untainted (*anāsrava*) karma leads to the attainment of nirvāṇa, one is thus able to know the group of those fixed in the right, the group fixed in the wrong, and the indeterminate group.
They know the power of causes and the power of karmic retribution; they know the causes and conditions for merit in past lives, and the causes and conditions for adornment in the present life.
They know those who are difficult to tame and those who are easy to tame; they provide concise explanations for the extensive and extensive explanations for the concise.
They know which sentient beings are capable of attaining liberation, and which sentient beings will not attain liberation.

Knowing those who are indeterminate, one teaches the Dharma according to what they should hear: that by encountering a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), they may abide in the group of those destined for rightness (samyaktva-niyāma);
yet if they do not obtain a virtuous friend, there will be no liberation. Having known this, one preaches the Dharma accordingly.
This is called the power of knowing the path that leads to the various destinations.

"Great King, you should know that as for the śramaṇa Gautama’s power of knowledge regarding meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi), he knows meditative concentrations, liberations (vimokṣa), samādhis, and attainments (samāpatti) as they truly are; he knows their defilement, their purification, their maintenance, and their increase. He knows that by these causes and conditions, sentient beings greedily delight in birth and death, and by these causes and conditions, they greedily delight in nirvāṇa."
What is called "cause" (hetu) and what is called "condition" (pratyaya)?

To know that the unwholesome thoughts of sentient beings are the cause and condition for birth and death: because of unwholesome thought, ignorance (avidyā) arises and grows; therefore, unwholesomeness is the cause and ignorance is the condition. Because of ignorance, volitional formations (saṃskāra) arise; therefore, ignorance is the cause and the various formations are the conditions. In this manner, up to: because of birth, there is old age, death, and other sufferings; therefore, birth is the cause and old age and death are the conditions.
Afflictions are the cause and various karmas are the condition;
various views are the cause and the fetter of craving is the condition;
afflictions are the cause and the five hindrances are the condition.
These are called causes and these are called conditions; yet all sentient beings, by means of these causes and conditions, crave and delight in birth and death.
For what cause and condition do they crave and delight in nirvana?
There are two causes and two dharmas that cause all sentient beings to delight in nirvana:
first, the joy of listening to the Dharma;
second, the joy of right reflection.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas: first, śamatha; second, vipaśyanā.
Furthermore, they know that through the causes and conditions of preaching the Dharma, one attains the samādhi of śrāvakas, the samādhi of pratyekabuddhas, and the samādhi of bodhisattvas.
Having known this, they preach the Dharma for others.
This is called the power of knowledge regarding the recollection of meditative concentrations.

"Great King, you should know that as for the Śramaṇa Gautama’s power of knowledge regarding past lives, he is able to know, according to reality, all his own past places of birth—whether with form or formless, their lineage and names, their food and drink, their complexion, appearance, and physical features, their suffering and happiness, and the length of their lifespans. He remembers how others pass away from one existence and are born into another; just as he knows his own past, so too does he know that of others."
He knows the karmic causes possessed by these sentient beings, and how these beings, having created such karmic causes, obtain other bodies.

He knows the minds and causal conditions of all sentient beings, and how, after such [conditions] have ceased, minds arise in succession; he fully knows that throughout the three periods of time there is neither beginning nor end. He exhorts all sentient beings to contemplate the fruits of retribution—suffering and joy—resulting from the good and evil deeds performed in the past.
Having known this, he preaches the Dharma according to what each being ought to hear.
This is called the power of knowledge of recollecting past lives.
"Great King, you should know!"

Regarding the śramaṇa Gautama’s power of knowledge through the divine eye: he knows and sees, according to reality, the birth, death, and falling away of all sentient beings; whether they experience beautiful forms or ugly forms, whether they are born into a good existence or a bad existence—he understands the causes of their various karmas with complete clarity. He knows that certain sentient beings have committed evil through body, speech, and mind, have slandered the noble ones, and increased their wrong views; because of these evil karmas, after casting off this body, they immediately fall into hell.

He also knows that certain sentient beings have performed good through body, speech, and mind, have not slandered the noble ones, and have increased their right views; by reason of these karmic conditions, after casting off this body, they are immediately born into a good existence.

They are able to see the worlds of the Buddhas of the ten directions as being without limit or boundary, just like space which is immeasurable; they see all sentient beings at the time of their birth and at the time of their death, and they see all worlds at the time of their formation and at the time of their destruction. They also know when sentient beings resolve upon Bodhicitta and at the time of its arising and ceasing. They see all Buddhas when they first attain perfect enlightenment, turn the wheel of the True Dharma, and enter Nirvana. They see the various Śrāvakas after they have realized liberation and taken Nirvana. They see the various Pratyekabuddhas using their supernormal powers to repay the kindness of the faithful offerings made by sentient beings.

Such matters as these cannot be seen by any of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas who possess the five supernormal powers. The śramaṇa Gautama’s divine eye has achieved such merit that, by means of this divine eye, he observes all sentient beings: who should be transformed and delivered by the Buddha, and who, moreover, should be transformed and delivered by a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
Having seen this, he manifests his body and preaches the Dharma according to those who are ready to be saved.
This is called the power of knowledge regarding the divine eye.
"Great King, you should know!"
Regarding the power of the śramaṇa Gautama’s knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows: since all his outflows have been exhausted and he is ultimately liberated, he proclaims:
"Birth for me has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further existence."
The Buddha’s knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows is pure and subtle.
It is called "pure" because it is free from habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). The wisdom of the śrāvakas, however, is limited and finite. Why is this?
Because there are residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*),
the wisdom of the pratyekabuddha is likewise limited. Why is this?
Because they lack great compassion.
The Buddha’s knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows is immeasurable and boundless. Why is this?

Because he knows all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), because he has fully accomplished all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), and because he has forever severed all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), he embraces the adornments of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and great compassion (*karuṇā*) and the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). Regarding all dharmas, he is free from the habit of grasping at signs; he cannot be surpassed by anything in the world, and whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, he is without any fault. He is like space—pure and unobstructed, unmixed with smoke or clouds.

The Buddha’s knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*) is likewise: because it is unmixed with any habitual tendencies of affliction (*kleśavāsanā*), he is able to preach the Dharma for all sentient beings, causing those who hear it to sever all afflictions; this is called the power of knowing the destruction of the outflows.

"Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished these ten kinds of powers of knowledge (*jñānabala*). Because he is adorned with them, he is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; therefore, what I have said is without fault."
And he spoke in verse:
“The Buddhas know, as they truly are, what is possible and what is impossible;
as great Honored Ones who speak the truth, they are therefore without fault.”
Regarding all past lives, his holy illumination is unimpeded;
regarding the future and the present, his wisdom is never deluded or lost.
Concerning karma and the retribution of karma, he possesses the knowledge of all causes and their effects.
He is able to know all things as they truly are; for this reason, he is called a Buddha.
Regarding the immeasurable natures of worldly beings, he knows them all in their various ways as they truly are;
being well-versed in these natures, he is called the Peerless One.
The various kinds of faith in the world, And those who possess immeasurable faith— He knows them through wisdom as they truly are; Therefore, his words do not differ from reality.
He knows those of inferior faculties as they truly are, And he knows those of middling faculties.
Knowing the ripening of the faculties as they truly are, he has attained mastery over the faculties.
The World-Honored One knows, as they truly are, the paths that lead to all destinations;
through his powers, supernormal knowledges, faculties, and meditative concentrations, he is the one who has awakened to the factors of enlightenment and liberation.
Knowing both defilement and purity, he understands their distinctions as they truly are;
the Tathāgata is without obstruction, for he is free from all hindrances.
Regarding his past immeasurable births, he perceives them through the power of various kinds of knowledge.
The wise know their own bodies and those of others as they truly are.
With the Buddha’s stainless, pure eye— which transcends the worlds of gods and humans—
he relies upon that purified vision to see beings being born and passing away.
The knowledge that all outflows are exhausted, And the knowledge of liberation— Whatever untainted realm there may be, The Noble One knows it as it truly is.
This power is unequaled; The Buddha, the World-Honored One, is sovereign.
Manifesting within a single mind, yet the mind remains without discrimination;
neither grasping nor rejecting, it appears spontaneously.
Like a wheel that turns of its own accord based on its original momentum, it revolves naturally.
In a single thought-moment, one knows truly all the mental activities of sentient beings;
regarding both the mind and sentient beings, one does not give rise to the two kinds of dualistic marks.
Within all phenomena, one is fully endowed with all virtues.
Therefore it is said: "Gautama is sovereign and free from fault.
The Great Sāṃkhyāyana Nirgrantha-putra Bhāṣita Sūtra, Scroll Eight.
