Chapter Eight, Part Four: The Tathāgata’s Faultless Merits.
"Great King, you should know!
“The śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately achieved the four fearlessnesses.
The king said, “Great Master!”
"What are the four fearlessnesses of the Tathāgata? He replied, "Great King!"

These are: the fearlessness of all-knowledge, the fearlessness of the exhaustion of outflows, the fearlessness regarding obstacles to the path, and the fearlessness regarding the path to the end of suffering.
"Great King, you should know this!"
Regarding the fearlessness of omniscience: the śramaṇa Gautama has fully awakened to and known all dharmas.
If any among the world—whether devas, humans, māras, brahmās, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas—should say, "The śramaṇa Gautama is unable to awaken to and know all dharmas," [he remains unshaken].
To say that one speaks according to reality in such a manner is impossible. Why is this?
Because the śramaṇa Gautama has fully awakened to the knowledge of all dharmas; therefore, he is called the Perfectly Enlightened One (Samyaksaṃbuddha).

That which is called the dharmas of ordinary persons, the dharmas of noble ones, the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of buddhas, the dharmas of bodhisattvas, the dharmas of those in training, the dharmas of those beyond training, mundane dharmas, supramundane dharmas, wholesome dharmas, unwholesome dharmas, tainted dharmas, untainted dharmas, conditioned dharmas, and unconditioned dharmas—to awaken to such dharmas is therefore called "Perfect Awakening."
As for "equality," it means equality in seeing emptiness, because phenomena are truly real;
equality in signlessness, because all signs are destroyed;
and equality in wishlessness, because one does not cling to the triple world.
The equality of non-arising, because of the nature of non-arising;
the equality of non-activity, because of the nature of non-activity;
the equality of non-emergence, because of the nature of non-emergence.
It is equal in having no destination, because its nature is to have no destination;
it is equal in reality, because there are no three periods of time;
it is equal in liberation, because it has no nature of ignorance.
Nirvana is equal, because it lacks the nature of birth and death.
For this reason, the śramaṇa Gautama is fully able to awaken to and know all dharmas, reaching the state of fearlessness.
With a heart of great compassion, he utters the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly and turns the Brahma-wheel of Dharma.
Among all those in the world—gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—none have ever been able to turn it in accordance with the Dharma; this is called the fearlessness of omniscience.
“Great King, you should know!

To speak thus according to reality is impossible. Why is this?

The śramaṇa Gautama has exhausted all outflows; regarding the outflow of desire, the outflow of existence, the outflow of ignorance, and the outflow of views, his mind has attained liberation, and all residual habit-energies have been extinguished.
Therefore, the Śramaṇa Gautama, having exhausted all outflows and attained the state of fearlessness, utters the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly and turns the Brahma wheel of Dharma.
No one in the entire world—whether devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas—has ever been able to turn it in such a manner; this is called the fearlessness of the exhaustion of outflows.
"Great King, you should know!
Regarding the fearlessness of one who obstructs the path: the śramaṇa Gautama knows that all sensual desires can obstruct the Noble Path;
therefore he says, 'Sensual desires can obstruct the path.'"
If any among the world’s devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas should say:
"These dharmas of sensual desire cannot obstruct the path," [one should know that they speak falsely].
"One who speaks thus is not speaking according to reality; such a thing is impossible. Why is this?
Because the śramaṇa Gautama has realized, exactly as they are, those dharmas that obstruct the path."
Regarding the dharmas that obstruct the path: it is said that the ten unwholesome karmic actions can obstruct the Noble Path. Śramaṇa Gautama!
You are able to know things as they truly are and have reached the state of fearlessness; you roar the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly and turn the Brahma wheel of Dharma.

In all the world—among gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brahmins—none have ever been able to turn it in accordance with the Dharma; this is called the fearlessness of proclaiming the obstacles to the path.
"Great King, you should know!
Regarding the fearlessness of the path to the exhaustion of suffering, the śramaṇa Gautama declares:
'By cultivating the noble path, one can reach the end of suffering and attain unsurpassed liberation.'"
If any among the world’s gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas should say:
"The cultivation of the noble path cannot lead to the ultimate exhaustion of the limits of all suffering," [one should know that this is not so].
To say that one who speaks thus is possible—that cannot be. Why is this?
Because the śramaṇa Gautama has already realized unsurpassed liberation and exhausted all suffering.
What is called the true noble path?
It is the so-called One Vehicle;
furthermore, there are two kinds, namely śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Furthermore, there are three kinds, namely the emptiness samādhi, the signless samādhi, and the wishless samādhi;
furthermore, there are seven dharmas, namely the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
This is called the ultimately true Noble Path.

As for the ultimate path, it neither increases nor decreases; it is without grasping or abandoning, without clinging or letting go; it is neither correct nor erroneous, neither one nor two. This is called the truly ultimate right path.
The śramaṇa Gautama, knowing reality as it truly is, has attained the state of fearlessness; amidst the great assembly, he roars the lion’s roar and turns the Brahma-wheel of Dharma.

Among all the worlds—gods, humans, Māras, Brahmas, śramaṇas, and brahmins—none have ever been able to turn it in accordance with the Dharma. This is called the fearlessness regarding the path to the exhaustion of suffering.

“Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished these four kinds of fearless wisdom and is able to roar the lion’s roar; therefore, what I have said is without fault.”
And he spoke in verse:
“Gautama is like a lion; Dwelling among the multitude, he speaks without fear.
In this world there is none equal to him, How much less could there be one who surpasses him?”
Gautama has realized all phenomena as they truly are, without falsehood;
because of this true vision, he utters the roar of the lion-king.
If anyone should say that what Gautama says is not correct, [they would be speaking falsely].
Gautama cannot see such a place; because he does not perceive such signs, he stands among gods and humans,
roaring the lion’s roar with mastery, emitting the wondrous sound of fearlessness.
Gautama’s outflows are exhausted; having attained the body of no-outflows, he has transcended the worlds of gods and humans; therefore, he is said to be peerless.
For the sake of sentient beings, Gautama teaches the various dharmas that obstruct the Path.
All things are exactly as they are, Therefore, I do not speak falsely.
Gautama teaches the path of progress; He speaks thus from his own realization.
For those who practice that Dharma, There shall be no obstacles whatsoever.
Gautama, knowing thus, has reached the supreme state of fearlessness;
having attained fearless, wondrous bliss, Gautama dwells in peace.
He turns the sublime Wheel of Dharma, which no other has ever turned before.
"Worldly people cannot turn it back, except for the Honored One among Two-legged Beings.
Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma)."
The king said: "Great Master!
What are the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) of a Tathāgata?"
He replied: "Great King!
The unique qualities of the śramaṇa Gautama are as follows: "
There is not a single fault whatsoever; this is called an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because the bodily actions (*kāyakarman*) of the śramaṇa Gautama are free from error.
The absence of all faults is called the "unshared quality" (āveṇika-dharma). Why is this?
Because the verbal karma of the śramaṇa Gautama is free from error.
The absence of all delusions is called the "unshared quality" (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because the mental action (*manas-karman*) of the śramaṇa Gautama is free from error.
The absence of various marks is called the "unshared dharma" (āveṇika-dharma). Why is this?
Because when the śramaṇa Gautama receives offerings, he does not give rise to pride, and when he receives insults or humiliation, he does not give rise to a sense of inferiority.
The state of having no unconcentrated mind is called an uncommon quality. Why is this?
Because the śramaṇa Gautama is always in meditative concentration whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, speaking, or remaining silent.
The mind that never fails to abide in equanimity is called the unique quality (āveṇika-dharma). Why is this?

Because the śramaṇa Gautama has cultivated the body, cultivated ethical discipline, cultivated the mind, cultivated wisdom, and severed delusion; therefore, this is called noble equanimity (āryopekṣā).
The desire for no rest is called the unique quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because the Śramaṇa Gautama teaches the Dharma with great loving-kindness and great compassion to deliver sentient beings, abiding securely in tranquility without increase or decrease.
Unceasing diligence is called an uncommon quality.
Why is this? Because the śramaṇa Gautama undergoes great suffering and affliction for the sake of all sentient beings throughout immeasurable kalpas, yet never gives rise to weariness or aversion.
The quality of mindfulness without cessation is called an uncommon dharma (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?

When the śramaṇa Gautama first attained the Way, he universally observed the minds of all sentient beings—past, future, and present—and subsequently taught them the Dharma without needing to observe them again, because he did not lose his prior mindfulness.
Wisdom that never ceases is called an uncommon quality (āveṇika-dharma). Why is this?
Because the śramaṇa Gautama recollects and does not forget throughout the three periods of time.
Liberation without cessation is called the unique quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?

The Śramaṇa Gautama did not learn from a teacher but attained spontaneous awakening; he is not like those of the Two Vehicles who learn from others, for [his realization] arises through causes and conditions.
The uninterrupted knowledge and vision of liberation is called the unique quality (āveṇika-dharma). Why is this?

Because the śramaṇa Gautama has attained unimpeded wisdom; he knows all meanings, all syllables, and all phrases, for he can explain the meaning of even a single phrase for immeasurable eons without ever reaching an end.
All bodily actions have wisdom as their basis; this succession of wisdom is called the "unshared dharma. Why is this?
Because all the bodily actions of the śramaṇa Gautama proceed in accordance with wisdom.
All vocal karma has wisdom as its basis; this successive unfolding is called the "unshared dharma. Why is this?
Because all the vocal karma of the śramaṇa Gautama proceeds in accordance with wisdom.
All mental actions have wisdom as their basis; this successive progression is called the "unshared dharma. Why is this?
Because all the mental actions of the śramaṇa Gautama proceed in accordance with wisdom.
Knowing the past without obstruction or hindrance is called an unshared quality (*āveṇika-dharma*).
Why is this? Because the śramaṇa Gautama possesses the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).
Knowing the future world without obstruction or hindrance is called the unique quality (āveṇika-dharma).
Why? Because the śramaṇa Gautama has attained the clarity of the divine eye (divyacakṣus).
Knowing the present world without obstruction or hindrance is called the unique quality (āveṇika-dharma).
Why is this? Because the śramaṇa Gautama has attained the clear knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya-vidyā).
The "unseen summit" is called an uncommon dharma. Why is this?
Because the Śramaṇa Gautama possesses a boundless body.
That which cannot be surpassed is called the "unshared dharma" (āveṇika-dharma). Why is this?
Because the śramaṇa Gautama has transcended all devas, humans, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
Sentient beings each perceive [the Buddha] as being before themselves; this is called the "unshared quality" (*āveṇika-dharma*).
Why is this? Because the body of the śramaṇa Gautama is inconceivable.
All his speech is called an uncommon quality because those who hear it give rise to wholesome states; why is this?
Because the śramaṇa Gautama has accomplished all virtues.
The sound of the teaching of the Dharma is called the "unshared quality" because it is heard according to the capacity of each recipient. Why is this?
Because the śramaṇa Gautama well knows that for others [who lack such capacity], hearing it would be of no benefit.
The purity of one’s speech is called an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because the śramaṇa Gautama never utters words that are not meaningful.
The fact that the words spoken by the Exponent of the Exit—whether harsh or gentle—are heard with joy by those who hear them is called an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because the mind of the Śramaṇa Gautama is impartial, being free from enmity toward enemies or affection for kin.
The spoken sounds and words, which those who hear never tire of, are called the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because the śramaṇa Gautama speaks with such subtle refinement.
Fearlessness when amidst the assembly is called an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because the Śramaṇa Gautama has purified all obstructions to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The absence of timidity when speaking before a multitude is called an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because the Śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
Speaking according to one's inclinations is called an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because the śramaṇa Gautama thoroughly knows the minds of all sentient beings.
The disciples’ tranquility is called an uncommon quality. Why is this?
Because all the followers of the śramaṇa Gautama comply with and receive his teachings.
That which causes those who see it to be free from affliction and eliminates all that is unwholesome is called the "unshared dharma" (āveṇika-dharma). Why is this?
Because the śramaṇa Gautama constantly vows that his body shall be like the king of medicinal trees.
That those who behold him never tire of doing so is called an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why?
Because the śramaṇa Gautama is able to cause all who see him to awaken to all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*).
Turning his body to look back like a great elephant king is called an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because the śramaṇa Gautama gazes like a dragon king, his majestic deportment being pure.
To be able to roar the lion’s roar amidst the fourfold assembly is called an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because the śramaṇa Gautama is fully endowed with the ten powers (*daśabala*) and is thus skilled at resolving the doubts of the multitude.
Constantly receiving supreme offerings is called the "unshared dharma. Why is this?
Because the śramaṇa Gautama is the unsurpassed field of merit.
Merit that is inexhaustible is called the "unshared dharmas. Why is this?
Because the various practices cultivated by the śramaṇa Gautama do not seek karmic retribution.
That which cannot be destroyed by any devas, humans, Māras, or Brahmās is called an "unshared dharma" (āveṇika-dharma).
Why is this? Because within each and every joint there is the strength of Nārāyaṇa.
The fact that the matters he records are free from error or falsehood is called the "unshared quality" (āveṇika-dharma).
Why is this? Because he thoroughly understands all the faculties (indriya) and underlying tendencies (anuśaya).
Knowing all conditioned phenomena is called the unique quality (āveṇikadharma). Why?
Because the śramaṇa Gautama has awakened to all phenomena.
All wisdom that is free from doubt and turbidity is called an uncommon quality (*āveṇikadharma*). Why is this?
Because the śramaṇa Gautama possesses pure knowledge of the three periods of time.
The exhaustion of the habitual tendencies of afflictions is called the unique quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because the śramaṇa Gautama is skillfully able to purify the causes of affliction.
To be the foremost teacher among all the world’s multitudes—gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—is called an uncommon quality (āveṇika-dharma). Why is this so?
Because the śramaṇa Gautama has thoroughly penetrated the characteristics of all dharmas,
the dharma-body he has attained is called the "unshared dharma. Why is this?
Because the lifespan of the śramaṇa Gautama is inexhaustible, seeing, hearing, and drawing near to him yield great benefit; this is called an uncommon quality (āveṇika-dharma). Why is this so?
Because the śramaṇa Gautama has accomplished wholesome dharmas and his three karmas are not in vain,
one who sheds his blood commits a crime of immediate retribution (ānantarya), which is termed an "unshared dharma" (asaṃdhāraṇa-dharma). Why is this?
"Because the śramaṇa Gautama has accomplished unsurpassed, supreme, and wholesome roots,
Great King, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has ultimately accomplished such uncommon qualities; therefore, what I have said is without fault."
And he spoke these verses:
"Gautama is without fault, Nor does he possess any habitual tendencies;
All his thoughts are pure— Such a wise one is without fault."
All things are without differing marks, yet the mind does not forget them;
the mind of equanimity is not without action, and all desires are never diminished.
With diligence free from indolence, mindfulness is never lost.
Liberated through wisdom, one does not fall back; right view is without loss or diminution.
Wisdom is unshakable, and the same is true for the actions of body and speech.
With wisdom as the root, they thus proceed in constant succession.
His constant wisdom is free from fault; it was so in the past, and likewise in the future and the present, unobstructed in all places.
Gautama is a wise one, possessing such virtues as these.
"There are further superior dharmas, O Lord of the Earth, which cannot be numbered.
The King said: "Great Master!"
Is the Tathāgata’s body, adorned with such perfected merits,
permanent or impermanent?
Are such merits subject to exhaustion?
"Is it for the sake of inexhaustibility? He replied, "Great King!"
The śramaṇa Gautama abides in these meritorious qualities; having reached the end of birth and death, this is his final body, a body that is eternally abiding and not impermanent.
Great King, you should know this!
"Do not regard the Gautama as being identical to impermanence.
The King said, "Great Master!"
"How should one contemplate such an eternal body?
He replied, "Great King!"
Just as one contemplates the body of one's own dharma-nature, so too does one contemplate the Dharma-body of Gautama.
This body is form, yet it cannot be seen as form;
this body is mind, yet it cannot be known as mind.
This body is a torch, for its nature is not dark;
this body is courageous and strong, for it subdues all evils;
this body is power, for there is nothing that can subdue it.
This body is without contradiction, for its nature is equal;
this body is empty, for it is free from seeing and hearing;
this body is signless, for it is free from applied and sustained thought.
This body is wishless, for it has transcended the triple world;
this body is of a single characteristic, for it is devoid of diverse characteristics;
this body is like empty space, for it has no resemblance.
This body is not born, because it arises from conditions;
this body does not perish, because it was originally unborn;
this body does not abide, because it does not belong to the three periods of time.
This body is not a spatial direction, yet it is not separate from spatial directions;
this body is not a sentient being, yet it is not separate from all sentient beings.
Great King, you should know this!
One who contemplates in this manner is said to contemplate the eternal body; they are said to see the Dharma-body.
Great King, you should know that such contemplation is called right contemplation.
"If one views it otherwise, it is called wrong view.
The King said, "Great Master!"
"How is it that that which is not born arises from conditions?
"Great King, you should know:
the Dharma-body is not born, because it arises from conditions."
The King said: "Great Master!
How does it arise from conditions?"
“Great King, you should know!

That which arises from conditions arises from immeasurable merit and wisdom; it arises from ethical discipline, from meditative concentration, from wisdom, from liberation, and from the knowledge and vision of liberation; it arises from loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; it arises from generosity, from maintaining ethical discipline, from patience, from diligence, from meditative absorption, and from wisdom; it arises from the liberations and samādhis, from all the skillful means and pāramitās, from the six supernormal powers, from the three types of clear knowledge, and from the four analytical knowledges; it arises from the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; it arises from the abandonment of all unwholesome dharmas and the accumulation of all wholesome dharmas; it arises from true wisdom and from heedfulness.
"Great King, you should know that [this body] is born from such immeasurable, pure, and virtuous dharmas.
Because the merits of Gautama’s body are inexhaustible, his Dharma-body is inexhaustible."
The King said, "Great Master!
Phenomena that arise are subject to cessation; how can there be arising without cessation?"
He replied: "Great King!
Because it is fundamentally unarisen, it is without exhaustion."
The king said:
"Great Master! Why is it that nothing is originally produced?"
He replied, "Great King!
The Dharma-body is not born, for it is primordially existent; yet, because it arises through conditions, it is designated as 'born'."
The king said: "Great Master!
Such conditions are immeasurable and boundless."
"If one wishes to practice, what is its foundation?
From what does it begin? He replied:
“Great King! All practices that assist the path toward merit—summarizing the essentials—they have precepts as their foundation and the observance of precepts as their beginning.
If one does not observe the precepts, one will not even attain the body of a scabby jackal, let alone attain a body of merit.”
"Great King, you should know this!
Because of the purity of their precepts, they do not sever the lineage of the Buddhas and achieve equal and perfect enlightenment;
they do not sever the lineage of the Dharma and discern the nature of phenomena."
"One does not sever the lineage of the Sangha and cultivates the unconditioned path.
Because one maintains pure precepts in continuous succession, one's merit is inexhaustible.
The King said:
“Great Master!
Are all virtuous precepts inexhaustible,
or are there some that are exhaustible?”
He replied: "Great King! It is not that all have perished, nor is it that none have perished."
"Why is this? Because when the continuity is severed, there is exhaustion; because it is not severed, there is no exhaustion.
The King said:
“Great Master! What is the continuity that is severed?
What is the continuity that is not severed?”
He replied: "Great King!
Because the continuity of pure precepts is uninterrupted, one's merit is inexhaustible."
Why is this? Because the precepts of ordinary persons are subject to exhaustion, for they are severed whenever one is reborn;
likewise, the karmic retribution obtained from the ten wholesome actions among humans is subject to exhaustion, for it is severed.
The merit and karmic rewards of the devas in the desire realm are subject to exhaustion because they are severed;
the meditative absorptions and immeasurable minds of the devas in the form realm are subject to exhaustion because they are severed;
and the entry into various concentrations by the devas in the formless realm is subject to exhaustion because it is severed.
All the precepts of the Śrāvakas, whether in training or beyond training, are subject to exhaustion because they are severed at the limit of Nirvāṇa;
the precepts of Pratyekabuddhas are also subject to exhaustion because they lack great compassion and are thus severed.
The precepts of all bodhisattvas reach as far as bodhi; because they bring about great compassion, their merit is inexhaustible. Why is this?

Within these precepts, all the precepts of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles are produced; just as a seed is inexhaustible, its fruit is likewise inexhaustible. Therefore, the seed of bodhi cannot be exhausted.
The king said: “Great Master!
Regarding such a Dharma-body, upon what dharma should one rely to perform such contemplation?”
He replied: "Great King!

One should contemplate based on the bodies of afflictions of all sentient beings; one should contemplate within the midst of sentient beings characterized by greed, hatred, and delusion; one should contemplate within the midst of sentient beings with the four inverted views; one should contemplate within the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; and one should contemplate within the various bodies of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and even asuras."
Why is this? Because this very body is the Tathāgatagarbha.
Great King, you should know this!

Within the treasury of all afflictions and impurities, the Tathāgata-nature is serenely and fully present, like gold within stone, fire within wood, water beneath the earth, curd within milk, oil within sesame seeds, a sprout within a seed, a treasure within a storehouse, an image within a mold, a fetus within a womb, and the sun within the clouds. Therefore, I say:
"Within the body of afflictions, there is the Tathāgatagarbha."
At that time, Saccaka the Nirgrantha spoke again in verse:
“Gautama’s Dharma-nature body, Its wondrous form is eternally serene;
Pure and eternally quiescent, Its characteristics are like space.”
"Such is the Dharma-nature body, equal and without distinction among all sentient beings;
this realm is profoundly deep, such that the followers of the two vehicles cannot know it.

At that time, King Ugratejas, having heard the Great Śāṭhyāyana Nirgrantha speak of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable merit and Dharma-body, gave rise to a heart of joy, a heart of exultation, a heart of leaping gladness, a heart of immeasurable joy, a heart of immeasurable faith and reverence, a heart of immeasurable affection, and a heart of immeasurable celebration.

In the presence of the great Śākyan Nirgrantha, he further conceived the thought that he was one who is inconceivable; he conceived the thought that he was one who is immeasurable; he conceived the thought that he was one worthy of honor; he conceived the thought that he was one worthy of veneration; he conceived the thought that he was one worthy of respect; he conceived the thought that he was one who well knows the path to enlightenment; he conceived the thought that he was one who possesses all-knowledge; he conceived the thought that he was one who has reached the other shore; he conceived the thought that he was one who is awakened; he conceived the thought that he was one who bestows mindfulness; and he conceived the thought that he was a bodhisattva abiding in inconceivable liberation.

Having given rise to such various inconceivable thoughts as these, he took necklaces worth hundreds of thousands of koṭis of asaṃkhyeyas and immeasurable, priceless, exquisite garments, and offered them to the Nirgrantha Saccaka, further saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Satyaka, Great Teacher!
You are able to expound such a supreme, great, and skillful Dharma-gate of expedient means.
He further spoke these words:
“Saccaka, Great Teacher!
The Dharma you teach is skillfully in accord with the knowledge of all modes; this Dharma can reach the stage of omniscience.
The Dharma you teach can ferry across all the worldly currents.”
The Dharma taught by the Master can wash away the defilements of all afflictions;
the Dharma taught by the Master can shatter all gates of envy and jealousy;
the Dharma taught by the Master can uproot the suffering of all evil realms.
The Dharma taught by the Master can skillfully employ expedient means to shatter and disperse all great mountains of arrogance;
the Dharma taught by the Master can completely dry up the great ocean of craving and desire in all worlds;
the Dharma taught by the Master can illuminate all dense forests of ignorance.
“The Dharma taught by the Teacher is such that it does not lose its proper time, nor does it miss the time for its reception.
At that time, Saccaka the Nirgrantha said to King Prasenajit: “So it is, so it is!”

"Great King! There is no deportment of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas that does not transform sentient beings; there is not a single dharma that cannot accord with the gates of the Mahāyāna; there is not a single dharma that cannot reach the stage of omniscience; there is not a single dharma that cannot sever all afflictions; there is not a single dharma that does not reveal all the faults of the world; there is not a single dharma that does not reveal the unsurpassed merit of Nirvāṇa; and there is not a single dharma that does not reveal the unsurpassed, supreme practices of a Bodhisattva."
"Great King, you should know that all the practices undertaken by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are for their own benefit, for the benefit of others, and for the benefit of both."

When the Nirgrantha Saccaka preached this Dharma-gate, King Ugratejas attained the great, firm, and non-retrogressive bodhicitta; the sixteen sons of the king attained what is called the state of joyful leaping faith; and eight thousand devaputras attained the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha’s Adornments.
At that time, thirteen thousand members of King Ugratejas’s retinue, along with the followers of the great Nirgrantha Saccaka and his own retinue, resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Those sentient beings each removed the upper garments they were wearing and offered them to the Nirgrantha Saccaka, saying:
"We have now truly attained supreme and great benefit, for by meeting the noble son Saccaka, we have been able to hear this sublime Dharma-gate of all-encompassing wisdom."

Chapter Nine: Approaching the Tathāgata. *The Mahāsāṃghika-sātrāntika-sūtra Spoken by the Nirgrantha Saccaka*, Chapter Nine: Approaching the Tathāgata. At that time, King Ugratejas and his retinue spoke these words:
“Saccaka, son of good family!
"Master, you should now go to the place where the Tathāgata resides to see the Buddha, the World-Honored One; pay homage to the Tathāgata and make offerings to the Tathāgata. Why is this?
Because at this moment, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is within my garden, preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the great assembly."
Saccaka the Nirgrantha said: “Excellent, Great King!

Now is the very time to see the Tathāgata. You may go together with the minor kings of the cities and towns within the kingdom, the heads of various villages, the ministers and princes, the elders and householders, as well as the king’s queen, the ladies of the inner palace, and the king’s powerful ministers—let such a multitude as these, with one mind, proceed together to the place where the Buddha is.”

At that time, King Ugratejas issued a decree to all the city governors and village chiefs throughout his realm, commanding them to lead their respective subjects and family members, and to adorn themselves all together, proceeding to the place where the Buddha was;
he declared that if anyone failed to go to the Tathāgata’s presence, their lives would be taken.

At that time, all the sons and daughters of good family, as well as the youths and maidens within the kingdom, having heard the king’s command, desired to go together with the Great Teacher Satyaka to the presence of the Buddha to pay their respects and make offerings. Their hearts were filled with joy, and each of them adorned themselves with exquisite and wonderful finery. They prepared every variety of incense, flowers, unguents, powdered incense, floral garlands, banners, and canopies; and taking up all manner of musical instruments, they departed from the city of Ujjayinī and waited for King Candana on the main road.
At that time, King Ugratejas mounted a palanquin adorned with cords of the seven treasures, with countless golden and silver vases filled with various flowers placed on both sides of it.

The King exerted great power, manifesting the majesty of a great king, performing the supernatural feats of a great king, and displaying the prowess of a great king. With elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, he engaged in the royal pastimes. He raised various kinds of banners, flags, and flowered parasols, and struck eight thousand types of drums of exquisite sound. Amidst various songs and dances, surrounded before and behind by ninety-eight million people—including the great Śākya Nirgrantha, ministers, princes, the King’s powerful queen, palace attendants, minor kings, elders, householders, and even gatekeepers and palace guards—he proceeded together to the park to visit the Tathāgata.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, they prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him three times.

Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha, together with his retinue, prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him countless hundreds of thousands of times; then, withdrawing to one side, they sat with single-minded palms joined, gazing at the Buddha without averting their eyes, remaining there in silence.

Chapter Ten: On Preaching the Dharma, Part One. From the *Mahāsātyaka-nirgrantha-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, Chapter Ten, Part One: On Preaching the Dharma. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra saw the great Nirgrantha Sātyaka seated before the Buddha, with his palms joined in single-minded devotion, gazing at the Buddha without wavering, remaining silent and dwelling in this thought:
"For what purpose has this Nirgrantha Sātyaka come to the presence of the Buddha?"
Having had this thought, he said to the mahāsaccaka nirgrantha:
"For what purpose have you come to the Buddha’s presence?
Is it to see the Buddha?"
"Is it for the sake of hearing the Dharma?
At that time, Satyaka Nirgranthaputra said to the Venerable Śāriputra: "Venerable Śāriputra!..."
I have now come to the presence of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, not for the sake of seeing the Buddha, nor for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
Venerable Śāriputra!
I have now come to the Buddha’s presence not for the sake of any dharmas whatsoever.
Why is this? Venerable Śāriputra!
It is not by seeing form that one is said to see the Tathāgata;
It is not by seeing feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness that one is said to see the Tathāgata;
it is not by seeing the nature of earth that one is said to see the Tathāgata;
it is not by seeing the nature of water, the nature of fire, or the nature of wind that one is said to see the Tathāgata.
It is not by seeing the self that one is said to see the Tathāgata;
it is not by seeing sentient beings that one is said to see the Tathāgata;
it is not by seeing the life-span that one is said to see the Tathāgata.
It is not by seeing the person that one is said to see the Tathāgata;
it is not by seeing the agent that one is said to see the Tathāgata;
it is not by seeing "mine" that one is said to see the Tathāgata.
One is said to see the Tathāgata not because of seeing the object seen,
nor because of seeing marks, nor because of seeing the markless. This is called seeing the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Venerable Śāriputra!
Not seeing any marks is called seeing the Tathāgata.
To see without attachment is called seeing the Tathāgata;
to not see objects is called seeing the Tathāgata;
to see according to reality is called seeing the Tathāgata.
Because one sees the limit of reality as no-limit, it is called seeing the Tathāgata;
because one is weary of the eye and weary of forms, it is called seeing the Tathāgata;
because one does not see the ear and does not hear sounds, it is called seeing the Tathāgata.
Not seeing the nose and not smelling fragrances is called seeing the Tathāgata;
not seeing the tongue and not knowing tastes is called seeing the Tathāgata;
not seeing the body and not perceiving tangibles is called seeing the Tathāgata.
"Because one does not perceive mental phenomena and does not differentiate mental phenomena,
this is called 'seeing the Tathāgata. Śāriputra said,
"Saccaka, Great Virtuous One!"
"If one sees or does not see the Tathāgata by means of such characteristics, how can this be called seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One?
Saccaka the Nirgrantha replied,
"Venerable Śāriputra!..."
One does not see the Tathāgata by seeing his family;
one does not see the Tathāgata by seeing his clan;
one does not see the Tathāgata by means of physical marks.
Because it is not the case that there is no characteristic, one is said to see the Tathāgata;
because it is not a dharma, one is said to see the Tathāgata;
because it is not the case that it is not a dharma, one is said to see the Tathāgata.
Because it is not real, one is said to see the Tathāgata;
because it is not unreal, one is said to see the Tathāgata;
because it is not through contemplation, one is said to see the Tathāgata.
Because it is not through non-contemplation, one is said to see the Tathāgata;
because it is not through recollection, one is said to see the Tathāgata;
because it is not through non-recollection, one is said to see the Tathāgata.
Because it is not through conceptual discrimination, one is said to see the Tathāgata;
because it is not through non-discrimination, one is said to see the Tathāgata;
because it is not conditioned, one is said to see the Tathāgata.
Because it is not unconditioned, one is said to see the Tathāgata;
because it is not a substantial entity, one is said to see the Tathāgata;
because it is not a non-entity, one is said to see the Tathāgata.
Because it is not through conjunction, one is said to see the Tathāgata;
because it is not through separation, one is said to see the Tathāgata;
because it is not form, one is said to see the Tathāgata.
One sees the Tathāgata not because of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
one sees the Tathāgata not because of grasping;
and one sees the Tathāgata not because of non-grasping.
"Because it is not born, one is said to see the Tathāgata;
because it is not unborn, one is said to see the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra spoke to the Mahāsaccaka Nirgrantha, saying:
“Saccaka, Mahāsthavira!
If one sees in this way, it is called seeing the Tathāgata.
Saccaka, Mahāsthavira!”
"How does one see the Buddha, the World-Honored One?
Saccaka the Nirgrantha replied,
"Venerable Śāriputra!..."
I do not see the Tathāgata by seeing form, nor do I see the Tathāgata apart from form; I do not see the Tathāgata by destroying or annihilating form.

Likewise, I do not see the Tathāgata by seeing feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor do I see the Tathāgata apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; I do not see the Tathāgata by destroying or annihilating feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
I do not see the Tathāgata as being subsumed within the mundane world, nor do I see the Tathāgata as being subsumed within that which transcends the mundane world.

I do not see the Tathāgata as being comprised of the aggregates (skandha), I do not see the Tathāgata as being comprised of the elements (dhātu), and I do not see the Tathāgata as being comprised of the sense-bases (āyatana);
I see the Tathāgata as being detached from all sounds and speech.

I now see the Tathāgata in this way: thus not seeing, yet not not seeing; not knowing and not discriminating; not arising and not manifesting; not being born and not increasing; not grasping and not abandoning; not conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); not forming signs (*nimitta*) and not not forming them; not making things and not not making them; not receiving and not protecting; not seeing by means of a mental construction, not seeing by means of spontaneity, not seeing by means of observation, not seeing by means of non-observation, not seeing as something expressible, and not seeing as something inexpressible.
To be free from all speech, names, phrases, and sounds is called seeing the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because he cannot be seen through such characteristics.
"Venerable Śāriputra!
The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perceive the Buddha in this way; I, too, perceive the Tathāgata in this same manner. Śāriputra said:
“Saccaka, Mahāsthavira!
If one can see the Tathāgata in such a manner, how then, Mahāsthavira, could you hear the Dharma being taught by the Tathāgata? He replied:
"Venerable Śāriputra! If I were to give rise to the notion of dharmas or the notion of non-dharmas, I would have to listen to the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata. Why is this?
Venerable Śāriputra!

When all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear the sound of the Dharma being preached regarding all names, phrases, and vocal expressions, they do not give rise to the mental conception of dharmas or the conception of non-dharmas.
"Why is this? Because it is detached from all characteristics of dharmas. Śāriputra said:
“Saccaka, Mahāsthavira!
Did you not come to the presence of the Buddha for the sake of the Dharma? He replied:
"Venerable Śāriputra!
I have come to the Buddha’s presence neither for the sake of dharmas nor for the sake of non-dharmas. Why is this?
Venerable Śāriputra! One who acts for the sake of the Dharma does not act for the sake of any phenomena; this is called acting for the sake of the Dharma. Venerable Śāriputra!
If there is someone who says they have come for the sake of the Dharma, that person does not cling to this Dharma—this is called the Buddha;
they do not perceive this Dharma—this is called the Dharma;
they do not cling to birth—this is called the Sangha.

Now, one who practices the Dharma does not do so for the sake of knowing suffering, nor for the sake of abandoning the origin, nor for the sake of cultivating the path, nor for the sake of realizing cessation; nor for the sake of transcending the realm of desire, nor for the sake of transcending the realm of form, nor for the sake of transcending the formless realm, nor for the sake of attaining nirvana.
"Venerable Śāriputra!
Relying on this Dharma, you should know that I have not come to the presence of the Buddha for the sake of the Dharma.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the great Sañjayin Nirgrantha, saying:
“Saccaka, Great Virtuous One!
Based on what dharma do you now speak in this way? He replied:
“Venerable Śāriputra! I do not rely upon even a single dharma at all when making such a statement. Why is this?
Within the dharma-realm there is no dependence; within the dharma-realm dependence cannot be found, nor can non-dependence be found within the dharma-realm.
Why is this? Because duality is not perceived.
Śāriputra said, "Venerable Satyaka!
Do you not now come and go in dependence upon the six realms of existence?"
He replied, "Venerable Śāriputra! If I were to perceive the characteristics of those six realms of existence, there would be coming and going."
If I were subject to birth, I too should undergo birth; if there were falling away, I should fall away; if there were going forth, I should go forth.
Venerable Śāriputra!
All dharmas are unmoving, non-rotating, non-going, non-falling-away, and unborn.
Śāriputra said: "Saccaka Nirgranthaputra!
If this is so, for what reason did the Tathāgata say, 'Bhikṣu, you are born, you age and die, and you both pass away and are reborn'?"
He replied: "Venerable Śāriputra!

The Tathāgata spoke thus based on his attachment to sentient beings within the six realms of existence; it was because he wished to uproot their reliance upon those six realms that the Tathāgata made such a statement."
"Venerable Śāriputra!
Within the Buddha-dharma, there is no going, no coming, no retreating, and no arising. Śāriputra said:
“Excellent, excellent, Venerable Satyaka!
Just as the Venerable Satyaka has spoken, he is a practitioner of the Mahāyāna who understands both the meaning and the words.”
Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha said: "Venerable Śāriputra!
Do you know what constitutes the meaning?"
"What is meant by 'name'? Śāriputra replied,
"O son of good family!"
I do not wish to speak; I wish to hear what is spoken.
Venerable sir, you should explain: what constitutes the meaning, and what constitutes the words?
At that time, Satyaka Nirgranthaputra addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"Venerable Śāriputra! That which is called 'meaning' is inexpressible."
That which cannot be spoken is called a "name" (nāman);
that which is expressed as meaning is called "inexpressible.
To speak of that [meaning] is called a "letter" (vyañjana).
That which is called "meaning" (artha) is that which cannot be named;
that which expresses it is called a "syllable" (vyañjana).

That which is called "meaning" is unmoving, unknowable, beyond frivolous conceptualization (prapañca), undifferentiable, unarisen, non-aggregated, neither a thing nor a reality, selfless, non-originated, ungraspable, and not a basis for reliance; it is utterly remote from all dependence upon language and names.
As for what is called "syllables" (vyañjana): it refers to that which, through reflection, enumeration, weighing, and investigation, causes others to understand; this is termed "syllables.
As for what is called "meaning" (artha): it refers to the unimpededness regarding meaning (arthapratisaṃvid).

What is called "syllables" refers to the unimpededness of dharmas (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), the unimpededness of expressions (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), and the unimpededness of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*). Venerable Śāriputra!
This is what is called a brief explanation of meaning and a brief explanation of syllables.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Nirgrantha Saccaka,
saying: "Excellent, excellent, Saccaka!"
Excellent, excellent!
If there are sons of good family who wish to preach the Dharma, they should preach it in this way!
Preach this Dharma-gate just as you have spoken.

At that time, among the assembly, three thousand devaputras heard the eloquent and inspired discourse of Mahāsaccaka the Nirgrantha and attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); twenty thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
The Scripture Spoken by the Great Śākyan Nirgrantha, Scroll Nine.
The Scripture Spoken by the Great Śākyan Nirgrantha, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
The Second Part of the Tenth Chapter on the Exposition of the Dharma.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many sentient beings has this Saccaka Nirgranthaputra, appearing in the guise of an externalist, taught and inspired to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana: “Maudgalyāyana!
If you were to ask me about this matter now, gods and humans who hear it spoken would all become bewildered and submerged, with the sole exception of the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.”
Maudgalyāyana!
I shall now speak of but a small portion of it, so that sentient beings may enter [the path].
The noble son Satyaka teaches and transforms sentient beings through various forms, various colors, and various modes of conduct, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Maudgalyāyana!

Suppose there were sentient beings as numerous as the atoms within Mount Sumeru dwelling in the teachings of external paths; the son of good family Satyaka, practicing the teachings of external paths, would teach and transform them, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

There are sentient beings equal in number to the atoms within the four continents who abide in the teachings of the heterodox Carakas; the noble son Satyaka practices the Caraka dharma, teaching and transforming them so that they resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Eighty-four thousand beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were dwelling in the teachings of the Pārivrajaka non-Buddhist sects; the noble son Satyaka practiced the Pārivrajaka non-Buddhist teachings and transformed them, causing them to resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

There are beings as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers who delight in the practice of the śrāvakas; the noble son Satyaka manifests the practice of a śrāvaka to teach and transform them, causing them to abide in the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, after which they resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having manifested bodies equal in number to those of the śrāvakas, they appear in the form of pratyekabuddhas to teach and transform others, causing them to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Countless sentient beings, through the practice of the bodhisattva path by the noble son Satyaka, were taught and transformed so that they resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
To those who should be transformed by seeing the body of Śakra, he manifests the body of Śakra to teach and transform sentient beings;
to those who should be transformed by seeing the body of Brahmā, he manifests the body of Brahmā to teach and transform sentient beings;
to those who should be transformed by seeing the body of a Cakravartin King, he manifests the body of a Cakravartin King to teach and transform sentient beings.
To those who should be transformed by seeing the body of a Four Heavenly King, he immediately manifests the body of a Four Heavenly King to teach and transform sentient beings;
to those who should be transformed by seeing the body of a Kiṃnara, he immediately manifests the body of a Kiṃnara to teach and transform sentient beings;
to those who should be transformed by seeing the body of an Asura, he immediately manifests the body of an Asura to teach and transform sentient beings.
To those who should be transformed by seeing the body of a garuḍa, he immediately manifests the body of a garuḍa to teach and transform sentient beings;
to those who should be transformed by seeing the body of a mahoraga, he immediately manifests the body of a mahoraga to teach and transform sentient beings;
to those who should be transformed by seeing the human body, he immediately manifests the human body to teach and transform sentient beings.
To those who should be transformed by seeing a female body, he manifests a female body to teach and transform sentient beings;
to those who should be transformed by seeing the bodies of young boys or young girls, he manifests the bodies of young boys or young girls to teach and transform sentient beings;
to those who should be transformed by seeing the body of a terrestrial deity (bhūmideva), he manifests the body of a terrestrial deity to teach and transform sentient beings.
To those who should be transformed by seeing the body of a co-natal deva, he immediately manifests the body of a co-natal deva to teach and transform sentient beings;
to those who should be transformed by seeing the body of a noble one (ārya), he immediately manifests the body of a noble one to teach and transform sentient beings;
to those who should be transformed by seeing the body of a māṇava, he immediately manifests the body of a māṇava to teach and transform sentient beings.
To those who should be transformed by seeing the bodies of bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs, he immediately manifests the body of a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī to teach and transform sentient beings;
to those who should be transformed by seeing the bodies of upāsakas or upāsikās, he immediately manifests the body of an upāsaka or upāsikā to teach and transform sentient beings.
Maudgalyāyana!
The noble son Satyaka manifests all such various and immeasurable bodily forms to teach and transform immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many Buddhas did the noble son Satyaka make offerings to?”
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana: “Maudgalyāyana!

The earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, and the realm of space can all be measured and calculated; however, the various bodies with which the noble son Satyaka has made offerings to the Buddha cannot be measured or calculated.”

Chapter Eleven: The Prediction The Scripture Spoken by the Great Śākyan Nirgrantha, Chapter Eleven: The Prediction At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the noble son Saccaka, saying: “Noble son!

You have already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas and have fully accomplished an immeasurable and boundless accumulation of all merits; for what reason do you not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Saccaka replied: "Venerable Kāśyapa!
If I had any view such as 'this is enlightenment' or 'this is the one who realizes it,' I would have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Kāśyapa said: "Saccaka, son of good family!

Among the immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, are there not some who have already attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, some who will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and some who are currently attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
Saccaka replied: "Venerable Kāśyapa!
As for what you have just said regarding those immeasurable and boundless sentient beings who will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, these are merely the numbers of conceited sentient beings."
Why is this? Venerable Kāśyapa!
Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), neither bodhi nor a bodhisattva can be apprehended.
For what reason? Venerable Kāśyapa!
That which is called *bodhi* is termed the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); *bodhi* is free from all numerical reckoning; *bodhi*...
This is not a material phenomenon; awakening is invisible. Awakening is not blue, not yellow, not red, not white, not crimson, not black, and not the color of crystal.
It is without form, without shape, without characteristics, and without manifestation; it transcends all marks, is without support, and is free from everything.
The basis is devoid of substance and free from all things; it is signless and free from all signs;
it is ineffable and inexpressible; it cannot be seen, nor can it be known through synthesis, nor can it be known through differentiation;
it is neither darkness nor light; it is formless, signless, and beyond observation; it is not speech.
It is beyond language; it cannot be touched, known, or heard. It is not sound, nor is it the path of speech.
It is without obstruction, without hindrance, without bondage, and without liberation.
It is neither hatred nor delusion; it cannot be manifested by any means and is ineffable.
Venerable Kāśyapa! Such is the nature of the essence of bodhi; it cannot be realized by the body, nor can it be known by the mind. Why is this?
Venerable Kāśyapa! This body is without cognition, like grass and wood;
this body is without sensation, like a stone wall.
This body is without consciousness, like a reflection in a mirror; therefore, one cannot attain bodhi by means of the body. Venerable Kāśyapa!
The mind, too, is invisible and cannot be demonstrated; therefore, one does not attain bodhi by means of the mind.
Venerable Kāśyapa!
Sentient beings cannot be seen, because there are no sentient beings; therefore, one does not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Venerable Kāśyapa! If all dharmas are thus, why do you say this:
'You have already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas and fulfilled immeasurable and boundless merits; for what reason have you not attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?'"

At that time, all the great assembly in the gathering—the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, Śakra-devānām-indra, the four heavenly kings, the Brahmā kings, and others—had this thought:
"O Tathāgata, World-Honored One!"
In order to eliminate our doubts and hesitations, and in accordance with the faith in our minds, you should bestow the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi upon the noble son Satyaka.
After how much time shall he attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?

In which eon, in which world-system, in which country, of which lineage, in which family, with what kind of retinue, by what manner of renunciation, and beneath what tree shall he attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
“Once you have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, what will be the name of that Buddha? For how long will he remain in the world? And how many assemblies of followers will gather?

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, Śakra-devānām-indra, the Four Heavenly Kings, the Brahmā kings, and others, and having discerned their various reflections and deliberations, addressed Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, saying: “Mañjuśrī!”
After this Bhadrakalpa and further beyond immeasurable and incalculable kalpas, this son of good family, Satyaka, shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha’s name is King of the Banner of True Wisdom, and the world is named Well-Contemplated Renown. In that world, there are no enemies or adversaries. Mañjuśrī!
That world, Well-Contemplated Renown, is adorned with rare, extraordinary, most exquisite, and delightful features.

That land was adorned with the seven treasures interspersed throughout; its city walls were encircled by hundreds of thousands of millions of layers of seven-jeweled ramparts. Within it, there were further seven hundred thousand million layers of great fragrant water-seas surrounding it on all sides;
seven hundred thousand million great *vaiḍūrya* mani-jewels formed its gates and towers;
and ten hundred thousand million *jāmbūnada* gold formed nets that covered the entire world.
Ten million billion *maṇi* jewels were interspersed throughout the palaces;
ten million billion *siṃhaprema-maṇi* jewels were suspended across all the halls as magnificent ornaments;
and ten million billion *siṃhadhvaja-maṇi* jewels adorned the streets.
Ten million billion fire-banner maṇi jewels constantly burn day and night, universally illuminating the world;
ten million billion bells made of the seven treasures constantly produce wondrous sounds that pervade all worlds;
and ten million billion high banners of maṇi jewels are erected, extending throughout the world.
"Hang banners made of ten, hundred, thousand, or ten-thousand koṭis of gold upon high flagstaffs. Mañjuśrī!..."

In that world, Well-Contemplated Renown (*Suvīkṣita-kīrti*), the ground is as level as the palm of a hand, covered everywhere by jewel trees, and the grasses are soft—curling to the right in graceful spirals like exquisite paintings, or like the feathers on a peacock’s neck; their touch is as soft as *kalaviṅka* birds, which completely cover the world. There are ten million billion exquisite and magnificent gardens pervading the world, and within each garden, there are ten million billion great jewel ponds, universally adorned. Along each side of every pond are eight paths, interspersed with eight-faceted *maṇi* jewels, with *jāmbūnada* gold sand spread across their bottoms. Within each pond, the water is filled with perfumed waters of eight flavors, and *padma* flowers made of the seven precious substances cover the surface of the water.
The *Kun-lun-ccha* birds and the *Ki-pa-ki-pa* birds constantly emit wondrous sounds that pervade all worlds.
"Mañjuśrī! In that world of Good Observation (*Sudarśana*), there are eighty million cities and villages, filling the land as its adornment."
Within one great city, there were ten hundred thousand million smaller cities serving as its adornments; all the towns and villages were likewise so.
In each town and each village, there were hundreds of thousands of millions of men, women, boys, and girls.
“Mañjuśrī! In that world called Well-Contemplated Renown, there is a four-continent system named World Delighting Those Who See It.
Among all the four continents, this one is the most excellent and sublime.
Its inhabitants are numerous, peaceful, secure, and happy; therein, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Real-Wisdom-Banner King has appeared in the world.
“Mañjuśrī! That Tathāgata Vimalabuddhaketurāja was born into a brahmin family; his mother’s name was Kṣipragāminī, just as my mother in the present world is named Māyā;
his father’s name was Brahmabhūti, just as my father in the present world is named King Śuddhodana.”
His son shall be named Yaśas, just as my present son Rāhula;
his wife shall be named Mahāmati, just as my present Śākyan wife Gopī;
and his wet nurse shall be named Mahāyaśas, just as my present Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
The attendant shall be named *Anuvartaka*, just as my attendant Candaka is in my present life;
the horse shall be named *Mahājavana*, just as my royal steed Kanthaka is in my present life.
The Tathāgata Real Wisdom Banner King mounted that Great Swift Steed to leave the city and renounce the world, just as I have now mounted the horse-king Kaṇṭhaka to renounce the world.
That Buddha’s place of enlightenment was named Dharmodgata; there, the Tathāgata Real Wisdom Banner King attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, just as I am now at the site of the path of tranquility.
That Bodhi tree had eight million hundred thousand billion trees as its retinue.
"Mañjuśrī! When the Tathāgata Real Wisdom Banner King appeared in the world during that kalpa, there were no maras, enemies, or retinues of maras."

“Mañjuśrī! When that Tathāgata Vimalaprajñādhvajarāja attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, all sentient beings in that world took up various kinds of flowers, incense, ointments, powdered incense, and scattered perfumes, and performed various kinds of music, song, and dance, proceeding at once to the Dharma-Excellence (Dharmaśreṣṭha) bodhimanda;
even all the celestial hosts in the Akaniṣṭha heaven performed various kinds of sublime celestial music and gathered at that bodhimanda.”
All the hosts of yakṣas performed various kinds of music and gathered at that place of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

All the hosts of gandharvas, all the hosts of asuras, all the hosts of garuḍas, all the hosts of kiṃnaras, and all the hosts of mahoragas in that world each performed hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of music and assembled with their retinues at the place of enlightenment.
Bodhisattvas from the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir have all come together in assembly from immeasurable and boundless worlds.

“Mañjuśrī! When the Tathāgata Real Wisdom Banner King first attained perfect enlightenment, for the sake of the great assembly gathered at that time, he preached this Great Dharma Gate of the Vigorous Display of the Skillful Means and Realm of Bodhisattva Practice, which has immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of sūtras as its retinue.”

“Mañjuśrī! When that Tathāgata King of the Banner of True Wisdom preached this Dharma-gate, sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained non-retrogression from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
“Mañjuśrī! When that Tathāgata Real Wisdom Banner King appeared in the world, he did not preach the teachings for converting beings through the three vehicles. Why was this?

In that Buddha-land there are no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; all sentient beings in that world believe in the One Vehicle and all believe in the supreme, wondrous, and victorious practices of bodhisattvas.

“Mañjuśrī! At the time of the first assembly of that Tathāgata Real Wisdom Banner King, there were immeasurable bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who had attained non-retrogression, who gathered there;
at the time of the second assembly, there were eighty billion hundred thousand million nayutas of bodhisattvas in their last birth before enlightenment who gathered there.”
During the third assembly, sixty *bimbara* of bodhisattvas gathered there.
"Mañjuśrī! Subsequently, at a later time, immeasurable and boundless sentient beings attained the non-retrogressive mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

“Mañjuśrī! After that Tathāgata Vimalaprajñādhvajarāja attained unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, he remained in the world for sixty intermediate kalpas preaching the Dharma, and subsequently entered parinirvāṇa.”

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for eighty thousand koṭis, hundreds of thousands of koṭis, and nayutas of kalpas, circulating and teaching and transforming sentient beings.
The number of people gathered and the benefits obtained were no different from those when the Buddha was in the world delivering beings. "Mañjuśrī!
When that Tathāgata Real Wisdom Banner King was on the verge of entering nirvana, he bestowed a prophecy upon the Bodhisattva Great Banner King, and only then did he enter parinirvāṇa."
He spoke these words:
"The Bodhisattva Mahādhvaja-rāja shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi after me; his name shall be Mahāvyūha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha."
At that time, the great assembly wished to know who among them was that Bodhisattva Mahādhvajarāja, who would attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* after that Tathāgata Vajradhvajarāja.
"What is meant by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahāvyūha?

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts and reflections in the minds of the assembly, and having understood their mental intentions, addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying: 'Mañjuśrī!'"
This son of good family, Satyaka, who is seated before you, is named the Māṇava Real Joy; he is the foremost among all the assembly of disciples.
This māṇava, at that time, became the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahāvyūha.
The adornments of that Buddha-world were most excellent and sublime, no different from the world of the Tathāgata Yathārthajñānaketudhvaja.
At that time, within the assembly, having heard the description of the supreme, wondrous, and magnificent merits and adornments of that Buddha-land,
sixty hundred thousand million billion nayutas of bodhisattvas made a vow to be born in that land,
saying: "When this Tathāgata Real Wisdom Banner King attains Buddhahood, may we be reborn in that Buddha-land."
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately bestowed upon them the prediction of enlightenment, saying that they would all be reborn in that Buddha-land.
A multitude of eighty million Nirgranthas then spoke with one voice, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I also vow to be reborn in that Buddha-land!
The World-Honored One then immediately bestowed predictions upon them all, saying:
"O sons of good family!..."
"All shall be born in that Buddha-land.
Eighty quadrillion nayutas of sons of gods in the realm of space spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!..."

We also vow that when the Tathāgata Real Wisdom Banner King attains bodhi, we shall all be reborn together in that world called Well-Contemplated Renown, where we may behold that Buddha’s inconceivable, merit-adorned, pure land.
Then the Buddha addressed those devaputras:
"O sons of good family!
You should all be born in that world called Renowned for Excellent Contemplation and make offerings to that Buddha."
"O sons of the gods!

You, too, shall be born in that world called Well-Contemplated Renown, where you will all attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Your various names, the duration of your lifespans remaining in the world, and the number of eons shall not differ from those of the Tathāgata Real Wisdom Banner King as he dwells in the world."

At that time, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and from the great earth there emerged hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *padma* lotuses. Their petals were made of Jāmbūnada gold, their calyxes of great blue *indranīla* jewels, their filaments of agate and *sūryakānta* (sun-light) jewels, and their stalks of great *vaiḍūrya* jewels.

Upon each and every one of those *padma* lotus flowers, he saw immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas sitting cross-legged, their bodies adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, all of whom together took refuge in the Tathāgata.
Those bodhisattvas each offered various jeweled clouds and nets to the Tathāgata, speaking these words:
“World-Honored One!

We have come from various worlds to the presence of the Buddha in order to hear the Buddha’s teaching on the inconceivable dharma-gate of the manifested merits of bodhisattvas; to see the Tathāgata, pay homage to the Tathāgata, and make offerings to the Tathāgata; to see the great good man Satyaka; and because we wish to see all the bodhisattvas present in this great assembly.”

When the Tathāgata preached this sublime Dharma-gate, immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas who had come from inconceivable Buddha-lands all attained non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"With single-mindedness, gather all your faculties And listen as I preach the sublime Dharma.
The Tathāgata speaks no falsehoods; The Buddhas do not speak in vain."
Saccaka and the great assembly, in future immeasurable ages,
after incalculable kalpas have passed, during the pure kalpa known as Unstained (Araṇa),
shall then attain Buddhahood, titled King of the Jewel-Wisdom Banner (Ratnajñānadhvaja-rāja).
At that time, the world was free from defilement and harm, and was thus called the Araṇa Kalpa;
the Buddha’s world at that time was named Sudarśana-kīrti,
endowed with all merits, and praised and revered by both devas and humans.
All the adornments of the realm are utterly exquisite;
the gates and towers are composed of hundreds of thousands of jewels.
Nets of Jambūnada gold cover them everywhere, reflecting one another in radiant splendor.
Its radiance shines eternally and universally, without distinction between day and night.
Hundreds of thousands of jewels are suspended, and the lion-banner is erected;
from jeweled bells a wondrous sound issues forth, proclaiming the Dharma of suchness.
Stainless jewel walls surpass all celestial palaces;
Springs, streams, and various ponds possess the eight excellent flavors.
There are *padma* flowers, *kukana* flowers, and others.
The clear waters fill all the ponds, unmixed with any dust or impurity.
That world’s dwelling place is the most excellent among the four continents;
it is fully endowed with wondrous adornments, and for this reason it is named "Delightful to Behold."
The Tathāgata was born in that place; he was a brahmin who left the household life.
His mother’s name was Śīghragāminī, his father’s name was Brahmabandhu, and his son’s name was Citra, just as Rāhula is mine.
That lady was of great wisdom, just as Gopī is mine today;
her wet nurse was of great renown, just as Prajāpatī is mine;
her attendant was named Anulā, and was also called Cchandikā.
Just as my attendant Channa, who follows my will with reverence,
is the foremost and most excellent horse named Kaṇṭhaka,
so too shall he bring forth the Tathāgata, just as I mounted Bālāha.
The bodhi tree of that Buddha is named Dharma-śreṣṭha;
its superior trees as its retinue number eight hundred million.
Beneath that tree is the Dharma-King, whose name is Buddha Truth-Benefit (Saddharmapriya).
Sitting beneath that tree of enlightenment, he attained great bodhi.
There were no hosts of Māras, nor were there any demonic activities;
within that Buddha-field, there were no thorns of enmity.
Immeasurable devas and humans gathered together in that pure land;
each holding exquisite flower garlands and hundreds of thousands of musical instruments,
they all approached the Tathāgata with hearts of reverence.
The Tathāgata, knowing their minds, preached for them various wondrous dharmas; with immeasurable sūtras as his retinue,
when that Buddha first gathered the assembly, those who heard this dharma-gate—
More numerous than the sands of the Ganges are those who do not regress from Bodhi.
Therein are no Śrāvakayāna followers, nor Pratyekabuddhas;
it is filled with courageous Bodhisattvas in that pure land.
In the second assembly, there were eighty nayutas of bodhisattvas who dwell for one more birth in the stage of being destined for enlightenment.
Those gathered in the third assembly were all great and supreme bodhisattvas.
Sixty *bimbara* [kalpas] he shall dwell in the state of suchness.
That Tathāgata will remain in the world for a lifespan of sixty kalpas;
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the lamp of the Dharma shall abide in the world.
The relics were widely disseminated, For eighty billion nayutas of kalpas;
They remained to benefit all sentient beings.
That Buddha bestowed a prophecy upon Mahādhvaja, And thereafter entered parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha’s name is Great Adornment, and his fame is manifest throughout the world.
The adornment of that world is no different from that of the Buddha Real Wisdom;
within that land, he has realized stainless enlightenment.
You all should believe me: my wisdom is like space;
its inexhaustible nature is eternally abiding, unimpeded in all places.
It can perceive the entirety of the future—both what has not yet occurred and what is yet to come.
How much more so regarding past kalpas— those that once existed but are no longer recorded.
Abiding in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) within the wisdom of reality as it is,
my words are free from falsehood, nor do I cause others to speak otherwise.
I now proclaim the truth, the exquisite Dharma of ambrosia;
therefore, you great assembly, upon hearing it, should receive it with earnest faith.
When the great assembly heard the Buddha’s teaching, they all gave rise to hearts of joy.
When that Buddha attained enlightenment, all vowed to be born in his land.
The World-Honored One granted predictions to all those immeasurable sentient beings, saying:
"When that Buddha appears in the world, you shall all be reborn there."
"You, in that world, shall teach and transform all sentient beings;
there you will attain enlightenment, and the world itself shall not be different.
When this Dharma-gate was spoken, the great earth shook in six ways.
The Bodhisattva within the lotus, with palms joined toward the Buddha, said:
"Excellent, World-Honored Buddha! You are inconceivable;
for the sake of immeasurable multitudes, you have skillfully expounded this Dharma-gate."
"We, the great assembly, have come from immeasurable worlds, all desiring to hear this most supreme and wondrous Wheel of Dharma. Chapter Twelve:

On the Merit of Faith *Sāṃkhyāyanapravāda-sūtra* At that time, the entire great assembly in the gathering was filled with immense joy and leaped for gladness. Each person removed the upper garment they were wearing and offered it to the Tathāgata, saying these words:
“Tathāgata, World-Honored One!
You now turn the Wheel of Dharma for the second time in the world.
In the past, the Tathāgata first turned the Wheel of Dharma in the city of Vārāṇasī; now, once again, you turn the Wheel of Dharma for the second time here in the city of Ujjayinī.”
They further spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!
We vow never to be separated from hearing this wondrous jewel Dharma-gate, and we vow never to be separated from the good man Satyaka."

At that time, the music of the devas in the void and the sound of exquisite drums resounded; the heavens rained down *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka*, and *vārṣika* flowers, filling the space beneath the Buddha’s feet.
In the sky, celestial beings let down clouds of precious robes as numerous as the heavens, and spoke these words:

"If there are good men or good women who are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, transcribe, and explain this sublime Dharma-gate for others, those people have certainly already attained immeasurable and boundless merit."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family is able to receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and widely explain this sublime Dharma-gate for others, how much merit will they accomplish?”
The Buddha addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying: "Mañjuśrī!

Suppose there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who were to count all the sentient beings in this trichiliocosm—whether with form or without form, whether with perception or without perception—and among all those sentient beings within the realm of beings, the Buddha’s wisdom knows that every single one of them simultaneously attains a human body."

Having attained human bodies, they shall all together cultivate the practices of the pāramitās and simultaneously achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; those Buddhas and others shall each remain in the world for one kalpa.

Suppose there were sons or daughters of good family who, for the duration of a full kalpa, made offerings to that many Buddhas and Tathāgatas—prostrating, revering, honoring, and praising them, providing every kind of supreme offering, including all flowers, incense, and music.
“Mañjuśrī, what do you think? Would those sons or daughters of good family obtain much merit? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Very much, Bhagavān! Very much, Sugata!
The merit obtained by those sons and daughters of good family is immeasurable and boundless; it cannot be measured, it cannot be numbered, it cannot be known, and it cannot be described.”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

“If there are sons or daughters of good family who receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, disseminate, and extensively explain to others this Dharma-gate of the Merit of the Bodhisattva’s Skillful Means, the merit they obtain will surpass that of those sons or daughters of good family who make offerings to all Buddhas; it is immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, and beyond comparison.”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How rare, Bhagavān! How rare, Sugata!”
"The Tathāgata has preached this Dharma-gate for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings. He further said:
"World-Honored One!"
"How long will this sublime Dharma-gate remain in Jambudvīpa?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"At the time of my parinirvāṇa, there will be eight great kings who, desiring to disseminate my relics, will divide them into eight portions at that time.
