These shall be placed within eight caskets; each person will take one casket and return to their own country, where they will erect great stūpas and temples to honor and make offerings to them."

"At that time, King Ajātaśatru shall obtain one portion of my relics; he shall write this sūtra upon golden cloth and, together with the relics, place them simultaneously within a casket made of the seven precious gems."
Outside the great city of Rājagṛha, he dug the earth to create a pit.
Within it, he erected a stūpa, adorned with exquisite beauty.

He placed the reliquary casket inside that stūpa and suspended hundreds of thousands of millions of asaṃkhyeya precious canopies, banners, and streamers. He scattered all manner of priceless incense and flowers, filled jars of the seven precious gems with fragrant oil, and lit great lamp wicks that remained burning for a full hundred years without extinguishing.

“Mañjuśrī! One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a King Aśoka born into the Mālava family who will appear in the world. He will become a Cakravartin king ruling over Jambudvīpa with sovereign power, possessing complete strength, and being well able to subdue those beings who are stubborn and fierce.”
"At that time, that king will surely observe me, be mindful of me, uphold my Dharma, and conceive a heart of reverence toward my person. Mañjuśrī!"
King Aśoka had a bhikṣu named Viśuddhavasu, who was born as a prince and left the household life to seek the Way.
King Aśoka regarded him as his gate-teacher; he possessed great supernatural powers and great majestic virtue, protecting all the Buddha-dharmas and protecting the Mahāvaipulya sūtras.

"Mañjuśrī! Because King Aśoka deeply respected and honored the bhikṣu Viśuddhavikrama, he did not allow him to go elsewhere, but kept him constantly at the royal palace, personally providing for his needs."

King Aśoka, desiring to disseminate the relics of my body for the benefit of all sentient beings, wished to bring forth from beneath the earth the precious casket containing the relics. Surrounded by a retinue of immeasurable great ministers, princes, elders, and householders, he arranged a magnificent display to manifest the power of a great king. Carrying incense, flowers, ointments, powdered incense, and scattered perfumes, and performing hundreds of thousands of kinds of exquisite music, he proceeded to the great city of Rājagṛha. There, having established all manner of supreme and wondrous offerings—immeasurable, boundless, and beyond calculation—he excavated the precious casket of relics from within the earth.

After seven days had passed, they made offerings and paid homage with all kinds of incense, all kinds of flowers, all kinds of flower garlands, all kinds of powdered incense, all kinds of unguents, and all kinds of music.

When the seven days had passed, throughout the various lands of Jambudvīpa—not sequentially, but in a single day, at a single moment, within a single kṣaṇa—he simultaneously established eighty-four thousand stūpas for the relics of the Buddha across the entirety of Jambudvīpa.
At that time, the bhikṣu Viśuddhavasu took this Dharma-gate from within that reliquary casket and widely proclaimed and disseminated it throughout a great kingdom in the northern region.

“Mañjuśrī! Although that Bhikṣu Viśuddhavaśitā has propagated it extensively, those who receive and uphold this Dharma-gate are few; many do not know it, many do not realize it, many do not embrace it, and many do not accept it. Rare are those who are able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this Dharma-gate.”
Why is this? Because this is a supreme Dharma, and sentient beings of meager merit should not hear it. "Mañjuśrī!..."
This sublime Dharma-gate is often kept secret and placed within the chests and various storehouses of the sutra repositories. Why is this?
Because those who are not vessels for the Dharma are unfit to plant the unsurpassed roots of goodness.
Why is this? Mañjuśrī!
Because this sublime Dharma-gate is difficult to believe, difficult to practice, and difficult to measure.

Mañjuśrī! All those people who have lacked roots of goodness from their past lives, and who, having heard the Mahāyāna in the past, gave rise to doubt and slander—because of this, when they hear this unsurpassed Dharma-gate, they are unable to give rise to faith and unable to enter it.

Mañjuśrī! In the future final age, when the Dharma is about to perish, there will be those who, upon hearing this Dharma-gate, are able to give rise to faith, are able to seek it out, and are able to understand and enter into it.

Mañjuśrī! You should know that this person has already made offerings to immeasurable and boundless Buddhas of the past; it is because they have skillfully practiced all manner of deeds that they are now able to believe in and enter this gateway of the Mahāyāna.

“Mañjuśrī! If there are good men or good women who, in the future final age, hear the name of this sutra and, upon hearing it, give rise to faith, and then receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and explain it, and having copied it, honor and make offerings to the scroll—”

Those sentient beings should reflect and know for themselves that, in the past, they have already seen immeasurable Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and have made offerings to and reverently honored those Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Mañjuśrī! Those sentient beings also see my body here in this garden preaching this Dharma-gate, and they also see this entire great assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "Ānanda!
You should receive, uphold, read, and recite this sublime Dharma-gate, and proclaim it extensively for the sake of all sentient beings."

When you observe that sentient beings possess the roots of the Mahāyāna and are capable of faith and acceptance, only then may you preach to them; you must not preach haphazardly without first making such an observation. Why is this?
Sentient beings of meager merit will give rise to disbelief upon hearing this, thereby incurring immeasurable transgression.

Ānanda! This Dharma-gate is called the Tathāgata’s treasury of true merit; it is called the Tathāgata’s secret treasury; it is called the Tathāgata’s treasury of pure and wondrous essence; it is called the Tathāgata’s treasury of the Dharma-seal; it is called the Tathāgata’s treasury protected by the mind; it is called the Tathāgata’s treasury of manifest faith.
Therefore, Ānanda! You should keep this secret and not proclaim it hastily, except to the sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. Why is this?

That son of good family has deeply planted roots of goodness in the presence of the Buddhas; he is able to protect the treasury of the Dharma, benefit himself, and also benefit others—therefore, you should speak for his sake.
Ānanda said: “World-Honored One!
I have already received this pure and wondrous Dharma-gate.”
“World-Honored One!
What is the name of this Dharma-gate now?
How should it be upheld?”

The Buddha told Ānanda: “This sublime Dharma-gate is named ‘The Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s Vigorous Display in the Sphere of Expedient Means’; it is named ‘The Profound Secret Treasury of the Tathāgata’; it is named ‘The Tathāgata’s Fulfillment of Merit’; it is named ‘The Profound Sphere of the Tathāgata’; it is named ‘The One Vehicle’; it is named ‘The Sūtra Spoken by Mañjuśrī’; it is named ‘The Sūtra of the Prediction for Satyaka Nirgrantha-putra’; it is named ‘The Sūtra Spoken by Satyaka Nirgrantha-putra. You should now uphold it in this manner.”

When the Tathāgata spoke this Dharma-gate, thirty billion nayutas of sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; sixty thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*); and immeasurable, boundless sentient beings became ultimately irreversible from the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, Śakra Devendra, the Four Heavenly Kings, Brahmā Devendra, and the devas, humans, asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Mahāsāṃghika-sāṃtīrthika-putra Sūtra, Scroll Ten.
